docs.title: About this book
docs.text: An introduction to political theory for readers meeting the subject for the first time. The book explains what political theory is and how it argues; the state and sovereignty; power, authority and legitimacy; liberty; equality; justice, including the theories of Rawls, Nozick and Sen; rights; democracy; citizenship and nationalism; and secularism. It then surveys the great ideologies (liberalism, conservatism, socialism and Marxism, feminism, environmentalism and others), the political thought of Kautilya, Gandhi, Ambedkar, Nehru and Tagore, and global justice and human rights. Each view is presented fairly with its main criticisms. Every chapter has learning outcomes, worked examples, figures or tables, a summary, exercises with answers and a quiz.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Citizenship and Nationalism
docs.text:
Who belongs, on what terms, and the idea of the nation

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • define citizenship and explain its three dimensions: status, rights and participation;
  • describe Marshall's account of civil, political and social citizenship and its criticisms;
  • compare liberal, republican, communitarian and differentiated conceptions of citizenship;
  • explain how citizenship is acquired (jus soli, jus sanguinis, naturalisation) and the problems of statelessness and refugees;
  • define nation and nationalism and compare civic and ethnic nationalism;
  • compare primordialist, modernist and ethno-symbolist theories of the nation, and assess the arguments for and against nationalism, including Tagore's critique.

docs.title: 9.1 What is citizenship?
docs.text:
Citizenship is full membership of a political community. To be a citizen is to belong, as an equal, to a state, with the rights and duties that membership brings. The idea has three dimensions.

  • Legal status. Citizenship is a legal relationship between a person and a state: a citizen has a passport, can enter and live in the country, cannot normally be deported, and is entitled to the state's diplomatic protection abroad.
  • Rights. Citizens enjoy civil, political and social rights, some of which (such as voting in national elections or holding certain offices) are often reserved to them.
  • Participation and identity. Citizenship also involves taking part in public life and a sense of belonging to a shared community.

The idea is ancient. Aristotle defined a citizen as one who shares in ruling and being ruled in turn, taking part in deliberation and judgement. Athenian citizenship was highly exclusive: women, slaves and resident foreigners were not citizens. The Roman Republic and Empire developed citizenship as a legal status that could be extended to conquered peoples; in 212 CE the emperor Caracalla extended it to almost all free inhabitants of the empire. Modern citizenship emerged with the nation-state and the democratic revolutions, which turned subjects of a king into citizens of a republic.

docs.title: Citizenship and nationality
docs.text: In everyday speech "citizenship" and "nationality" are often used interchangeably to mean legal membership of a state. In political theory "nationality" can also mean belonging to a nation in the cultural sense discussed in section 9.5. The two do not always coincide: a state may contain citizens of several national groups, and members of one national group may be citizens of several states.

docs.title: 9.2 Marshall: civil, political and social citizenship
docs.text:
The British sociologist T. H. Marshall, in the essay Citizenship and Social Class (1950), gave the most influential modern account of citizenship. He defined citizenship as a status bestowed on those who are full members of a community, all of whom are equal with respect to the rights and duties with which the status is endowed. Studying England, he argued that citizenship developed in three stages, each adding a new element.

  1. Civil rights (mainly the eighteenth century): the rights necessary for individual freedom: liberty of the person, freedom of speech, thought and faith, the right to own property and make contracts, and the right to justice. Their institution is the courts.
  2. Political rights (mainly the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries): the right to take part in the exercise of political power, as a voter or a member of a governing body. Their institutions are parliament and local councils.
  3. Social rights (mainly the twentieth century): the right to a modicum of economic welfare and security, and to share in the social heritage and live the life of a civilised being according to the standards prevailing in the society. Their institutions are the education system and the social services.
Figure 9.1 Marshall's three elements of citizenship. A timeline of Marshall's three elements of citizenship in England: civil rights developing mainly in the eighteenth century through the courts, political rights in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries through parliament and the extension of the franchise, and social rights in the twentieth century through education and the welfare state.

Marshall's central argument concerned the relation between citizenship and class. Capitalism produces inequality of class; citizenship is a principle of equality of status. Social rights, he argued, modify the inequalities of the market by guaranteeing all citizens a basic standard of life, so that equal citizenship can coexist with, and soften, class inequality.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text:
• Ethnocentric. The sequence describes England, not a universal law. In many countries political rights came before secure civil rights, or social rights were introduced by authoritarian rulers (Bismarck's Germany introduced social insurance in the 1880s before full democracy).
  • Gender. The sequence describes the experience of men. Women in England gained many civil rights (such as married women's property rights) and political rights after men, and social rights were often designed around a male breadwinner. Feminists such as Ruth Lister and Carole Pateman criticised the neglect of the private sphere.
  • Too optimistic. Marshall seemed to assume steady progress; the retreat of welfare provision in some countries from the 1980s showed that social rights can be reduced.
  • Neglect of duties and participation. Critics on the right (and republicans) argued that Marshall's account is all rights and no responsibilities, encouraging passive citizenship.

docs.title: Liberal citizenship
docs.text: For liberals, citizenship is above all a status carrying rights. Citizens are free and equal individuals, protected by the state in pursuing their own ideas of the good life. Participation in politics is a right, not a duty; a citizen who prefers private life is not failing in any civic obligation. Critics say this produces a thin, passive citizenship of consumers rather than participants.

docs.title: Republican citizenship
docs.text: The civic republican tradition, from Aristotle and the Roman republic through Machiavelli and Rousseau, sees citizenship as active participation in self-government. Citizens should have civic virtue: concern for the common good, willingness to serve and to take part in public deliberation. Liberty depends on citizens being vigilant against corruption and domination (Chapter 4). Critics worry that demanding civic virtue may be oppressive, that it assumes a homogeneous community, and that most people in large modern societies cannot or do not wish to be active citizens all the time.

docs.title: Communitarian citizenship
docs.text: Communitarians emphasise the community's shared values and traditions, the duties citizens owe to one another and the importance of belonging. They criticise a rights-centred individualism that, they argue, weakens social bonds.

docs.title: Differentiated and multicultural citizenship
docs.text:
Iris Marion Young (1989) argued that the ideal of a universal citizenship, in which all citizens are treated identically and set aside their particular identities, in practice favours dominant groups, whose perspective is presented as neutral. She proposed differentiated citizenship, with special representation for oppressed groups. Will Kymlicka (Multicultural Citizenship, 1995) distinguished national minorities (groups such as indigenous peoples that were incorporated into a larger state and have a claim to self-government) from immigrant groups (which generally seek integration with accommodation of their cultural practices), and argued that liberal principles support group-differentiated rights for both. Critics, such as Brian Barry in Culture and Equality (2001), replied that equal treatment under common laws is fairer and that group rights can entrench divisions.

Conception Core idea of citizenship Emphasis Main criticism Liberal Status bearing equal rights Individual freedom Passive, thin Republican Active participation in self-government Civic virtue, common good Too demanding; assumes homogeneity Communitarian Membership of a community of shared values Belonging, duties May suppress diversity and dissent Differentiated Equal membership that recognises group differences Inclusion of marginalised groups May entrench group divisions

Table 9.1. Four conceptions of citizenship.

Key idea

Citizenship combines legal status, rights and participation. Liberals stress rights, republicans participation and virtue, communitarians belonging, and theorists of differentiated citizenship the inclusion of groups whom universal citizenship has marginalised.

docs.title: Rules of acquisition
docs.text:
States use two basic principles, usually combined.

  • Jus soli (right of the soil): citizenship by birth on the territory. The United States and many countries of the Americas grant citizenship to almost anyone born on their soil.
  • Jus sanguinis (right of blood): citizenship by descent from a citizen parent, wherever one is born. Many European and Asian countries rely mainly on this principle.
  • Naturalisation: acquisition by a foreigner after a period of residence and other conditions (language, knowledge of the country, good character, an oath of allegiance).

In India citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution was dealt with in Part II, and acquisition and loss since then are governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955, as amended. Indian law began close to jus soli and, through amendments, moved towards requiring that a parent also be a citizen (with further conditions), a combination of soil and descent.

docs.title: Dual citizenship
docs.text: Some states permit citizens to hold another citizenship; others require them to give up any other. India does not permit dual citizenship, but offers the status of Overseas Citizen of India to many persons of Indian origin who are citizens of other countries, giving them rights such as visa-free travel and residence, but not political rights.

docs.title: Statelessness and refugees
docs.text:
A stateless person is someone not considered a national by any state. Statelessness can result from the break-up of states, discriminatory laws, gaps between nationality laws, or lack of birth registration. Stateless people may be unable to work legally, go to school, travel or receive health care.

A refugee, under the Refugee Convention of 1951 (as extended by its Protocol of 1967), is a person who is outside his or her country and unable or unwilling to return owing to a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion. The core principle of refugee law is non-refoulement: a refugee must not be returned to a country where he or she faces persecution. India is not a party to the 1951 Convention, though it has hosted large numbers of refugees.

Reflecting on the stateless people of interwar Europe in The Origins of Totalitarianism (1951), Hannah Arendt argued that the supposedly universal rights of man had turned out to be unenforceable for those who belonged to no political community. The most fundamental right, she wrote, is the right to have rights: the right to belong to a community that will protect one's other rights.

Worked example 9.1: Applying the rules of citizenship

Situation. A child is born in Country P to parents who are both citizens of Country Q. Country P grants citizenship only by descent; Country Q grants citizenship only to children born on its territory.

Analysis. Country P applies jus sanguinis: the child's parents are not P citizens, so the child does not acquire P citizenship. Country Q applies jus soli: the child was not born in Q, so the child does not acquire Q citizenship either. The child is stateless at birth, an example of how gaps between nationality laws produce statelessness. The 1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness asks states to grant nationality to children born on their territory who would otherwise be stateless, precisely to close such gaps.

docs.title: What is a nation?
docs.text:
A nation is a large group of people who see themselves as a community sharing a common identity, often based on some combination of language, history, culture, religion, territory and political aspirations, and who usually seek some form of self-government. A nation-state is a state whose population is (or is held to be) a single nation.

No single objective feature defines a nation. Switzerland is a nation with four official languages; Arabic speakers form many states; India is home to many languages and religions. The French historian Ernest Renan, in a lecture of 1882, "What Is a Nation?", argued that a nation is a soul, a spiritual principle, made of shared memories of the past (including the forgetting of past violence) and a present will to live together. The existence of a nation, he said, is "a daily plebiscite".

Nationalism has two meanings: (1) a sentiment of attachment to one's nation, and (2) a doctrine or political movement holding that the nation is the primary unit of political loyalty and that each nation should have its own state or self-government. In the classic formulation of Ernest Gellner, nationalism is primarily a political principle that holds that the political and the national unit should be congruent.

The distinction is useful but too neat. Civic nations have usually been built around a dominant language and culture, and ethnic nations can become more inclusive. Many scholars prefer to see civic and ethnic elements as present in different proportions in all nationalisms.

docs.title: Theories of the nation
docs.text:
Where do nations come from?

  • Primordialism. Nations are ancient and natural, rooted in kinship, language and culture going back far into history. This is how many nationalists see their own nations. Critics point out that many supposedly ancient nations are recent creations.
  • Modernism. Nations are products of modernity. Ernest Gellner (Nations and Nationalism, 1983) argued that industrial society needs a mobile, literate workforce sharing a standardised high culture, spread by mass education; nationalism provides it. Benedict Anderson (Imagined Communities, 1983) called the nation an imagined community: imagined because members will never meet most of their fellow members, yet each holds an image of their communion. He linked its rise to print capitalism: newspapers and novels in vernacular languages created a reading public that imagined itself as one community. Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger (The Invention of Tradition, 1983) showed how many "ancient" national traditions were invented in the nineteenth century.
  • Ethno-symbolism. Anthony D. Smith argued that modernists go too far: modern nations are built on pre-existing ethnic communities (ethnies) with their own myths, memories, symbols and attachment to a homeland. Nations are modern, but not created from nothing.

'Imagined' does not mean 'false'

Anderson did not claim that nations are fake. "Imagined" means that a nation exists in the shared understanding of its members, as all large communities do, since no one can know personally the millions of fellow members. Imagined communities can be extremely real in their effects: people work, vote, sacrifice and die for them.

docs.title: 9.6 Self-determination
docs.text:
The principle of national self-determination holds that a nation has the right to decide its own political status, including independence. It was championed after the First World War by the American president Woodrow Wilson, and appears in the United Nations Charter (1945), which names respect for the principle of equal rights and self-determination of peoples among the purposes of the United Nations. In the period of decolonisation it became the basis of the claims of colonised peoples to independence.

The principle raises hard questions.

  • Who is the "self"? Most states contain more than one group that could claim to be a nation. If every group could secede, states would fragment endlessly.
  • Secession. International law generally recognises a right to independence for colonised peoples, but is very reluctant to recognise a right of secession from existing states, emphasising their territorial integrity. Some theorists defend a remedial right to secede only for groups suffering grave injustice; others defend a broader right for any group that democratically chooses independence.
  • Internal self-determination. Many claims can be met by autonomy, federalism or minority rights within an existing state, rather than independence.

docs.title: Arguments for
docs.text:
• Belonging and identity. National membership gives people a sense of belonging, a shared history and a cultural context in which their choices make sense. Liberal nationalists such as Yael Tamir and David Miller argue that national identity is compatible with liberal values and supports them.
  • Solidarity. A shared national identity may motivate the trust and solidarity needed for democracy and for redistribution: people are more willing to pay taxes for the welfare of those they see as fellow members.
  • Freedom from foreign rule. Nationalism was the driving force of the movements that ended colonial rule in Asia and Africa. The Indian national movement combined demands for self-rule with ideas of democracy, rights and social reform.

docs.title: Arguments against
docs.text:
• Exclusion and conflict. Nationalism defines insiders and outsiders, and has fuelled discrimination against minorities, wars of expansion and ethnic cleansing. The extreme ultranationalism of fascism and Nazism led to aggression and genocide (Chapter 12).
  • Arbitrariness. Why should the accident of birth into a nation determine one's moral obligations? Cosmopolitans argue that our fundamental moral concern should extend to all human beings equally (Chapter 14).
  • Suppression of internal diversity. Building a nation-state has often meant imposing one language and culture on all.

docs.title: Tagore's critique
docs.text:
The poet Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941), who received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913, delivered a series of lectures in Japan and the United States in 1916–17, published as Nationalism (1917). Tagore was deeply committed to India's freedom and to the dignity of its people, but he distinguished between a people's genuine self-respect and what he called the Nation: the political and commercial organisation of a people for power and profit, a machine that subordinates human beings to its purposes. He saw the aggressive nationalism of the Western powers as the source of imperialism and of the First World War, and he warned Indians and Japanese against imitating it. India's problem, in his view, was social rather than merely political, and its contribution to the world should be a spirit of unity in diversity and openness to all humanity. Critics accused Tagore of idealism and of underestimating the need for political struggle against colonial rule; admirers see his warnings about aggressive nationalism as prophetic. Gandhi, for his part, described his own patriotism as compatible with love of humanity and the service of others (Chapter 13).

Worked example 9.2: Civic or ethnic?

Situation. Two imaginary countries revise their citizenship laws. Country R grants citizenship to anyone who has lived there legally for eight years, speaks one of its official languages and pledges loyalty to the constitution. Country S grants automatic citizenship to anyone, anywhere in the world, who can show descent from the country's historic ethnic group, but makes naturalisation for long-term residents of other origins very difficult.

Analysis. R's law reflects civic nationalism: membership is open to those who share residence, a language and loyalty to political institutions. S's law reflects ethnic nationalism: membership depends on descent. A liberal would worry that S treats long-settled residents as permanent outsiders. A defender of S might argue that it protects a diaspora's connection to its homeland. Real countries often combine elements of both, for instance granting easier naturalisation to people of shared descent alongside a residence route for others.

Summary

  • Citizenship is full membership of a political community: legal status, rights and participation. Aristotle defined it as ruling and being ruled in turn.
  • Marshall described civil, political and social citizenship emerging in England over three centuries, with social rights softening class inequality; critics note its ethnocentrism, gender blindness and neglect of duties.
  • Liberal citizenship stresses rights, republican citizenship participation and virtue, communitarian citizenship belonging; Young and Kymlicka defend differentiated, multicultural citizenship, and Barry criticises it.
  • Citizenship is acquired by jus soli, jus sanguinis or naturalisation; statelessness and refugee status show the importance of Arendt's "right to have rights".
  • A nation is a self-identifying community seeking self-government; nationalism is both a sentiment and a doctrine. Civic and ethnic nationalism differ in the basis of membership.
  • Primordialists see nations as ancient, modernists (Gellner, Anderson, Hobsbawm) as modern creations, ethno-symbolists (Smith) as modern but rooted in older communities.
  • Nationalism has supported belonging, solidarity and liberation from colonial rule, but also exclusion and war; Tagore criticised the aggressive Nation while valuing freedom and humanity.

docs.title: 9.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

List Marshall's three elements of citizenship with the institutions associated with each.

Answer

Civil rights (individual freedom, property, justice): the courts. Political rights (voting, holding office): parliament and local councils. Social rights (economic welfare and security, a share in the social heritage): the education system and social services.

Exercise 2

Give two criticisms of Marshall's account.

Answer

Any two: (1) it is ethnocentric, describing English history rather than a universal sequence; (2) it ignores gender, since women gained rights later and differently and social rights assumed a male breadwinner; (3) it is too optimistic about steady progress, as later cuts to welfare showed; (4) it neglects duties and participation, encouraging passive citizenship.

Exercise 3

Compare liberal and republican citizenship. How would each view a citizen who never votes or takes part in public life?

Answer

Liberal citizenship is a status with rights; participation is a right, not a duty, so a non-voter is exercising his freedom and is not failing as a citizen. Republican citizenship requires active participation and civic virtue; the non-voter fails in a civic duty and contributes to the corruption of self-government.

Exercise 4

Explain jus soli and jus sanguinis, and show how their combination can produce statelessness.

Answer

Jus soli grants citizenship by birth on the territory; jus sanguinis by descent from a citizen parent. A child born in a jus sanguinis country to parents from a jus soli country acquires neither citizenship: not the first, because the parents are not its citizens, and not the second, because the child was not born on its soil. The child is stateless.

Exercise 5

What did Anderson mean by calling the nation an "imagined community", and what role did print capitalism play?

Answer

The nation is imagined because its members will never know most of their fellow members, yet each holds an image of their shared communion; it is a community because it is conceived as a deep comradeship. Print capitalism, the mass production of books and newspapers in vernacular languages, created reading publics who could imagine themselves as sharing a language, a time and a common fate, laying the basis for national consciousness.

Exercise 6

Distinguish civic from ethnic nationalism, and explain why some scholars think the distinction is too neat.

Answer

Civic nationalism bases the nation on shared citizenship and political values and is open to anyone who adopts them; ethnic nationalism bases it on descent, ethnicity, language or religion. The distinction is too neat because "civic" nations are usually built around a dominant language and culture (an ethnic core), while ethnic nations can become more inclusive; most real nationalisms mix the two.

Exercise 7

Summarise Tagore's critique of nationalism and one criticism of his view.

Answer

Tagore distinguished a people's self-respect from the Nation as a political and commercial machine organised for power and profit, which he blamed for imperialism and war; he urged India to value unity in diversity and openness to humanity rather than imitate aggressive Western nationalism. Criticism: he was accused of idealism and of underestimating the need for organised political struggle against colonial rule.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Democracy
docs.text:
Rule by the people: its meaning, its models, its forms and its critics

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain the meaning of democracy and the main arguments for and against it, from Plato to the present;
  • compare direct and representative democracy, and the main theories of representation;
  • describe the main models of democracy: protective, developmental, elitist, pluralist, participatory and deliberative;
  • explain the danger of the tyranny of the majority and the idea of liberal constitutional democracy;
  • compare majoritarian and consensus forms of democracy, and the main electoral systems;
  • analyse a voting cycle (Condorcet's paradox) and explain what it shows about majority rule.

docs.title: 8.1 What is democracy?
docs.text:
The word democracy comes from the Greek dēmos (the people) and kratos (power or rule): rule by the people. The most famous modern definition is Abraham Lincoln's, from his Gettysburg Address of 1863: government "of the people, by the people, for the people". Each phrase points to a different element: the people are the source of authority, they take part in governing, and government serves their interests.

Today nearly every government claims to be democratic, which shows the prestige of the word but also how elastic it has become. For most of history the word was a term of abuse. Plato and Aristotle regarded democracy as rule by the ignorant poor; the framers of the American Constitution spoke of a republic rather than a democracy; and many nineteenth-century liberals feared that universal suffrage would threaten property and liberty. Only in the twentieth century, after long struggles by workers, women, colonised peoples and racial minorities, did universal adult suffrage become the norm.

Two broad understandings of democracy can be distinguished.

  • Procedural (or minimal) democracy defines democracy by its procedures: free and fair elections, universal suffrage, competing parties, freedom of speech and association, and peaceful transfer of power.
  • Substantive democracy adds conditions about outcomes or social conditions: protection of rights, social and economic equality, real participation, and government that actually serves the people's interests.

docs.title: Dahl's criteria
docs.text:
Robert Dahl, in On Democracy (1998), listed five criteria that an ideal democratic process would meet among the members of an association:

  1. effective participation: all members have equal and effective opportunities to make their views known;
  2. voting equality: every member has an equal and effective opportunity to vote, and all votes count as equal;
  3. enlightened understanding: each member has opportunities to learn about the alternatives and their likely consequences;
  4. control of the agenda: members decide which matters are placed on the agenda;
  5. inclusion of adults: all, or most, adult permanent residents have full rights of citizens.

No real state meets these perfectly. Dahl used the term polyarchy for the actual regimes that approximate them, characterised by elected officials, free and fair elections, inclusive suffrage, the right to run for office, freedom of expression, alternative sources of information and freedom of association.

docs.title: Arguments for
docs.text:
• Equality. Democracy expresses the equal worth of citizens: each counts for one in deciding the laws all must obey.
  • Freedom and self-government. Citizens who make their own laws are, in a sense, free (positive liberty; Chapter 4). Democracy also protects negative liberty, since rulers who can be removed have reason to respect citizens' rights.
  • Protection of interests. Each person is usually the best judge and guardian of his or her own interests. Those excluded from power tend to have their interests neglected, as J. S. Mill argued about the working class and women.
  • Peaceful change. Democracy allows governments to be removed without bloodshed. Karl Popper emphasised this as its central merit.
  • Better decisions. The "wisdom of crowds" argument holds that the judgements of many people, pooled together, are often better than those of a few. The Condorcet jury theorem (1785) shows mathematically that if each voter is more likely than not to be right on a yes-or-no question, and votes independently, the probability that the majority is right approaches certainty as the number of voters grows.
  • Development of citizens. Taking part in government educates citizens and widens their sympathies (Mill, Rousseau, participatory democrats).

docs.title: Arguments against
docs.text:
• Incompetence. Plato compared the state to a ship: we would not choose the captain by a vote of the passengers, so why choose rulers that way? Governing well requires knowledge most citizens lack. A modern version, sometimes called epistocracy, proposes giving more weight to better-informed voters.
  • Tyranny of the majority. A majority may oppress minorities (section 8.5).
  • Instability and demagogy. Ancient critics feared that democracy leads to rule by flatterers and eventually to tyranny.
  • Elite rule in disguise. Elite theorists argued that every society is in fact ruled by a minority. Gaetano Mosca held that there is always a ruling class; Vilfredo Pareto spoke of the circulation of elites; Robert Michels, studying socialist parties, formulated an iron law of oligarchy (1911): any large organisation, however democratic in principle, comes to be controlled by a small leadership.
  • Marxist critique. In a capitalist society political equality coexists with economic inequality, so that democracy is formal and the wealthy dominate in practice.

docs.title: Direct democracy
docs.text: In direct democracy citizens make decisions themselves. Athens in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE is the classic example: the assembly (ekklēsia) of adult male citizens met frequently to decide on laws, war, finance and the punishment of officials; many offices were filled by lot rather than election, on the view that selection by lot treats citizens equally. Modern forms include referendums, citizens' initiatives (in which a set number of citizens can force a vote on a proposal), recall of officials and local assemblies. In India the gram sabha, the assembly of all registered voters of a village panchayat area, gives a role for direct participation in local government.

docs.title: Representative democracy
docs.text: In representative democracy citizens elect representatives who make decisions on their behalf. It is the only practical form for large states, but its advocates also defended it on its own merits. James Madison, in Federalist No. 10 (1787), argued that representation would refine and enlarge public views by passing them through a chosen body of citizens. Rousseau, by contrast, held that sovereignty cannot be represented, and that the English were free only during elections and enslaved between them.

docs.title: Theories of representation
docs.text:
What does it mean for one person to represent others?

  • Trustee model. The representative uses his or her own judgement on behalf of constituents. Edmund Burke, in his speech to the electors of Bristol (1774), argued that a representative owes the people his judgement, and betrays them if he sacrifices it to their opinion.
  • Delegate model. The representative follows the instructions or wishes of constituents.
  • Mandate model. A party that wins an election has a mandate to carry out the programme it presented to voters.
  • Descriptive (or mirror) representation. A representative body should resemble the population in its composition, by sex, caste, religion, region or class. This is one argument for reserved seats for women or for disadvantaged groups. Critics argue that resembling a group does not guarantee acting in its interests; defenders reply that some experiences are best understood by those who share them, and that presence matters symbolically.

The political theorist Hanna Pitkin, in The Concept of Representation (1967), distinguished formal, descriptive, symbolic and substantive representation, and argued that the core idea is acting in the interest of the represented, in a manner responsive to them.

docs.title: 8.4 Models of democracy
docs.text:
Political theorists, notably David Held in Models of Democracy (1987), have identified several models that differ in why they value democracy and how much participation they expect.

Model Key thinkers What democracy is for Role of citizens Classical (direct) Athens; Rousseau Collective self-government Active participation in decisions Protective Bentham, James Mill Protecting citizens against rulers and from each other Vote to hold rulers accountable Developmental J. S. Mill Developing citizens' capacities Participate and deliberate, with weight for the educated in Mill's own proposal Competitive elitist Schumpeter Choosing between competing leaders Vote, then leave governing to leaders Pluralist Dahl Balancing the interests of many groups Join groups that compete for influence Participatory Pateman, Macpherson Extending self-government to workplaces and communities Active participation in many spheres Deliberative Habermas, Joshua Cohen Reaching decisions through public reasoning Exchange reasons in public debate

Table 8.1. Models of democracy.

docs.title: Protective democracy
docs.text: Jeremy Bentham and James Mill defended representative democracy on utilitarian grounds: rulers, like everyone else, pursue their own interests, so they must be made accountable to the governed through regular elections, a free press and the secret ballot, or they will use power for themselves.

docs.title: Developmental democracy
docs.text: J. S. Mill, in Considerations on Representative Government (1861), valued democracy not only as protection but as a school of citizenship that develops people's intellectual and moral capacities. He supported extending the vote, including to women, and proportional representation to give minorities a voice. But he also proposed plural voting (extra votes for the educated), fearing the rule of an ignorant majority, a proposal few democrats now accept.

docs.title: Competitive elitism
docs.text: The economist Joseph Schumpeter, in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy (1942), rejected what he called the classical doctrine, which assumed a "common good" and a "will of the people" that democracy expresses. Ordinary citizens, he argued, know and care little about most political issues. Democracy is better understood as a method: an institutional arrangement for arriving at political decisions in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote. The voters' role is to choose and remove governments, not to govern. Critics argue that this reduces democracy to choosing masters, and that citizens' apathy may be a product of their exclusion rather than a fixed fact.

docs.title: Pluralism
docs.text: Pluralists such as Dahl saw democracy as a process in which many organised groups (business, labour, farmers, professions, religious and ethnic groups) compete and bargain, so that power is dispersed and no single group dominates. Critics, including Dahl himself in later work, noted that groups are unequal in resources and that business enjoys a privileged position (Chapter 2).

docs.title: Participatory democracy
docs.text: Carole Pateman (Participation and Democratic Theory, 1970) and C. B. Macpherson argued that democracy should extend beyond voting to active participation in decisions in the workplace, the neighbourhood and the community. Participation educates people and builds the confidence and skills that democracy needs. Examples include participatory budgeting, first developed in the Brazilian city of Porto Alegre in 1989, in which residents help decide how part of the municipal budget is spent.

docs.title: Deliberative democracy
docs.text:
Deliberative democracy, developed from the 1980s by Jürgen Habermas, Joshua Cohen, Amy Gutmann, Dennis Thompson and others, holds that democratic legitimacy comes not simply from counting votes but from public reasoning: free and equal citizens exchanging arguments, listening to one another and seeking decisions that all could accept. Its supporters advocate institutions such as citizens' assemblies and deliberative polls, in which randomly selected citizens learn about an issue, deliberate and make recommendations. Ireland used a citizens' assembly in 2016–2018 to discuss questions including abortion before referendums were held. Critics argue that deliberation favours the articulate and educated, may silence those who express themselves differently, and is hard to scale up to whole societies.

Key idea

Democracy means rule by the people, but theories differ about what that requires: choosing leaders (Schumpeter), balancing group interests (Dahl), taking part directly (Pateman) or reasoning together in public (Habermas).

docs.title: The tyranny of the majority
docs.text: The French writer Alexis de Tocqueville, in Democracy in America (1835 and 1840), warned of the tyranny of the majority: in a democracy the majority's opinion can become so dominant that it crushes dissent, not only through law but through social pressure. J. S. Mill took up the warning in On Liberty (Chapter 4). The danger is greatest where a society is divided into permanent groups, by religion, language, caste or ethnicity, so that a minority can never become part of a majority.

docs.title: Liberal constitutional democracy
docs.text:
The common response is liberal democracy (or constitutional democracy): majority rule within limits set by a constitution that protects individual rights and minority interests, separates powers, provides for judicial review and can be changed only by special procedures. Some decisions, on this view, are taken off the table of ordinary majority politics.

Critics of strong constitutional limits, such as the legal theorist Jeremy Waldron, argue that when citizens disagree in good faith about rights, it is more democratic to let elected legislatures decide than to give final authority to unelected judges. Defenders reply that democracy itself requires certain rights (free speech, the vote, equal citizenship), which courts protect, and that minorities need protection against majorities that might otherwise violate them.

docs.title: Condorcet's paradox
docs.text:
A deeper puzzle about majority rule was discovered by the Marquis de Condorcet in 1785: majority preferences may be intransitive, so that there is no option a majority prefers to every other.

Voter group (one-third of voters each) First choice Second choice Third choice Group 1 A B C Group 2 B C A Group 3 C A B

Table 8.2. Preferences that produce a voting cycle.

Worked example 8.1: A voting cycle

Situation. A town council must choose one of three projects: A (a library), B (a park) or C (a road). Its members fall into three equal groups with the preferences in Table 8.2, and it votes on pairs of options.

Analysis. Compare each pair by majority vote.

  • A against B: Groups 1 and 3 prefer A to B, so A beats B by two-thirds.
  • B against C: Groups 1 and 2 prefer B to C, so B beats C.
  • C against A: Groups 2 and 3 prefer C to A, so C beats A.

The majority prefers A to B, B to C and C to A: a cycle. There is no option that beats all others (no Condorcet winner). The final outcome depends on the order in which pairs are voted on. If the council first votes A against B and then the winner against C, C wins; if it first votes B against C and then the winner against A, A wins. Whoever controls the agenda can determine the result.

In 1951 the economist Kenneth Arrow proved a much more general result, Arrow's impossibility theorem: when there are at least three options, no method of turning individual rankings into a social ranking can satisfy a small set of reasonable conditions at once (including that the method works for any preferences, respects unanimous preferences, makes the ranking of two options depend only on how voters rank those two, and is not a dictatorship). Some theorists, such as William Riker in Liberalism against Populism (1982), concluded that there is no meaningful "will of the people" for democracy to express, and that democracy is valuable chiefly as a way of removing rulers. Others reply that cycles are less common in practice than in theory, that deliberation can shape preferences so that cycles disappear, and that the results show only that democratic procedures must be designed with care.

docs.title: Parliamentary and presidential systems
docs.text:
Feature Parliamentary system Presidential system Executive Prime minister and cabinet, drawn from and responsible to the legislature President, separately elected for a fixed term Head of state Separate from the head of government (monarch or president) The president is both Removal Government falls if it loses the confidence of the legislature President can be removed only by impeachment for serious misconduct Relation of powers Fusion of executive and legislature Separation of powers Examples United Kingdom, India, Japan United States, Brazil, Mexico

Table 8.3. Parliamentary and presidential systems.

Defenders of parliamentary systems point to flexibility (an unpopular government can be replaced without waiting for an election) and to the absence of deadlock between executive and legislature. Defenders of presidential systems point to the stability of a fixed term, a clear choice of executive by voters and checks between separate branches. The political scientist Juan Linz argued that presidentialism carries risks of deadlock and winner-take-all politics; others dispute how far this is borne out.

docs.title: Majoritarian and consensus democracy
docs.text: Arend Lijphart, in Patterns of Democracy (1999), contrasted two ideal types. Majoritarian democracy concentrates power in the hands of the majority: single-party governments, a dominant executive, two main parties, first-past-the-post elections and a unitary, centralised state (the "Westminster model"). Consensus democracy disperses power: coalition governments, a balance between executive and legislature, multiple parties, proportional representation, federalism and strong judicial review. Lijphart argued that consensus democracy works better in deeply divided societies, where he recommended consociational arrangements such as power-sharing among groups.

docs.title: Electoral systems
docs.text:
• First-past-the-post (plurality): the candidate with the most votes in each constituency wins. It is simple, produces clear constituency representatives and often single-party governments, but can give a party a majority of seats with a minority of votes and under-represent smaller parties. It is used for elections to the Lok Sabha.
  • Proportional representation: seats are allocated in proportion to votes, often through party lists. It is fairer to smaller parties and minorities but usually produces coalition governments and may weaken the link between a representative and a locality.
  • Mixed systems combine the two, as in Germany and New Zealand.
  • Preferential systems let voters rank candidates; the single transferable vote is used, for example, in the election of the President of India by an electoral college.

Worked example 8.2: Votes and seats

Situation. Three parties contest 10 single-member constituencies of equal size. In every constituency Party X wins 40 per cent of the vote, Party Y 35 per cent and Party Z 25 per cent.

Analysis. Under first-past-the-post, X wins all 10 seats with 40 per cent of the vote; Y and Z win none. Under proportional representation with these national totals, X would win 4 seats, Y about 3 or 4 and Z 2 or 3, depending on the counting formula. The example is extreme (real votes vary between constituencies), but it shows how first-past-the-post can magnify the largest party's lead, while proportional systems mirror the distribution of votes.

docs.title: 8.7 Democracy and its present challenges
docs.text:
Political theorists today discuss several challenges to democratic systems, which this book states in general terms.

  • Participation. Declining party membership and turnout in some democracies raise questions about how engaged citizens are.
  • Money and power. Large inequalities of wealth may translate into unequal political influence, through campaign finance, lobbying and media ownership.
  • Information. The spread of misinformation and the fragmentation of public debate online may weaken the shared basis of facts that deliberation needs.
  • Populism. Political scientists use the term for movements that present politics as a struggle between a virtuous "people" and a corrupt "elite", and claim to speak for the people as a whole. Scholars disagree on whether such movements threaten liberal democracy by attacking checks and balances, or express legitimate grievances that established parties neglected.
  • Democratic backsliding. Researchers have studied cases in which elected governments gradually weaken courts, the press and electoral bodies while keeping elections.

Summary

  • Democracy is rule by the people; procedural accounts focus on free elections and rights, substantive accounts add equality and real participation. Dahl's criteria define an ideal; real regimes are polyarchies.
  • Arguments for democracy rest on equality, freedom, protection of interests, peaceful change and better decisions; criticisms come from Plato, elite theorists (Mosca, Pareto, Michels) and Marxists.
  • Direct democracy (Athens, referendums, gram sabhas) and representative democracy coexist; representatives may act as trustees (Burke), delegates, mandate-holders or descriptive mirrors.
  • Models include protective, developmental, competitive elitist (Schumpeter), pluralist (Dahl), participatory (Pateman) and deliberative (Habermas) democracy.
  • Tocqueville and Mill warned of the tyranny of the majority; liberal constitutional democracy limits majorities. Condorcet's paradox and Arrow's theorem show that majority preferences can cycle and agenda control matters.
  • Democracies may be parliamentary or presidential, majoritarian or consensus (Lijphart), and use plurality, proportional, mixed or preferential electoral systems.

docs.title: 8.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Distinguish procedural from substantive democracy. Could a country be democratic in one sense but not the other?

Answer

Procedural democracy is defined by procedures: free and fair elections, universal suffrage, competing parties, civil liberties. Substantive democracy also requires outcomes or conditions such as protection of rights, real equality and government that serves people's interests. Yes: a country with regular free elections but deep social exclusion of some groups may be procedurally democratic but substantively weak.

Exercise 2

Explain Schumpeter's definition of democracy and one criticism of it.

Answer

Schumpeter defined democracy as a method in which individuals acquire the power to decide by means of a competitive struggle for the people's vote; citizens choose and remove leaders but do not govern. Criticism: it reduces democracy to choosing between elites and treats citizen apathy as natural, when it may result from exclusion; participatory democrats argue that democracy should involve citizens much more actively.

Exercise 3

Contrast Burke's trustee model of representation with the delegate model. Which better describes a representative who votes against a popular measure because she thinks it unwise?

Answer

A trustee uses independent judgement for constituents' good; a delegate follows their instructions or wishes. A representative who votes against a popular measure because she judges it unwise acts as a trustee, as Burke recommended in his speech to the electors of Bristol (1774).

Exercise 4

Five voters rank three options: two voters rank A > B > C, two rank B > C > A, and one ranks C > A > B. Is there a Condorcet winner?

Answer

Compare pairs. A vs B: A is preferred by 2 + 1 = 3 voters, B by 2: A beats B. B vs C: B by 2 + 2 = 4, C by 1: B beats C. A vs C: A by 2, C by 2 + 1 = 3: C beats A. The majority prefers A to B, B to C and C to A, a cycle: there is no Condorcet winner.

Exercise 5

What is deliberative democracy, and what is one practical institution its supporters recommend? Give one criticism.

Answer

Deliberative democracy holds that legitimacy comes from public reasoning among free and equal citizens seeking decisions all could accept, not just from counting votes. Supporters recommend citizens' assemblies or deliberative polls of randomly selected citizens. Criticism: deliberation may favour the educated and articulate, and is hard to extend to whole societies.

Exercise 6

Give two advantages and two disadvantages of first-past-the-post compared with proportional representation.

Answer

Advantages: (1) simplicity and a clear link between a representative and a constituency; (2) it often produces single-party governments that are stable and clearly accountable. Disadvantages: (1) disproportionality: a party can win a majority of seats with a minority of votes; (2) smaller parties and dispersed minorities are under-represented, and many votes are wasted.

Exercise 7

What is the tyranny of the majority, and how does liberal constitutional democracy respond to it?

Answer

The tyranny of the majority (Tocqueville, Mill) is the oppression of minorities or dissenters by a majority, through law or through social pressure. Liberal constitutional democracy responds by limiting majority rule: a constitution entrenches rights, separates powers, provides for judicial review and requires special procedures for amendment, so that some matters are protected from ordinary majorities.

docs.title: Chapter 5: Equality
docs.text:
Equal worth, equal rights, equal chances and the question "equality of what?"

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain the idea of equal moral worth and why it is the starting point of most modern political theory;
  • distinguish formal, political, social and economic equality;
  • compare equality of opportunity (formal and fair) with equality of outcome;
  • explain the "equality of what?" debate: welfare, resources and capabilities;
  • describe luck egalitarianism and relational equality, and the alternatives of priority and sufficiency;
  • discuss the arguments for and against affirmative action and reservations.

docs.title: 5.1 Equal in what sense?
docs.text:
People are obviously unequal in many ways: in height, strength, talent, health, wealth and luck. When political theorists say that people are equal, they do not deny these facts. They make a moral claim: that every person has equal moral worth, and that their interests and choices deserve equal consideration. This idea was not always accepted. Many societies were built on hierarchies of birth, caste, race or sex, justified by the claim that some people were naturally superior.

The modern idea of equality has several roots: the religious belief that all are equal before God; the Stoic idea of a common human reason; the social contract theorists' claim that people are naturally free and equal; the revolutionary declarations of the late eighteenth century; and the struggles of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries against slavery, caste, colonialism and the subordination of women. Today almost every political theory accepts equal moral worth. Ronald Dworkin argued that the real disagreements are about what treating people as equals requires, a phrase he distinguished from treating them equally (identically). A parent who gives medicine only to the sick child treats both children as equals, though not identically.

Key idea

Equality in political theory is a moral claim about equal worth and equal consideration, not a factual claim that people are the same. The hard question is what equal consideration requires in practice.

docs.title: 5.2 Dimensions of equality
docs.text:
Equality can be sought in different spheres of life.

Dimension What is equalised Examples Formal or legal equality Status before the law Equality before the law; abolition of legal privileges based on birth; the same laws for everyone Political equality Voice in collective decisions Universal adult franchise; one person, one vote; equal right to stand for office Social equality Status and respect in social life Absence of caste, class or gender hierarchies; equal access to public places Economic equality Income, wealth or resources Progressive taxation; social insurance; limits on inequality

Table 5.1. Four dimensions of equality.

These can come apart. A country may have formal and political equality while social hierarchies and great economic inequality persist. B. R. Ambedkar made this point forcefully when presenting the draft Constitution of India: political equality (one person, one vote, one value) would coexist with social and economic inequality, and he warned that this contradiction could endanger political democracy itself (Chapter 13). Marxists argue more generally that legal and political equality in a capitalist society hides deep economic inequality, which shapes real power.

docs.title: Formal equality
docs.text: Formal equality is the principle that like cases should be treated alike. It goes back to Aristotle, who held that justice requires treating equals equally and unequals unequally, in proportion to the relevant difference. The principle is necessary but empty until we know which differences are relevant. Race is irrelevant to the right to vote; age is relevant. Sex is irrelevant to holding public office; a medical condition may be relevant to driving a bus. Much of the history of equality consists in showing that differences once thought relevant, such as caste, race and sex, are not.

docs.title: 5.3 Equality of opportunity and of outcome
Equality of opportunity
docs.text:
Equality of opportunity means that positions and rewards in society should be open to all on the basis of fair competition, not reserved for those of a particular birth or group. Two versions are usually distinguished.

  • Formal equality of opportunity ("careers open to talents"): there should be no legal or official barriers to anyone competing for any position, and positions go to the best qualified. It ended aristocratic privilege and is widely accepted.
  • Fair (or substantive) equality of opportunity: people with similar talents and willingness to use them should have similar chances of success, whatever their social background. This requires more than removing barriers; it requires public education, health care and other measures to offset the advantages of a privileged upbringing. Rawls made fair equality of opportunity part of his second principle of justice (Chapter 6).

The metaphor of a race is often used. Formal equality of opportunity says that everyone may enter the race. Fair equality of opportunity says that everyone should start from the same line. Critics then ask further questions: even with a fair start, differences of natural talent are a matter of luck; why should those born with talents in demand earn much more? And is a society organised as a race the best kind of society at all?

docs.title: Equality of outcome
docs.text:
Equality of outcome (or of condition) aims at equal results: similar levels of income, wealth or well-being, whatever people's starting points or choices. Few theorists defend strict equality of outcome, but many argue that inequalities of outcome should be reduced. Their reasons include:

  • great inequalities of outcome undermine equality of opportunity for the next generation, since wealthy parents can buy advantages for their children;
  • economic inequality turns into political inequality, as the rich gain more influence;
  • large inequalities damage social relations, creating hierarchy, envy, humiliation and a sense that citizens do not share a common life;
  • many inequalities reflect luck rather than desert.

Critics reply that equality of outcome would require intrusive interference with people's choices and with the results of free exchange (Nozick's argument in Chapter 6), would weaken incentives to work and innovate, would ignore differences of effort and choice, and could be achieved only by levelling down: making the better-off worse off without making anyone better off.

Figure 5.1 Three ideas of equality. Three panels comparing formal equality of opportunity, fair equality of opportunity and equality of outcome. In the first, runners start from different lines but no one is barred. In the second, runners start from the same line. In the third, everyone finishes together.

Caution: equality of opportunity can justify large inequality

Equality of opportunity is sometimes presented as a moderate alternative to equality of outcome. But it is compatible with very large inequalities of outcome, as long as they result from fair competition. The British socialist R. H. Tawney, in Equality (1931), mocked what he called the "Tadpole Philosophy": the idea that the misery of many tadpoles is consoled by the fact that a few of them will one day become frogs. A society that offers everyone a chance to rise, he argued, is not thereby a society of equals. Whether this is a criticism depends on one's view of whether unequal outcomes from fair competition are just.

docs.title: 5.4 Equality of what?
docs.text: In a lecture of 1979 entitled "Equality of What?", Amartya Sen pointed out that every serious theory of justice wants equality of something. Libertarians want equal rights to liberty; utilitarians give equal weight to everyone's happiness; egalitarians want equal income or resources. The real question is what the right currency of equality is. Three main answers have been defended.

docs.title: Equality of welfare
docs.text: One might aim to make people equally well off in terms of welfare: happiness, preference satisfaction or well-being. This seems to focus on what ultimately matters. But it faces objections. A person with expensive tastes (who is miserable without fine wine) would be entitled to more resources than a person with modest tastes, which seems unfair to the latter. And a person who has adapted to deprivation and learned to be content with very little (Sen's problem of adaptive preferences) would be entitled to nothing more, which seems to reward oppression.

docs.title: Equality of resources
docs.text: Ronald Dworkin argued instead for equality of resources. Imagine shipwrecked people on a desert island who divide its resources by an auction in which each starts with an equal number of shells. The result passes an envy test if no one prefers anyone else's bundle of resources to their own. Dworkin added a hypothetical insurance scheme to compensate for handicaps and bad luck in talents. His aim was a distribution that is ambition-sensitive (reflecting people's choices about work and leisure) but endowment-insensitive (not reflecting unchosen differences in natural ability or circumstance).

docs.title: Equality of capability
docs.text:
Sen's own answer was capability: the real freedom people have to achieve functionings they have reason to value, such as being well nourished, being healthy, being educated, moving about freely and taking part in community life. Resources matter only as means, and people differ in their ability to convert resources into functionings. A person who uses a wheelchair needs more resources to achieve the same mobility as others; a pregnant woman needs more food to be well nourished. Equalising resources would leave them worse off in what they can actually do and be. Chapter 6 discusses the capability approach in more detail.

Currency What is equalised Main strength Main objection Welfare Happiness or preference satisfaction Focuses on what people care about Expensive tastes; adaptive preferences Resources (Dworkin) Bundles of goods and opportunities, with insurance for bad luck Respects responsibility for choices Ignores differences in converting resources into well-being Capability (Sen) Real freedoms to achieve valued functionings Sensitive to human diversity Which capabilities count, and how to weigh them?

Table 5.2. Three currencies of equality.

docs.title: Luck egalitarianism
docs.text:
Dworkin's distinction between choice and circumstance inspired a family of views called luck egalitarianism, defended in different forms by G. A. Cohen, Richard Arneson and others. Its core claim is that it is unjust for some people to be worse off than others through no fault or choice of their own. Inequalities that result from brute luck (being born disabled, being born into poverty, being struck by lightning) should be corrected; inequalities that result from option luck (losing a deliberate gamble, choosing more leisure over more income) may stand.

The idea has intuitive appeal: we resent unfairness that comes from the accident of birth more than unequal results of free choices. But it faces strong objections.

  • Harshness. If a person crashes a motorbike while riding without a helmet, does luck egalitarianism imply that he should be left untreated because his misfortune resulted from choice? Most luck egalitarians try to avoid this conclusion, but critics argue that the theory's logic points towards it.
  • Intrusiveness. To separate choice from circumstance, the state would have to investigate and judge people's responsibility for their condition, which can be demeaning.
  • The point of equality. In an influential article of 1999, "What Is the Point of Equality?", Elizabeth Anderson argued that luck egalitarianism mistakes the point of equality altogether.

docs.title: Relational equality
docs.text: Anderson and others (Samuel Scheffler, Jonathan Wolff) defend relational or democratic equality. The aim of equality, on this view, is not to distribute goods according to luck and choice, but to create a society in which people relate to one another as equals: where no one is dominated, exploited, marginalised, humiliated or treated as inferior. Historically, egalitarian movements fought against hierarchies of caste, race, class and gender, not against bad luck. Relational egalitarians want everyone to have what they need to function as an equal citizen (adequate income, education, health, access to public spaces and a voice in decisions), but do not require that every unchosen disadvantage be compensated. Critics ask whether relational equality can say anything about inequalities between people who never interact, or about large inequalities of wealth that leave everyone above the threshold of equal citizenship.

docs.title: Priority and sufficiency
docs.text:
Some theorists doubt that equality as such is what matters.

  • Prioritarianism, set out by Derek Parfit in a lecture of 1991, "Equality or Priority?", holds that benefits matter more the worse off the person who receives them. What matters is not how people compare with each other but how badly off they are.
  • Sufficientarianism, defended by Harry Frankfurt in "Equality as a Moral Ideal" (1987), holds that what matters is that everyone has enough. Once everyone is above a threshold of sufficiency, inequalities above it are of no special concern.

docs.title: The levelling-down objection
docs.text:
These alternatives are partly motivated by the levelling-down objection. Suppose an inequality could be removed only by making the better-off worse off, without making anyone better off: for example, by blinding the sighted so that they are equal with the blind. Pure egalitarianism seems to say that this is in one respect an improvement, since it reduces inequality. Many find this absurd. Egalitarians reply that equality is one value among others; levelling down is better in one respect (equality) but worse overall.

Distribution Group 1 Group 2 Group 3 Total Worst-off A 10 50 90 150 10 B 30 30 30 90 30 C 25 40 60 125 25 D 10 10 10 30 10

Table 5.3. Four possible distributions of well-being among three equal groups.

Worked example 5.1: Comparing distributions

Situation. A society of three groups of equal size can choose among the four distributions of Table 5.3. The numbers are levels of well-being (higher is better); a level of 20 is the threshold of a decent life.

Analysis. A utilitarian maximising the total picks A (150). A strict egalitarian concerned only with equality ranks B and D as the most equal and is indifferent between them on equality alone, though any plausible egalitarian also cares about well-being and prefers B. The move from A to D is levelling down: Groups 2 and 3 lose, and Group 1 gains nothing. A prioritarian gives extra weight to the worst off and would probably choose B or C, depending on how much extra weight. Rawls's maximin rule (Chapter 6) picks the distribution whose worst-off group is best off: B (30). A sufficientarian wants everyone above 20: B and C both qualify, and among them C has the higher total. The example shows that "equality" covers several distinct principles that give different answers.

docs.title: 5.6 Equality and difference
docs.text: Treating people identically can sometimes produce inequality. A building with only stairs treats everyone the same but excludes people who use wheelchairs. A test in a language some candidates do not speak well measures language skill rather than the ability it claims to test. Feminist and multicultural theorists have therefore argued that genuine equality sometimes requires recognising differences: special provisions, accommodations or group rights (Chapters 9 and 12). Iris Marion Young argued in Justice and the Politics of Difference (1990) that a supposedly neutral standard often reflects the norms of dominant groups. Critics worry that emphasising group differences can entrench them, and that special treatment can conflict with the principle of treating individuals on their merits.

docs.title: 5.7 Affirmative action and reservations
docs.text: Affirmative action (called positive discrimination in some countries, and reservation or compensatory discrimination in India) refers to policies that give some preference to members of disadvantaged groups in education, employment or political representation. The Constitution of India permits special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Articles 15(4) and 16(4)), and reserves seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies (Articles 330 and 332).

docs.title: Arguments for
docs.text:
• Compensation. Groups that suffered historical injustice, such as caste-based exclusion, are owed redress.
  • Fair equality of opportunity. Present disadvantages of education, wealth and social networks mean that formal equality of opportunity is not fair; preferences help to level the starting line.
  • Diversity and representation. Institutions that include people from all sections of society serve everyone better, gain legitimacy and break stereotypes.
  • Dismantling hierarchy. On a relational view, preferences help to end the social hierarchy that excluded some groups from positions of respect and power.

docs.title: Arguments against
docs.text:
• Merit. Positions should go to the best qualified individuals; group preferences can mean that a better-qualified candidate loses out.
  • Individual versus group. Benefits may go to the better-off members of a disadvantaged group (in India, the "creamy layer" concept addresses this), while poor members of other groups receive nothing.
  • Stigma and division. Preferences may stigmatise beneficiaries as less able and entrench group identities in politics.
  • Temporary or permanent? Critics ask when such measures should end; supporters reply that they should continue as long as the disadvantage persists.

Courts and legislatures have tried to balance these concerns: for example, the Supreme Court of India in Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992) upheld reservations for Other Backward Classes, excluded the creamy layer and held that reservations should not ordinarily exceed fifty per cent.

Worked example 5.2: Two views of a scholarship scheme

Situation. A university reserves a share of its scholarships for students from groups historically excluded from higher education, admitting some students with lower entrance scores than others who were not admitted.

A merit-based critic argues that the higher-scoring students have been treated unfairly: they were judged by group membership, not individual achievement.

A defender using fair equality of opportunity replies that entrance scores reflect not only talent and effort but unequal schooling and family resources; a student who scored slightly lower despite much worse conditions may have shown more ability. A relational egalitarian adds that a university in which some groups are almost absent reproduces social hierarchy.

What the debate turns on. Whether "merit" is accurately measured by the test, whether group membership is a good proxy for disadvantage, and whether the scheme is designed to reach those who need it most.

Summary

  • Modern political theory starts from equal moral worth: people are to be treated as equals, which is not always the same as treating them identically.
  • Equality has legal, political, social and economic dimensions, which can come apart; Ambedkar warned of the contradiction between political equality and social and economic inequality.
  • Formal equality of opportunity removes barriers; fair equality of opportunity seeks equal chances for equally talented people whatever their background; equality of outcome seeks equal results and faces objections about choice, incentives and levelling down.
  • Sen's question "equality of what?" leads to rival currencies: welfare, resources (Dworkin) and capabilities (Sen).
  • Luck egalitarians would neutralise brute luck but not choice; relational egalitarians (Anderson) want people to relate as equals; prioritarians (Parfit) give priority to the worse off; sufficientarians (Frankfurt) want everyone to have enough.
  • Affirmative action and reservations are defended as compensation, fair opportunity, diversity and the dismantling of hierarchy, and criticised in the name of individual merit and for their side effects.

docs.title: 5.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Explain Dworkin's distinction between treating people equally and treating them as equals, with an example.

Answer

Treating people equally means giving them identical treatment or shares. Treating them as equals means showing equal concern and respect for each, which may require different treatment. Example: in a flood, a government that sends the same amount of aid to every district treats them equally; one that sends more aid to the worst-hit districts treats their residents as equals.

Exercise 2

Distinguish formal from fair equality of opportunity. Which would require public spending on schools in poor areas, and why?

Answer

Formal equality of opportunity requires only that positions be open to all, with no legal barriers and selection on qualifications. Fair equality of opportunity requires that people with similar talent and motivation have similar chances whatever their social background. Fair equality of opportunity would require spending on schools in poor areas, because unequal schooling gives children of equal ability unequal chances.

Exercise 3

State two objections to equality of welfare as the currency of equality.

Answer

(1) Expensive tastes: someone who needs costly goods to be satisfied would claim more resources than someone with modest tastes, which seems unfair. (2) Adaptive preferences: someone who has adjusted to deprivation and is content with little would be owed nothing more, so equality of welfare could endorse the results of oppression.

Exercise 4

What is the difference between brute luck and option luck, and why does it matter to luck egalitarians? Give one criticism of the view.

Answer

Brute luck is fortune that is not the result of a deliberate gamble (being born with a disability); option luck is the outcome of a deliberate, calculated risk (losing an investment). Luck egalitarians hold that inequalities from brute luck should be corrected, but those from option luck may stand, since people are responsible for their choices. Criticism: the view seems to imply abandoning people whose misfortune results from bad choices (the uninsured reckless driver), and it requires intrusive judgements about responsibility (Anderson).

Exercise 5

In Worked example 5.1, which distribution would a sufficientarian with a threshold of 20 regard as acceptable, and which would a prioritarian probably choose? Explain.

Answer

A sufficientarian accepts any distribution in which everyone has at least 20: B and C. A prioritarian gives extra weight to gains for the worse off; A has a very low worst-off level (10), and D is low for everyone. The prioritarian would choose B or C, depending on how much extra weight is given: with strong priority B (worst-off 30); with weaker priority C, whose total is higher and whose worst-off level (25) is still decent.

Exercise 6

What is the levelling-down objection, and how do egalitarians reply?

Answer

The levelling-down objection says that if equality has value in itself, making the better-off worse off without benefiting anyone would be in one respect an improvement, which seems absurd. Egalitarians reply that equality is one value among several: levelling down is better in respect of equality but worse overall, so egalitarianism need not recommend it. Others move to prioritarianism, which avoids the objection.

Exercise 7

Give two arguments for and two against reservations in public employment.

Answer

For: (1) compensation for historical exclusion; (2) fair equality of opportunity in a society where background shapes qualifications (also: representation and diversity in public institutions; breaking social hierarchy). Against: (1) it can override individual merit; (2) benefits may go to the better-off members of beneficiary groups while poor members of other groups are excluded (also: stigma; entrenching group identities).
