docs.title: Chapter 12: Feminism, Environmentalism and Other Ideologies
docs.text:
New questions for political theory: gender, nature, culture, authority and empire

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain the key concepts of feminism (patriarchy, sex and gender, the public–private divide) and its main waves and varieties, including intersectionality;
  • describe feminist thought in India from the nineteenth century;
  • explain the core ideas of environmentalism, including the distinction between shallow and deep ecology, sustainable development and environmental justice;
  • outline anarchism, multiculturalism and communitarianism, with their main criticisms;
  • describe fascism as a historical ideology and explain why it is condemned;
  • explain the main ideas of postcolonial thought.

docs.title: 12.1 Beyond the classical ideologies
docs.text: The ideologies of Chapter 11 were shaped by the conflicts of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries: monarchy against representative government, tradition against reason, capital against labour. In the twentieth century other questions forced their way onto the political agenda. Why had half of humanity been excluded from political life? Could the earth sustain unlimited economic growth? How should states treat cultural minorities? What did the end of empire mean for the ideas of the colonisers? This chapter surveys the ideologies that grew from these questions, together with older ideologies, anarchism and fascism, that sit outside the usual left–right line.

docs.title: 12.2 Feminism
docs.text: Feminism is the belief that women have been, and are, unjustly disadvantaged because of their sex, and the commitment to ending that disadvantage. Feminists disagree about the causes of women's subordination and the remedies, but they share two claims: that the relations between the sexes are political (shaped by power and open to change) and that they have been unjust.

docs.title: Key concepts
docs.text:
• Patriarchy. Literally "rule of the father", the term is used by feminists for a social system in which men as a group hold power over women, in the family, the economy, the state and culture.
  • Sex and gender. Many feminists distinguish sex (biological differences) from gender (the social roles, behaviour and expectations attached to being a man or a woman). Gender roles vary between societies and change over time, which shows they are not fixed by nature. Simone de Beauvoir, in The Second Sex (1949), expressed this in a famous phrase: one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
  • The public–private divide. Liberal political theory traditionally separated a public sphere of politics and the market, where justice applies, from a private sphere of the family, regarded as natural and outside politics. Feminists argued that this division hid domestic violence, unequal division of labour and male authority from political scrutiny. The slogan of the 1960s and 1970s, "the personal is political", expressed the claim that private life is shaped by power.

docs.title: Waves of feminism
docs.text:
Historians often describe feminism in waves, though the metaphor simplifies a continuous history.

  • First wave (mid-nineteenth to early twentieth century): demands for legal and political equality, above all the right to vote, and rights to property, education and the professions. Early landmarks include Mary Wollstonecraft's A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), which argued that women's apparent inferiority was the result of their lack of education, and J. S. Mill's The Subjection of Women (1869), written with ideas developed with Harriet Taylor Mill, which argued that the legal subordination of women was wrong in itself and a hindrance to human improvement. Women won the vote in New Zealand in 1893, in Britain on equal terms with men in 1928, and in many countries only after the Second World War.
  • Second wave (1960s to 1980s): with legal equality largely won in many Western countries, feminists turned to discrimination in work, sexuality, reproduction, the family and culture. Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963) described the dissatisfaction of educated housewives; radical feminists analysed patriarchy as a pervasive system.
  • Third wave (from the 1990s): emphasis on diversity among women, on identity, and on the different experiences of women of different races, classes, sexualities and nations.
  • Some writers speak of a fourth wave from the 2010s, using online activism against sexual harassment and violence.

docs.title: Varieties of feminism
docs.text:
Variety Cause of women's subordination Remedy Liberal feminism Unequal rights and opportunities; prejudice Equal legal and political rights; equal opportunity in education and work Socialist and Marxist feminism Capitalism and the economic dependence of women; unpaid domestic labour Transform economic structures as well as gender relations Radical feminism Patriarchy as the most basic form of oppression, present in all spheres including sexuality and the family Transform all social relations; sometimes separate women's organisation Black and intersectional feminism Interlocking systems of oppression by gender, race, class and others Address the specific experience of women facing several forms of oppression Postcolonial feminism Colonial and global inequalities, alongside local patriarchies Challenge Western feminism's claim to speak for all women

Table 12.1. Varieties of feminism.

Intersectionality, a term introduced by the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989, describes how different forms of discrimination (by sex, race, class, caste, disability, sexuality) intersect, so that the experience of, say, a Black woman or a Dalit woman cannot be understood simply by adding the experience of race or caste to that of gender. The postcolonial scholar Chandra Talpade Mohanty, in the essay "Under Western Eyes" (1984), criticised Western feminist writing that portrayed "Third World women" as a single, passive, victimised group.

docs.title: Feminism in India
docs.text: Indian feminism has its own history. In the nineteenth century social reformers campaigned against practices such as sati and child marriage and for widow remarriage and women's education. Savitribai Phule and Jyotirao Phule opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848, challenging both caste and gender hierarchies. Tarabai Shinde's Stri Purush Tulana (A Comparison of Women and Men, 1882) is an early, sharp critique of the double standards applied to women. Pandita Ramabai campaigned for the education and welfare of widows and wrote The High-Caste Hindu Woman (1887). Women took part in large numbers in the national movement, and the Constitution of 1950 granted universal adult franchise, so that Indian women voted on equal terms with men from the first general election. Since independence, women's movements have campaigned on issues including dowry, violence against women, equal pay, representation and land rights. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) reserved one-third of seats in panchayats and municipalities for women, and the 106th Amendment (2023) provides for reserving one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies for women, to come into effect after a fresh delimitation.

docs.title: Criticisms of feminism
docs.text:
• Conservatives argue that differences between men's and women's roles reflect nature or valuable tradition, and that feminism undermines the family.
  • Some liberals worry that feminist proposals for regulating private life or speech conflict with individual liberty.
  • Within feminism, women of colour, working-class women and women from the global South have criticised mainstream feminism for generalising from the experience of educated, Western, middle-class women; intersectional and postcolonial feminism grew from this criticism.
  • There are continuing debates within feminism, for example about pornography, sex work and the relation between sex and gender identity.

Key idea

Feminism holds that relations between the sexes are political and have been unjust. Its varieties differ on the causes of women's subordination (unequal rights, capitalism, patriarchy, intersecting oppressions) and therefore on the remedies.

docs.title: 12.3 Environmentalism
docs.text: Environmentalism (or ecologism) is the ideology that places the relation between human beings and the natural world at the centre of politics. It grew from the 1960s in response to pollution, the destruction of habitats and species, the depletion of resources and, later, climate change. Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962), on the effects of pesticides, is often seen as a starting point of the modern movement.

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
• Ecology. All living things, including humans, are part of interdependent ecosystems. Damage in one place has effects elsewhere.
  • Limits to growth. Infinite economic growth on a finite planet is impossible. The report The Limits to Growth (1972), commissioned by the Club of Rome, used computer models to argue that continued growth in population and production would exhaust resources.
  • Sustainability. The report of the World Commission on Environment and Development, Our Common Future (1987, known as the Brundtland Report), defined sustainable development as development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
  • Responsibility to future generations and to other species. Environmentalists extend moral concern beyond the present generation and, in some versions, beyond human beings.

docs.title: Shallow and deep ecology
docs.text:
The Norwegian philosopher Arne Naess distinguished in 1973 between shallow and deep ecology.

Shallow (light green) ecology Deep (dark green) ecology Moral centre Anthropocentric: nature matters because it matters to humans Ecocentric: nature and all living things have value in themselves Aim Protect the environment for human health and prosperity Respect the intrinsic value of the whole of nature Means Reform within existing economic and political systems: regulation, green technology, pricing pollution Fundamental change in values, lifestyles and economic systems Attitude to growth Sustainable or "green" growth is possible Sceptical of growth; may favour reduced consumption

Table 12.2. Shallow and deep ecology.

docs.title: Varieties
docs.text:
• Reformist environmentalism works within liberal democratic and market systems: environmental regulation, carbon taxes, emissions trading and renewable energy.
  • Eco-socialism argues that capitalism, with its drive for profit and growth, is the root cause of environmental destruction.
  • Eco-feminism connects the domination of nature with the domination of women; the Indian scholar and activist Vandana Shiva (Staying Alive, 1988) argued that development models had marginalised both women's knowledge and nature.
  • Eco-anarchism and social ecology (Murray Bookchin) favour small, decentralised, self-governing communities living in harmony with their environment.

docs.title: Environmental justice and India
docs.text: The environmental justice movement points out that environmental harms (pollution, toxic waste, displacement by dams and mines) fall disproportionately on the poor, on indigenous peoples and on marginalised communities, while the benefits of resource use go mostly to others. In India the Chipko movement, which began in the Himalayan region of what is now Uttarakhand in 1973, saw villagers, many of them women, embrace trees to prevent them from being felled by contractors. The historian Ramachandra Guha and others have described an "environmentalism of the poor" in which struggles over forests, water and land are struggles for livelihood as well as for nature. At the global level, debates about climate change raise questions of climate justice: how to share the burden of reducing emissions between rich countries that have emitted most in the past and poorer countries that need to develop (Chapter 14).

docs.title: Criticisms of environmentalism
docs.text:
• Economic costs. Critics argue that strict environmental regulation slows growth and harms the poor, who most need development; environmentalists reply that environmental damage itself harms the poor most.
  • Anti-human? Deep ecology is criticised for valuing nature over human needs; some critics have called it misanthropic.
  • Authoritarianism. Some fear that the urgency of environmental crisis could justify restrictions on democratic freedoms.
  • Technological optimism. Others argue that innovation will solve environmental problems without radical changes in lifestyle.

docs.title: 12.4 Anarchism
docs.text:
Anarchism (from the Greek anarchos, without a ruler) is the belief that the state is unnecessary and harmful, and that society can and should be organised on the basis of voluntary cooperation without coercive authority. Anarchists do not favour chaos; they believe that order can arise from free association.

  • Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (1809–1865), the first to call himself an anarchist, wrote in What Is Property? (1840) that "property is theft", attacking property that allows some to live off the labour of others, and proposed mutualism, a society of small producers exchanging through cooperative banks.
  • Mikhail Bakunin (1814–1876) clashed with Marx in the First International, warning that a workers' state would become a new tyranny of a ruling elite.
  • Peter Kropotkin (1842–1921), in Mutual Aid (1902), argued against social Darwinism that cooperation, not only competition, is a factor in evolution, and envisaged anarcho-communism.
  • Individualist anarchism and anarcho-capitalism (associated with Murray Rothbard) reject the state from the opposite direction, favouring private property and markets for all services, including protection.

Gandhi described himself at times as a philosophical anarchist, valuing a stateless society of self-governing villages as an ideal while accepting that some state was needed in practice (Chapter 13). Criticisms: anarchism is said to be utopian, underestimating human selfishness and the need for coordination and protection against aggression; anarcho-capitalism is criticised for leaving the weak at the mercy of the strong.

docs.title: Multiculturalism
docs.text:
Multiculturalism, as a political theory, holds that cultural diversity within a state should be recognised and accommodated, not merely tolerated, and that members of minority cultures may be entitled to special rights or protections. Its leading theorists include:

  • Charles Taylor, whose essay "The Politics of Recognition" (1992) argued that identity is shaped by recognition from others, and that misrecognition (being seen through a demeaning image) can inflict real harm; equal respect may require recognising distinct identities.
  • Will Kymlicka, who defended group-differentiated rights on liberal grounds (Chapters 7 and 9).
  • Bhikhu Parekh, in Rethinking Multiculturalism (2000), who argued that cultures should engage in an open dialogue in which no single culture, including liberalism, is taken as the standard.

Criticisms come from several sides. Liberal egalitarians such as Brian Barry argue that it is fairer to apply the same laws to all and that group rights can entrench inequality. Feminists such as Susan Moller Okin, in "Is Multiculturalism Bad for Women?" (1997), argued that defending minority cultures can mean defending practices that subordinate women within them. Others worry that multicultural policies may weaken social cohesion; defenders reply that recognition strengthens minorities' attachment to the wider society.

docs.title: Communitarianism
docs.text: Communitarianism (Sandel, MacIntyre, Walzer, Taylor; Chapter 6) emphasises that individuals are shaped by their communities and that the common good, shared values and social responsibilities deserve more weight than liberal individualism allows. Political communitarians in the 1990s, such as Amitai Etzioni, called for balancing rights with responsibilities and strengthening families, neighbourhoods and civil society. Critics worry that communitarianism can be conservative, suppressing dissent and diversity within communities, and that "community" is often defined by its most powerful members.

docs.title: 12.6 Fascism
docs.text: Fascism was a political ideology and movement of the twentieth century, which rose to power in Italy under Benito Mussolini (from 1922) and, in its Nazi form, in Germany under Adolf Hitler (from 1933). It is studied in political theory both as a historical phenomenon and as a warning.

docs.title: Main features
docs.text:
Historians and political theorists have identified a cluster of features, though fascist movements differed among themselves:

  • extreme nationalism: the nation (or, in Nazism, a supposed race) is the highest value, and its glory and expansion the supreme goal;
  • rejection of liberal democracy, individualism and rights, and of the Enlightenment ideas of reason and equality;
  • anti-communism combined with hostility to liberal capitalism, while in practice cooperating with business;
  • totalitarianism: the state, controlled by a single party, seeks to control every area of life, including culture, education, youth and the economy;
  • the leader principle: a charismatic leader embodies the will of the nation;
  • glorification of violence, struggle and war;
  • scapegoating of minorities and, in Nazism, a racial ideology of antisemitism.

docs.title: Why it is condemned
docs.text:
Fascist regimes destroyed democratic institutions, suppressed all opposition, launched wars of aggression and, in the case of Nazi Germany, carried out the Holocaust, the systematic murder of some six million Jews, together with the murder of Roma, disabled people, political opponents and many others. The defeat of fascism in the Second World War shaped the post-war order, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) and the commitment of many constitutions to human dignity (Chapter 14). Political theorists such as Hannah Arendt (The Origins of Totalitarianism, 1951) studied how such regimes arose and how they used terror and ideology to atomise and dominate whole societies.

Caution: using the word 'fascist' carefully

"Fascist" is often used loosely as a term of abuse for any opponent. In political theory the term refers to a specific historical ideology with the features listed above. Analysing whether a movement shares some of those features is a legitimate scholarly question, but it requires evidence and care, not labels.

docs.title: 12.7 Postcolonialism
docs.text:
Postcolonial theory studies the cultural, political and intellectual legacies of colonialism, and criticises the ways in which Western knowledge represented colonised peoples.

  • Frantz Fanon (1925–1961), a psychiatrist from Martinique who joined the Algerian struggle for independence, analysed in Black Skin, White Masks (1952) and The Wretched of the Earth (1961) the psychological damage of colonial racism and the dynamics of decolonisation. He also warned that a new national elite might simply replace the colonisers.
  • Edward Said (1935–2003), in Orientalism (1978), argued that Western scholarship, literature and art constructed an image of "the Orient" as exotic, backward, irrational and unchanging, in contrast to a rational, progressive West, and that this knowledge was bound up with colonial power.
  • The Subaltern Studies group of historians, founded in the early 1980s by Ranajit Guha and others, set out to write the history of colonial India from the perspective of peasants, workers and other subordinated groups, rather than of colonial rulers or nationalist elites. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak's essay "Can the Subaltern Speak?" (1988) asked whether intellectuals can represent the voices of the most marginalised without silencing them.
  • Partha Chatterjee, in Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986), examined how Indian nationalism both challenged and borrowed from the categories of colonial thought.

Postcolonial thought has influenced political theory by questioning the universality of concepts developed in Europe, drawing attention to the colonial context of liberal thinkers, and encouraging comparative political theory. Critics argue that it can be obscure, that it sometimes treats "the West" as monolithic, and that it may neglect the agency of colonised peoples, or the role of local hierarchies, in favour of an exclusive focus on colonial discourse.

Worked example 12.1: One issue, several ideologies

Issue. A large dam is proposed that would generate electricity and irrigate farmland, but flood forests and displace several thousand villagers, many of them from tribal communities.

How each ideology might frame it. A neo-liberal would ask whether the project is economically efficient and whether the displaced are properly compensated through market-based valuation. A social democrat would support development that reduces poverty, with fair compensation and rehabilitation. A shallow ecologist would weigh environmental costs against human benefits and look for less damaging alternatives. A deep ecologist would emphasise the intrinsic value of the forest and its species. An environmental justice perspective would ask why the costs fall on poor and tribal communities while benefits go elsewhere. A feminist would ask how displacement affects women's work, land rights and security. A multiculturalist would ask whether the project respects the distinct way of life and land rights of tribal communities. An anarchist would ask why the decision is made by the state rather than by the affected communities themselves.

Summary

  • Feminism holds that gender relations are political and unjust; key concepts are patriarchy, sex and gender, and the public–private divide. Its waves run from Wollstonecraft and suffrage to second-wave, third-wave and fourth-wave feminism, and its varieties include liberal, socialist, radical, intersectional (Crenshaw) and postcolonial (Mohanty) feminism. Indian feminism includes Savitribai Phule, Tarabai Shinde and Pandita Ramabai.
  • Environmentalism stresses ecology, limits to growth and sustainability (Brundtland, 1987). Naess distinguished anthropocentric shallow ecology from ecocentric deep ecology; varieties include reformism, eco-socialism, eco-feminism and social ecology; Chipko exemplifies the environmentalism of the poor.
  • Anarchism (Proudhon, Bakunin, Kropotkin) rejects the state in favour of voluntary cooperation.
  • Multiculturalism (Taylor, Kymlicka, Parekh) seeks recognition and accommodation of cultural diversity; critics include Barry and Okin. Communitarianism stresses community and responsibilities.
  • Fascism was a twentieth-century ideology of extreme nationalism, totalitarianism, the leader principle and violence; Nazism added racial antisemitism and carried out the Holocaust.
  • Postcolonialism (Fanon, Said, Subaltern Studies, Spivak, Chatterjee) examines colonial legacies and questions the universality of Western categories.

docs.title: 12.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Explain the distinction between sex and gender and why it matters to feminists.

Answer

Sex refers to biological differences; gender to the social roles, behaviours and expectations attached to being a man or woman. The distinction matters because it shows that many differences between men's and women's lives are socially created and changeable, not fixed by nature, so they can be criticised as unjust and reformed.

Exercise 2

What does "the personal is political" mean? Give an example.

Answer

It means that relations in private life, especially in the family and sexuality, are shaped by power and are proper subjects of political debate and action. Example: the division of unpaid housework and childcare, often regarded as a private matter, affects women's opportunities in paid work and politics, so it is a question of justice.

Exercise 3

Distinguish liberal, radical and intersectional feminism.

Answer

Liberal feminism attributes women's disadvantage to unequal rights and opportunities and seeks equal legal and political rights. Radical feminism sees patriarchy as a pervasive system of male domination present in all areas of life, including the family and sexuality, requiring deep social transformation. Intersectional feminism (Crenshaw) holds that gender oppression intersects with race, class, caste and other forms of oppression, so that women's experiences differ and must be understood in their specific combinations.

Exercise 4

Compare shallow and deep ecology on (a) the value of nature and (b) attitudes to economic growth.

Answer

(a) Shallow ecology is anthropocentric: nature is valuable for its use to humans. Deep ecology is ecocentric: nature has intrinsic value. (b) Shallow ecology believes sustainable or green growth is possible through reform; deep ecology is sceptical of growth and favours changes in values and reduced consumption.

Exercise 5

What is environmental justice? Illustrate with the Chipko movement.

Answer

Environmental justice concerns the fair distribution of environmental harms and benefits; it notes that the poor and marginalised often bear the costs of pollution and resource extraction while others gain the benefits. In Chipko (from 1973), villagers in the Himalayan region, many of them women, embraced trees to stop commercial felling that threatened their forests and livelihoods: an "environmentalism of the poor" in which protecting nature meant protecting livelihoods.

Exercise 6

Summarise Okin's criticism of multiculturalism and one reply a multiculturalist might give.

Answer

Okin argued that group rights for minority cultures can protect practices that subordinate women within those cultures, since many cultures are patriarchal and the group's leaders are usually men. Reply: multiculturalists such as Kymlicka support external protections but not internal restrictions that limit members' basic liberties, so a liberal multiculturalism can protect women's rights while accommodating culture.

Exercise 7

What was Said's argument in Orientalism?

Answer

Said argued that Western scholarship, literature and art constructed "the Orient" as exotic, backward, irrational and unchanging, in contrast to a rational, progressive West, and that this body of knowledge was bound up with colonial power, helping to justify and administer domination.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Global Justice and Human Rights
docs.text:
Do justice and rights stop at the border?

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe the origins and content of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the main international human rights instruments;
  • discuss the debate between universalism and cultural relativism, including the "Asian values" debate;
  • compare cosmopolitan, statist and nationalist positions on global justice;
  • explain Singer's argument about famine and affluence, Pogge's argument about institutional harm and Rawls's Law of Peoples;
  • discuss humanitarian intervention and the responsibility to protect;
  • apply theories of global justice to climate change and migration.

docs.title: 14.1 From domestic to global justice
docs.text:
Most of this book has asked what justice and rights require within a political community. Yet we live in a world of about two hundred states with vastly different levels of wealth, security and freedom. A child's chances of surviving to adulthood, going to school or living free from violence depend heavily on the country of birth, a fact as morally arbitrary, in Rawls's sense, as the family or class into which one is born. Problems such as climate change, pandemics, financial crises and refugee flows cross borders. Political theorists have therefore asked whether principles of justice apply globally, and what we owe to people in other countries.

Two developments shape the discussion: the creation, after the Second World War, of an international system of human rights; and the growth, from the 1970s, of philosophical debate about global justice.

docs.title: The Universal Declaration
docs.text:
The horrors of the Second World War, including the Holocaust, convinced many that the treatment of people by their own governments could no longer be left entirely to those governments. The Charter of the United Nations (1945) committed member states to promote respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December 1948, a date now observed as Human Rights Day. It was drafted by a commission chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, with important contributions from members from many countries, including the Lebanese philosopher Charles Malik, the Chinese diplomat Peng-chun Chang, the French jurist René Cassin and the Indian educator Hansa Mehta, who is credited with helping to change the draft wording "all men are born free and equal" to "all human beings are born free and equal". The Declaration was adopted with no votes against and eight abstentions.

Its 30 articles proclaim civil and political rights (life, liberty, security, freedom from slavery and torture, equality before the law, fair trial, privacy, freedom of movement, asylum, nationality, marriage, property, thought, conscience, religion, opinion, expression, assembly and participation in government) and economic, social and cultural rights (social security, work, rest and leisure, an adequate standard of living, education and participation in cultural life). Its first article states that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

The Declaration was not a treaty and did not create binding legal obligations by itself. It was followed by two binding covenants adopted in 1966 and in force from 1976: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (ICESCR). Together with the UDHR they are often called the International Bill of Human Rights.

docs.title: Other instruments and institutions
docs.text:
Further conventions address particular rights or groups, among them the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (1948), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (1965), the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women (1979), the Convention against Torture (1984), the Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) and the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (2006). Regional systems include the European Convention on Human Rights (1950) with its court, and inter-American and African systems.

The International Criminal Court, established by the Rome Statute (1998) and operating since 2002, can try individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression, where national courts are unwilling or unable to do so. Not all states are parties to it; India, for example, is not.

The Vienna Declaration of the World Conference on Human Rights (1993) affirmed that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated (Chapter 7).

Figure 14.1 The international human rights framework. A diagram of the international human rights framework. At the top, the UN Charter of 1945. Below it, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948. Below that, two branches: the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, both of 1966. Further below, specialised conventions on genocide, racial discrimination, women, torture, children and disability, and the International Criminal Court.

docs.title: 14.3 Universalism and cultural relativism
docs.text: Are human rights truly universal, or are they the expression of one culture, the liberal West, imposed on others?

docs.title: The relativist challenge
docs.text:
Cultural relativists argue that moral values are rooted in particular cultures and that there is no neutral standpoint from which to judge them all. In 1947, while the UDHR was being drafted, the American Anthropological Association submitted a statement warning that a declaration conceived only in terms of the values of Western Europe and America could not be applicable to all human beings. Critics argue that human rights, with their focus on individuals, reflect Western liberal individualism, while many cultures emphasise duties, community and harmony.

In the 1990s some political leaders in East and Southeast Asia advanced the idea of "Asian values": that Asian societies give priority to family, community, order and economic development over individual rights and political freedoms, so that Western criticism of their human rights records was cultural imperialism.

docs.title: Universalist replies
docs.text:
• Overlapping consensus. Human rights need not rest on Western philosophy. People from many traditions can endorse them for their own reasons, as the drafters of the UDHR, drawn from many cultures, did.
  • Diversity within cultures. Cultures are not uniform. Every culture contains debates and dissenters, and the people who invoke "culture" to deny rights are often those who hold power. Amartya Sen, in essays such as "Human Rights and Asian Values" (1997), pointed out that Asian traditions contain strong defences of tolerance and freedom (he cited Aśoka and Akbar, among others), while Western traditions contained much authoritarianism; there is no single set of "Asian" or "Western" values.
  • The victims' perspective. Those whose rights are violated rarely accept that their suffering is justified by their culture.
  • Relativism undermines itself. If all values are relative, the value of respecting other cultures is relative too, and the relativist cannot criticise cultural imperialism either.

docs.title: Moderate positions
docs.text:
Many theorists take a middle position. Human rights express universal moral standards, but their interpretation and implementation may legitimately vary between societies. Rights should be few and basic enough to command broad agreement, and the language of rights can be translated into, and enriched by, other traditions. The philosopher Abdullahi An-Na'im, for example, has argued for an internal cultural dialogue in which human rights are legitimated from within religious and cultural traditions.

Key idea

Universalists hold that human rights apply to all people by virtue of their humanity; relativists that values depend on culture. Most theorists defend universal basic rights while allowing variety in how they are interpreted and realised, and point out that cultures are internally diverse.

docs.title: 14.4 Theories of global justice
docs.text:
What do the rich owe to the poor across borders? Positions can be grouped in three broad families.

Position Main claim Key thinkers Implication Cosmopolitanism Every human being has equal moral standing; principles of justice apply to all people, whatever their nationality Peter Singer, Thomas Pogge, Charles Beitz, Simon Caney Strong duties to reduce global poverty and inequality; reform of global institutions Statism (or political conception) Demanding principles of distributive justice apply only within states, where people share coercive institutions Thomas Nagel, the later Rawls Duties of humanitarian assistance abroad, but not global equality Nationalism (liberal nationalism) Nations are ethical communities whose members owe special duties to one another David Miller, Yael Tamir Basic human rights for all; deeper redistributive duties among co-nationals

Table 14.1. Three positions on global justice.

docs.title: Cosmopolitanism
docs.text:
The word comes from the Greek for "citizen of the world", a phrase associated with the ancient Cynic philosopher Diogenes. In modern philosophy Immanuel Kant, in Perpetual Peace (1795), proposed a federation of free states and a "cosmopolitan right" of hospitality to strangers. Contemporary cosmopolitans hold that what matters morally is individual human beings, each counting equally, and that national borders have no fundamental moral significance for justice.

Peter Singer's argument. In "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" (1972), written during the famine and refugee crisis accompanying the war of 1971 in what became Bangladesh, the philosopher Peter Singer argued from a simple case. If you pass a shallow pond and see a child drowning, you ought to wade in and save the child, even if it means ruining your clothes. The cost to you is small compared with the death of a child. Singer then argued that distance and the number of other people who could help make no moral difference. If we can prevent something very bad from happening without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to do it. Since people in affluent countries can, by giving money to effective aid agencies, prevent deaths from poverty at modest cost, they are morally obliged to give much more than they do; giving is a duty, not an act of charity.

Criticisms: the argument seems extremely demanding, potentially requiring people to give until they are nearly as poor as those they help; critics also question whether aid is as effective as the argument assumes, and whether individual giving is the right response to problems that are institutional and political.

Pogge's argument. Thomas Pogge, in World Poverty and Human Rights (2002), argued that the relation between rich and poor countries is not one of mere failure to help, but of harm. The global institutional order, shaped by powerful states (rules of trade, intellectual property, lending and the recognition of governments' rights to sell their countries' resources and borrow in their name, whoever those governments are), foreseeably contributes to severe poverty. Since we are harming the poor by imposing these institutions, we have negative duties, the strongest kind, to reform them, not merely positive duties of charity. Criticisms: critics dispute Pogge's empirical claims about how much global institutions cause poverty, as opposed to domestic factors such as governance and conflict.

Beitz and the global original position. Charles Beitz (Political Theory and International Relations, 1979) argued that if Rawls's reasoning is sound, it should be applied globally: since the world economy is a scheme of cooperation and the natural resources a country happens to have are as morally arbitrary as natural talents, parties in a global original position would choose a global difference principle.

docs.title: Statism and Rawls's Law of Peoples
docs.text:
John Rawls himself rejected a global difference principle. In The Law of Peoples (1999) he imagined a second original position in which representatives of peoples (not individuals) choose principles for relations among them. The principles include respect for peoples' independence, observance of treaties, non-intervention except in self-defence and to protect human rights, observance of the laws of war, honouring of a short list of basic human rights, and a duty of assistance to "burdened societies" whose unfavourable conditions prevent them from having just or decent institutions. The duty of assistance has a target: once a society can manage its own affairs as a just or decent society, the duty ends. Rawls argued that a country's wealth depends mainly on its political culture and institutions rather than its resources, and that requiring continuing redistribution between peoples would fail to respect their responsibility for their own choices.

Thomas Nagel ("The Problem of Global Justice", 2005) argued that demanding principles of justice, such as equality, arise only among people who are jointly subject to a coercive state in whose name laws are made; absent a world government, there is no global justice in this full sense, though there are humanitarian duties to relieve extreme suffering.

Criticisms: cosmopolitans reply that the global economy and international institutions are already coercive and shape people's lives deeply, so the conditions that trigger duties of justice exist globally; and that Rawls's view of the causes of poverty underestimates international factors.

docs.title: Liberal nationalism
docs.text:
David Miller (National Responsibility and Global Justice, 2007) argued that nations are ethical communities whose members share a public culture and have special obligations to one another, and that nations can be held responsible for their own choices and outcomes. Everyone, everywhere, is owed respect for basic human rights, which generates real duties for outsiders when rights are not met; but deeper principles of distributive equality apply within nations. Criticisms: cosmopolitans ask why the accident of nationality should determine one's share of the world's resources, and whether it is fair to hold individuals responsible for the decisions of their nations.

Worked example 14.1: Three answers to one question

Question. A wealthy country is considering whether to increase its foreign aid budget substantially, at the cost of slightly higher taxes for its citizens.

Singer (cosmopolitan, utilitarian): yes, and individuals should give privately too; preventing deaths from poverty at modest cost is a moral duty.

Pogge (cosmopolitan, institutional): aid is welcome, but the main duty is to reform the trade, finance and resource rules from which the country benefits and which harm the poor.

Rawls (Law of Peoples): the country has a duty of assistance to help burdened societies build just or decent institutions, but not a duty to equalise wealth between countries; aid should aim at institutional capacity, and ends when that target is met.

Miller (liberal nationalist): the country must help ensure that basic human rights are met everywhere, but may legitimately give priority to its own citizens beyond that threshold.

docs.title: 14.5 Humanitarian intervention and the responsibility to protect
docs.text:
What should the international community do when a government commits mass atrocities against its own people, or fails to prevent them? The principle of sovereignty and the UN Charter's prohibition on the use of force (except in self-defence or when authorised by the Security Council) seem to forbid intervention. Yet the failure to prevent the genocide in Rwanda in 1994 and the massacre at Srebrenica in Bosnia in 1995 led many to ask whether sovereignty should shield such crimes.

In 2001 an International Commission on Intervention and State Sovereignty proposed the doctrine of the responsibility to protect (often abbreviated R2P). The 2005 World Summit of the United Nations endorsed a version of it:

  1. each state has the responsibility to protect its population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity;
  2. the international community should help states fulfil this responsibility;
  3. if a state is manifestly failing to protect its population, the international community should be prepared to take collective action, through the Security Council, in accordance with the UN Charter, using peaceful means first and force as a last resort.

R2P reframes sovereignty as responsibility rather than merely a right to non-interference.

docs.title: Arguments for and against intervention
docs.text:
For: there is a moral duty to prevent mass atrocities; sovereignty exists to protect people and loses its moral force when a government turns on them; failure to act in Rwanda showed the cost of indifference.

Against: intervention can be a cover for powerful states' strategic interests; it may make matters worse, causing civilian deaths and prolonged instability; it is applied selectively, depending on the interests of the permanent members of the Security Council; it threatens the sovereignty that protects weaker states. Many countries of the global South, with memories of colonial rule, have been wary of doctrines that license intervention by powerful states. Just war theory, which goes back to Augustine and Aquinas, offers criteria often used in these debates: just cause, right intention, last resort, legitimate authority, proportionality and reasonable prospect of success.

docs.title: Climate justice
docs.text:
Climate change raises questions of justice between countries, between generations and between rich and poor. The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (1992) recognised the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities: all countries share responsibility for addressing climate change, but developed countries, which have emitted most greenhouse gases historically and have greater resources, should take the lead. The Paris Agreement (2015) set the goal of holding the rise in global average temperature to well below 2 °C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C, with each country setting its own nationally determined contributions.

Theorists have proposed several principles for sharing the burden.

  • Polluter pays (or contribution): those who caused the problem should bear the cost, in proportion to historical emissions. Objection: past emitters often did not know the harm, and many are dead.
  • Beneficiary pays: those who benefited from emission-intensive development should pay, whether or not they caused it.
  • Ability to pay: the burden should fall on those best able to bear it.
  • Equal per-capita shares: each person has an equal right to the atmosphere's capacity to absorb emissions, so countries' allowances should be proportional to population.

Worked example 14.2: Comparing burden-sharing principles

Situation. Imagine two countries. Country N has a small population, high income per person and high historical and current emissions per person. Country S has a large population, low income per person and low emissions per person, but its total current emissions are growing as it develops.

Analysis. Under polluter pays (historical) and ability to pay, most of the burden of reducing emissions and financing adaptation falls on N. Under equal per-capita shares, S is entitled to a much larger total allowance because of its population, while N must cut its emissions per person sharply. A principle that looked only at current total emissions would put more pressure on S, which S would reject as unfair given its lower historical responsibility and its need for development. The principle of common but differentiated responsibilities is an attempt to combine these considerations.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
Do states have the right to control who enters their territory? Most states and many theorists say yes: self-determination includes deciding who becomes a member, as clubs and families choose their members (Michael Walzer, Spheres of Justice, 1983). Supporters of this view add arguments from the protection of a national culture, the integrity of welfare systems and democratic control. Cosmopolitan critics such as Joseph Carens ("Aliens and Citizens: The Case for Open Borders", 1987) argue that citizenship in a rich country is like feudal privilege, an inherited status that greatly enhances one's life chances, and that restrictions on movement are hard to justify given the equal moral worth of all persons; at least, there is a strong presumption in favour of freedom of movement. Between these positions lie views that accept state control of borders but insist on duties to refugees (Chapter 9), on fair treatment of migrants already resident, and on the effects of migration policies on poorer countries.

Summary

  • The UN Charter (1945), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (10 December 1948) and the two Covenants (1966, in force 1976) form the core of international human rights law; specialised conventions, regional courts and the International Criminal Court (Rome Statute, 1998) extend it. The Vienna Declaration (1993) affirmed that rights are universal and indivisible.
  • Relativists and proponents of "Asian values" question the universality of human rights; universalists reply with overlapping consensus, the internal diversity of cultures (Sen) and the perspective of victims.
  • Cosmopolitans (Singer, Pogge, Beitz) extend principles of justice to all humanity; Singer argues from the drowning child, Pogge from institutional harm, Beitz for a global difference principle. Statists (Nagel, the later Rawls) confine full distributive justice to states; Rawls's Law of Peoples includes a duty of assistance with a target. Liberal nationalists (Miller) defend basic rights for all and special duties among co-nationals.
  • The responsibility to protect (endorsed in 2005) treats sovereignty as responsibility and permits collective action through the Security Council against genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity; intervention remains controversial.
  • Climate justice debates how to share burdens (polluter pays, beneficiary pays, ability to pay, equal per-capita shares) under the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities; migration debates set self-determination against freedom of movement.

docs.title: 14.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Why is the Universal Declaration of Human Rights not legally binding by itself, and which instruments made its rights binding?

Answer

The UDHR was adopted as a resolution of the General Assembly, which does not create binding treaty obligations. Its rights were made binding through treaties, above all the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (both 1966, in force 1976), and through later specialised conventions. Many of its provisions are also widely regarded as part of customary international law.

Exercise 2

State the "Asian values" argument and Sen's reply to it.

Answer

The Asian values argument held that Asian societies prioritise family, community, order and development over individual rights and political freedoms, so Western human rights criticism is cultural imperialism. Sen replied that there is no single set of Asian (or Western) values: Asian traditions include strong defences of tolerance and freedom (e.g. Aśoka, Akbar), Western traditions include much authoritarianism, and those who invoke cultural values to deny rights are often those in power.

Exercise 3

Summarise Singer's drowning-child argument and one objection to it.

Answer

If you can save a child drowning in a shallow pond at the cost of ruining your clothes, you ought to do so. Distance and the presence of others who could help make no moral difference. So if we can prevent something very bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we ought to: affluent people should give much more to relieve poverty abroad. Objection: the argument is extremely demanding, seeming to require giving until one is nearly as badly off as those helped; others question aid effectiveness or prefer institutional reform to individual charity.

Exercise 4

How does Pogge's argument differ from Singer's?

Answer

Singer argues from positive duties to help those in need, whatever the cause of their need. Pogge argues that the affluent are harming the poor by imposing a global institutional order (trade, lending, resource and intellectual property rules) that foreseeably produces severe poverty; this violates negative duties not to harm, the strongest kind of duty, and requires institutional reform.

Exercise 5

What is Rawls's duty of assistance, and why does it have a "target"?

Answer

In The Law of Peoples, well-ordered peoples have a duty of assistance to burdened societies whose unfavourable conditions prevent them from having just or decent institutions. It has a target: to help them become able to manage their own affairs as just or decent societies. Once that is achieved the duty ends, because Rawls held that a society's wellbeing depends mainly on its political culture and that continuing redistribution between peoples would not respect their responsibility for their own choices.

Exercise 6

State the three elements of the responsibility to protect as endorsed in 2005, and give one argument against humanitarian intervention.

Answer

(1) Each state is responsible for protecting its population from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity. (2) The international community should help states meet this responsibility. (3) If a state manifestly fails, the international community should be prepared to take collective action through the Security Council, peacefully first and by force as a last resort. Argument against: intervention may serve the strategic interests of powerful states, is applied selectively, and can worsen the situation it aims to remedy.

Exercise 7

Explain the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities, and why a poorer, populous country might reject a burden-sharing rule based on current total emissions.

Answer

The principle (UNFCCC, 1992) holds that all countries share responsibility for addressing climate change, but developed countries, with greater historical emissions and capabilities, should take the lead. A poorer, populous country might reject a rule based on current total emissions because its emissions per person and its historical emissions are low, it needs development to reduce poverty, and such a rule would ignore the responsibility of countries that grew rich by emitting earlier.
