docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms used in this book, with the chapter where each is explained

docs.title: A–C
docs.text: Ahiṃsā Non-violence, understood by Gandhi as active love that excludes hatred of the opponent; the basis of satyagraha. (Chapter 13) Alienation In Marx, the estrangement of workers under capitalism from the product and activity of their labour, from their human nature (species-being) and from one another. (Chapter 11) Anarchism The belief that the state is unnecessary and harmful and that society can be organised by voluntary cooperation. (Chapter 12) Arthaśāstra The Sanskrit treatise on statecraft attributed to Kauṭilya, describing administration, law, economy and foreign policy. (Chapter 13) Authority The recognised right to command and be obeyed; power accepted as rightful. Weber distinguished traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority. (Chapter 3) Basic structure For Rawls, the main political, economic and social institutions of a society, which are the primary subject of justice. In Indian constitutional law, the essential features of the Constitution that amendment cannot destroy. (Chapters 6 and 10) Capability In Sen and Nussbaum, a person's real freedom to achieve valued functionings (beings and doings). (Chapters 5 and 6) Citizenship Full membership of a political community, combining legal status, rights and participation. (Chapter 9) Civic nationalism Nationalism that bases the nation on shared citizenship and political values, open to those who adopt them. (Chapter 9) Civil disobedience Public, non-violent, conscientious breach of law aimed at changing a law or policy, with acceptance of the penalty. (Chapter 3) Communitarianism The view that individuals are shaped by their communities and that the common good and shared values deserve more weight than liberal individualism allows. (Chapters 6 and 12) Condorcet's paradox The possibility that majority preferences over three or more options form a cycle, so that no option beats all others. (Chapter 8) Conservatism The ideology that values tradition, organic society, gradual change and authority, and is sceptical of abstract reason in politics. (Chapter 11) Cosmopolitanism The view that every human being has equal moral standing and that principles of justice apply to all people regardless of nationality. (Chapter 14) Cultural relativism The view that moral values are rooted in particular cultures and cannot be judged by a universal standard. (Chapter 14)

docs.title: D–H
docs.text: Daṇḍa Literally "rod": coercive authority and punishment in ancient Indian thought; also one of the seven limbs of the state (the army) and one of the four means (force). (Chapter 13) Deliberative democracy The view that democratic legitimacy comes from public reasoning among free and equal citizens, not only from counting votes. (Chapter 8) Democracy Rule by the people; procedural accounts stress free elections and rights, substantive accounts also equality and participation. (Chapter 8) Descriptive claim A claim about what is the case, true or false as a matter of fact. (Chapter 1) Difference principle Rawls's principle that social and economic inequalities must work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged. (Chapter 6) Dharma Cosmic order, moral law and duty in Indian thought; government was expected to uphold it. (Chapter 13) Domination Being subject to the arbitrary will of another; republicans define freedom as its absence. (Chapter 4) Entitlement theory Nozick's theory that a distribution is just if it arises from just acquisition and just transfer, whatever its pattern. (Chapter 6) Equality of opportunity The principle that positions should be open to all; in its fair version, that people of similar talent and effort should have similar chances whatever their background. (Chapter 5) Essentially contested concept A concept, such as democracy or justice, that is evaluative, complex and open to rival interpretations, so that disputes about its use cannot be settled by definition. (Chapter 1) Ethnic nationalism Nationalism that bases the nation on shared descent, ethnicity, language or religion. (Chapter 9) Fascism A twentieth-century ideology of extreme nationalism, totalitarian rule, the leader principle and glorification of violence. (Chapter 12) Feminism The belief that women have been unjustly disadvantaged because of their sex and the commitment to ending that disadvantage. (Chapter 12) Functioning In the capability approach, an achieved state of being or doing, such as being nourished or literate. (Chapter 6) General will In Rousseau, the will of citizens directed at the common good, as distinct from the sum of private wills (the will of all). (Chapter 2) Hegemony In Gramsci, rule by consent through culture and ideas as well as by coercion. (Chapter 3) Historical materialism Marx's theory that the economic base (forces and relations of production) shapes the rest of society and drives historical change. (Chapter 11)

docs.title: I–M
docs.text: Ideology A more or less coherent set of ideas offering a description of society, a vision of a better one and a programme of action. (Chapter 11) Imagined community Anderson's description of the nation: a community whose members cannot know one another personally but share an image of their communion. (Chapter 9) Interest theory of rights The view that rights protect important interests of the right-holder. (Chapter 7) Intersectionality The way different forms of discrimination (by gender, race, class, caste and others) combine to shape distinctive experiences. (Chapter 12) Jus sanguinis Citizenship by descent from a citizen parent. (Chapter 9) Jus soli Citizenship by birth on a state's territory. (Chapter 9) Laïcité The French model of secularism, which keeps religion out of public institutions. (Chapter 10) Legitimacy The rightfulness of a political order; understood sociologically as belief in its rightfulness or normatively as its justification. (Chapter 3) Liberalism The ideology that puts the free individual first and values liberty, reason, equality, toleration and government by consent. (Chapter 11) Luck egalitarianism The view that inequalities resulting from unchosen circumstances (brute luck) are unjust, while those resulting from choices may stand. (Chapter 5) Maṇḍala theory Kauṭilya's account of a king's international environment as circles of enemies and allies. (Chapter 13) Maximin The decision rule of choosing the option whose worst outcome is best; used by Rawls to defend the difference principle. (Chapter 6) Multiculturalism The view that cultural diversity should be recognised and accommodated, sometimes through group-differentiated rights. (Chapters 9 and 12)

docs.title: N–R
docs.text: Nation A large group of people who see themselves as sharing a common identity and political destiny, usually seeking self-government. (Chapter 9) Negative liberty Freedom as the absence of deliberate interference by other people. (Chapter 4) Normative claim A claim about what ought to be the case, which needs an argument about values. (Chapter 1) Original position Rawls's hypothetical situation in which parties behind a veil of ignorance choose principles of justice. (Chapter 6) Paternalism Interference with a person's liberty for his or her own good; soft paternalism checks that choices are informed and voluntary, hard paternalism overrides them. (Chapter 4) Pluralism Several distinct ideas: the dispersal of authority among associations (pluralist theory of sovereignty), competition among groups (pluralist democracy), and the existence of many irreducible values (value pluralism). (Chapters 2, 4 and 8) Political obligation The moral duty, if any, to obey the law of one's state because it is the law. (Chapter 3) Positive liberty Freedom as self-mastery or self-government. (Chapter 4) Power The capacity to bring about outcomes, especially to get others to do what they would not otherwise do; Lukes described three dimensions. (Chapter 3) Primary goods In Rawls, goods any rational person wants whatever else they want: rights and liberties, opportunities, income and wealth, and the social bases of self-respect. (Chapter 6) Principled distance Bhargava's description of the Indian model of secularism: no established religion, with flexible engagement with religions guided by liberty and equality. (Chapter 10) Prioritarianism The view that benefits matter more the worse off the person who receives them. (Chapter 5) Reflective equilibrium The method of testing principles against considered judgements about cases and revising each until they cohere. (Chapter 1) Responsibility to protect The doctrine, endorsed by the UN in 2005, that states must protect their populations from mass atrocities and that the international community may act collectively when they manifestly fail. (Chapter 14) Right A justified entitlement that belongs to a holder, imposes duties on others and carries special weight. (Chapter 7)

docs.title: S–Z
docs.text: Saptāṅga The seven limbs of the state in the Arthaśāstra: ruler, ministers, territory and people, fort, treasury, army and ally. (Chapter 13) Sarvodaya "The welfare of all": Gandhi's ideal of a society serving the good of every person, including the least. (Chapter 13) Satyagraha "Truth-force": Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance that seeks to convert the opponent through willing self-suffering. (Chapter 13) Secularism The political doctrine that the state should not be governed by or identified with any religion, and that citizens' rights should not depend on religion. (Chapter 10) Self-determination The principle that a people has the right to decide its own political status. (Chapter 9) Social contract The idea that political authority is justified by the actual or hypothetical agreement of those subject to it. (Chapter 2) Socialism A family of ideologies valuing community, equality, need and, in many versions, common ownership. (Chapter 11) Sovereignty Supreme authority: internal (over everyone within the territory) and external (independence from other states); legal, political or popular. (Chapter 2) State In Weber's definition, a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory. (Chapter 2) Sufficientarianism The view that what matters is that everyone has enough, not that everyone has the same. (Chapter 5) Surplus value In Marx, the value produced by workers beyond the value of their wages, appropriated as profit. (Chapter 11) Swaraj Self-rule; for Gandhi both individual self-control and collective self-government. (Chapter 13) Tyranny of the majority The oppression of minorities or dissenters by a majority, through law or social pressure (Tocqueville, Mill). (Chapters 4 and 8) Universal Declaration of Human Rights The declaration of 30 articles adopted by the UN General Assembly on 10 December 1948. (Chapter 14) Utilitarianism The theory that the right action or policy is the one that produces the greatest total happiness or well-being. (Chapter 6) Veil of ignorance In Rawls's original position, the restriction that prevents the parties from knowing their own place in society, talents or conception of the good. (Chapter 6) Will theory of rights The view that rights give their holders control over the duties of others. (Chapter 7)

docs.title: Chapter 13: Indian Political Thought
docs.text:
Kauṭilya, Gandhi, Ambedkar, Nehru, Tagore and the Indian conversation about power and justice

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • describe the main themes of ancient Indian political thought: dharma, rājadharma, daṇḍa and early ideas of kingship by agreement;
  • explain Kauṭilya's theory of the state in the Arthaśāstra: the seven limbs (saptāṅga), the maṇḍala theory and the four means (upāya), and the debate about its date and character;
  • explain Gandhi's ideas of swaraj, satyagraha, ahiṃsā, sarvodaya, trusteeship and decentralisation, with criticisms;
  • explain Ambedkar's critique of caste, his idea of social democracy and constitutional morality, and his conversion to Buddhism, with criticisms;
  • explain Nehru's ideas of democracy, secularism, planning, non-alignment and scientific temper, with criticisms;
  • explain Tagore's humanism, his critique of nationalism and his educational ideas;
  • place other modern Indian thinkers on the map of ideas.

docs.title: 13.1 An Indian conversation
docs.text:
Indian thinkers have reflected on power, order and justice for well over two thousand years. Their writings answer the same basic questions as those of other traditions (Chapter 1): what the purpose of government is, what limits a ruler, how a society of many groups can live together, and when resistance is justified. They also bring distinctive concepts, and the modern thinkers in this chapter worked in a distinctive situation: a society of great religious, linguistic and caste diversity, under colonial rule, seeking both freedom from foreign domination and freedom from internal hierarchies.

This chapter treats each thinker fairly: it sets out what each argued in their own terms, and then the main criticisms made by others. The thinkers often disagreed sharply with one another, and their disagreements are among the most illuminating debates in modern political thought.

Figure 13.1 A timeline of Indian political thought. A timeline of Indian political thought. Ancient: Vedic assemblies, the dharmaśāstras and the Arthaśāstra attributed to Kauṭilya. Nineteenth century: Rammohun Roy, Jyotirao and Savitribai Phule, Pandita Ramabai. Twentieth century: Tagore (1861–1941), Gandhi (1869–1948), Nehru (1889–1964) and Ambedkar (1891–1956), with the Constitution of 1950.

docs.title: Dharma, daṇḍa and rājadharma
docs.text:
Three concepts run through ancient Indian political thought.

  • Dharma has many meanings: cosmic order, moral law, duty and righteous conduct. Each person had duties according to their stage of life and, in the brahmanical texts, their varṇa (social order). Government was expected to uphold dharma.
  • Daṇḍa literally means "rod" or "staff" and stands for coercive authority and punishment. Without daṇḍa, many texts warn, society would fall into mātsya-nyāya, the "law of the fishes", in which the big fish eat the small. This is an Indian counterpart to the Hobbesian state of nature (Chapter 2).
  • Rājadharma is the duty of the king: to protect his subjects, maintain order, administer justice impartially, and promote their welfare. The king was not above dharma; a king who failed in his duty could be condemned, and some texts even justify resistance to a tyrant.

The dharmaśāstra texts, of which the Manusmṛti is the best known, set out law and the duties of the king within a hierarchical social order. They have been sharply criticised, by Ambedkar among many others, for sanctioning the caste hierarchy and the subordination of women.

docs.title: Assemblies and kingship by agreement
docs.text: The Vedic texts mention assemblies called the sabhā and samiti, whose exact composition and powers are debated by historians. Between about the sixth and fourth centuries BCE, Buddhist and other sources describe gaṇa-saṅghas: polities governed by assemblies of members of ruling clans rather than by a single king. Buddhist texts also contain an early contractual account of kingship: in the Aggañña Sutta, when people's growing greed leads to theft and disorder, they choose from among themselves a person to maintain order in return for a share of the harvest. He is called Mahāsammata, "the great elect". Historians caution against reading modern democracy into these sources, but they show that the idea of authority grounded in agreement was not foreign to Indian thought.

docs.title: The text and its date
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra ("the science of material well-being" or "of polity") is a long Sanskrit treatise on statecraft in fifteen books. Tradition attributes it to Kauṭilya, identified with Cāṇakya, the minister of Candragupta Maurya, founder of the Mauryan empire in the late fourth century BCE. The text was lost to modern scholarship until a manuscript reached the Sanskrit scholar R. Shamasastry, who published it in 1909 and an English translation in 1915.

Its date is debated. Many scholars, including Thomas Trautmann and Patrick Olivelle, have argued on linguistic and historical grounds that the text as we have it was compiled and revised over a long period, probably between the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE, drawing on older material and earlier schools of statecraft that it often cites. Others defend a closer link with the Mauryan period. What is not in doubt is that the Arthaśāstra is the most systematic ancient Indian work on government.

docs.title: Artha and the purposes of the state
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra treats artha (material well-being, wealth and power) as the foundation on which dharma and kāma (pleasure) depend. Its subject is how a king acquires, protects and expands territory, and how he governs it for the welfare of his subjects. The science of government is daṇḍanīti, the science of the rod: the right use of coercion, neither too harsh nor too mild, so that subjects are protected and order maintained.

The text insists that the king's own good depends on that of his people. In Shamasastry's translation: "In the happiness of his subjects lies his happiness; in their welfare his welfare." The king is to be disciplined, educated, and constantly active; a large part of the text describes his daily timetable and his duty to hear the complaints of subjects.

docs.title: The seven limbs of the state (saptāṅga)
docs.text:
Book 6 describes the state as having seven limbs (aṅga), or constituent elements, an organic conception in which the health of the whole depends on each part.

Figure 13.2 The seven limbs of the state (saptāṅga). Seven limbs of the state in the Arthaśāstra arranged in a circle: svāmin (the ruler), amātya (ministers and officials), janapada (territory and people), durga (fortified city), kośa (treasury), daṇḍa (army and coercive force) and mitra (ally). Each is described in a short phrase. Limb Meaning Comparison with modern elements of the state Svāmin The ruler or king Government (the executive) Amātya Ministers and officials Bureaucracy Janapada Territory with its people Territory and population Durga Fortified city or fort Defence installations, the capital Kośa Treasury Public finance Daṇḍa Army; coercive force Armed forces and police Mitra Ally Foreign relations

Table 13.1. The seven limbs of the state.

The list is often compared with the modern elements of the state (Chapter 2). Interestingly, it includes allies, recognising that a state exists among other states, and it does not include an abstract idea of sovereignty separate from the ruler.

docs.title: The maṇḍala theory and foreign policy
docs.text:
The maṇḍala (circle) theory describes a king's international environment as concentric circles of states. At the centre is the vijigīṣu, the king who seeks to conquer or expand. His immediate neighbour is his natural enemy (ari); the state beyond the enemy is his natural ally (mitra), since it shares an enemy; beyond that lie the enemy's ally, and so on. The theory also considers a middle king (madhyama) and a neutral, more powerful king (udāsīna). The underlying principle, sometimes summarised as "the enemy of my enemy is my friend", is a realist analysis of the balance of power.

The text also describes six policies (ṣāḍguṇya) for relations with other states: peace (sandhi), war (vigraha), remaining stationary (āsana), marching (yāna), seeking shelter with another (saṃśraya) and the dual policy of peace with one and war with another (dvaidhībhāva), chosen according to whether the king is stronger, equal or weaker.

docs.title: The four means (upāya)
docs.text: To deal with opponents, the Arthaśāstra lists four means, in an order commonly read as from mildest to harshest: sāma (conciliation, persuasion), dāna (gifts, concessions), bheda (sowing dissension, dividing opponents) and daṇḍa (force). The text also describes in detail a system of spies and secret agents.

docs.title: Interpretation and criticism
docs.text:
Because of its frank discussion of espionage, deception and the use of force, Kauṭilya is often compared with Machiavelli and called a realist. Max Weber remarked that, compared with the Arthaśāstra, Machiavelli's The Prince is harmless. But the comparison can mislead. The Arthaśāstra also gives detailed attention to welfare, administration, justice, regulation of trade and labour, care for the vulnerable, and the moral education and self-discipline of the ruler, and it places statecraft within a framework in which dharma remains important. Critics have objected to its acceptance of deception and secret killings as tools of state, and to its assumption of a hierarchical social order; admirers point to its sophisticated analysis of administration and of the relations between states.

Key idea

The Arthaśāstra sees the state as an organism of seven limbs, government as the disciplined use of daṇḍa for the protection and welfare of subjects, and foreign policy as the management of a circle (maṇḍala) of friends and enemies by four means and six policies.

docs.title: 13.4 The nineteenth-century awakening
docs.text: Under colonial rule, Indian thinkers responded to Western ideas while re-examining their own traditions. Raja Rammohun Roy (1772–1833) campaigned against sati and for press freedom and modern education, and founded the Brahmo Samaj (1828). Jyotirao Phule (1827–1890), in Gulamgiri (Slavery, 1873), attacked caste hierarchy and brahmanical dominance, and with Savitribai Phule founded schools for girls and for children of oppressed castes. Swami Vivekananda (1863–1902) combined a universalist interpretation of Vedānta with a call for service to the poor and national regeneration. Early nationalists such as Dadabhai Naoroji analysed the "drain of wealth" from India to Britain. By the early twentieth century the national movement contained moderates who sought reform through constitutional means and extremists such as Bal Gangadhar Tilak, who demanded swaraj as a birthright.

docs.title: Life and method
docs.text: Gandhi trained as a lawyer in London, worked in South Africa from 1893 to 1914, where he developed his method of non-violent resistance against racial discrimination, and returned to India to lead the national movement. Among his campaigns were Champaran (1917), the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22), the Salt March and civil disobedience (1930), and the Quit India Movement (1942). He wrote extensively, above all in his journals and in Hind Swaraj (1909), a short dialogue that contains the core of his political thought. He was assassinated in January 1948.

docs.title: Swaraj
docs.text: Swaraj means self-rule. For Gandhi it meant much more than political independence. In Hind Swaraj he argued that if Indians merely replaced English rulers with Indian ones while keeping the same institutions, they would have "English rule without the Englishman". True swaraj is self-rule in two senses: individual self-control, the mastery of one's desires, and collective self-government by self-reliant communities. It is a moral as well as political ideal.

docs.title: Critique of modern civilisation
docs.text: Hind Swaraj contains a radical critique of modern industrial civilisation, which Gandhi saw as driven by the multiplication of wants, material greed and the worship of the machine. Railways, lawyers and doctors, as institutions of modernity, came in for criticism. Gandhi did not reject all technology, but he insisted that machines should serve human beings rather than displace them, and favoured simple living and handicrafts, symbolised by the spinning wheel (charkha) and hand-spun cloth (khadi).

docs.title: Satyagraha and ahiṃsā
docs.text: Satyagraha ("holding firmly to truth" or "truth-force") is Gandhi's method of resisting injustice. Its basis is ahiṃsā, non-violence, understood not merely as refraining from violence but as active love, including love for the opponent. The satyagrahi seeks to convert the opponent, not to defeat him, by appealing to his conscience through willing self-suffering, and must be prepared to accept the consequences of disobedience. Gandhi distinguished satyagraha from passive resistance, which he saw as a weapon of the weak that does not exclude hatred. Its methods included non-cooperation, civil disobedience, strikes, boycotts and fasting. Gandhi's view of the relation between means and ends was central: impure means, he held, corrupt the ends they serve, so good ends must be pursued only by good means.

docs.title: Sarvodaya, trusteeship and decentralisation
docs.text:
• Sarvodaya ("the welfare of all") was the title of Gandhi's Gujarati paraphrase (1908) of John Ruskin's Unto This Last. It expresses the principle that the good of the individual is contained in the good of all, that all work has equal value, and that the life of labour is the life worth living. Unlike utilitarianism's "greatest good of the greatest number", sarvodaya aims at the good of all, including the least.
  • Trusteeship was Gandhi's answer to economic inequality. The wealthy should regard their surplus wealth as held in trust for society and use it for the common good. He hoped to achieve this by persuasion, but accepted that the state might regulate it.
  • Decentralisation and gram swaraj. Gandhi envisaged India as a federation of largely self-sufficient, self-governing village republics, with power flowing upward from the village rather than down from the centre, an image he described as an "oceanic circle" rather than a pyramid. He was suspicious of the centralised state, which he saw as violence in concentrated form, and described himself at times as a philosophical anarchist whose ideal was a society that needed little government.

docs.title: Religion, caste and untouchability
docs.text: Gandhi was a deeply religious Hindu who held that all religions are true and all imperfect, and who worked throughout his life for Hindu–Muslim unity. He campaigned against untouchability, which he called a sin, calling the communities subjected to it Harijan ("people of God"), a name later rejected by many Dalits as patronising. His views on caste changed over his life: in earlier writings he defended an idealised varṇa system of hereditary occupations without hierarchy, while opposing untouchability; later he became more critical of caste restrictions.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text:
• Ambedkar argued that Gandhi's defence of varṇa and his opposition to separate electorates for the depressed classes in 1932 (which led to the Poona Pact, providing instead for reserved seats in joint electorates) reflected a reformist paternalism that left caste intact. Calling for a change of heart among caste Hindus, he argued, was no substitute for legal rights and political power for the oppressed.
  • Modernisers, including Nehru, regarded Gandhi's critique of industrial civilisation and his idealisation of village life as unrealistic for a poor country that needed industry, science and modern institutions.
  • Marxists argued that trusteeship left property relations untouched and relied on the goodwill of the rich.
  • Critics questioned whether non-violence could succeed against opponents without a conscience to appeal to, and whether it was suitable for defending a state.
  • Feminist scholars have debated Gandhi's legacy: he drew women into public political life in large numbers, but also idealised women's self-sacrifice and held views on sexuality that many find troubling.

Gandhi's admirers reply that his ideas of non-violent resistance, means and ends, and decentralised self-government have influenced movements across the world, including the American civil rights movement, and that his critique of consumerism and centralisation has gained relevance with environmental concerns.

docs.title: Life
docs.text: Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar was born into a family of the Mahar community, which was treated as untouchable. He experienced caste discrimination throughout his education, yet earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics and qualified as a barrister. He led movements for the rights of the depressed classes, such as the Mahad satyagraha (1927) to assert the right to draw water from a public tank, founded political parties, served as Labour Member in the Viceroy's Executive Council, became the first Law Minister of independent India, and chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly. In 1956, shortly before his death, he converted to Buddhism with a very large number of followers in Nagpur.

docs.title: The critique of caste
docs.text:
In Annihilation of Caste (1936), a speech written for an anti-caste conference in Lahore but never delivered because the organisers objected to its content, Ambedkar argued that caste is not merely a division of labour but a division of labourers, a hierarchy imposed by birth that prevents people from choosing occupations according to their abilities. Caste destroys public spirit and the sense of community, since it makes people loyal to their caste rather than to the whole society. Because caste is sanctioned by religious texts that people regard as sacred, he argued, it cannot be abolished without challenging the authority of those texts. Reform of untouchability alone is insufficient; what is needed is the annihilation of the caste system.

Ambedkar's ideal society was one based on liberty, equality and fraternity, which he said he derived not from the French Revolution but from the teachings of the Buddha. Fraternity, the sense of common brotherhood, was in his view the foundation of the other two; without it, liberty and equality would be no deeper than coats of paint.

docs.title: Social democracy and constitutional morality
docs.text:
For Ambedkar, democracy was not merely a form of government but a mode of associated living. Political democracy (one person, one vote) cannot last unless there lies at its base social democracy, a way of life that recognises liberty, equality and fraternity as principles of life. In his final speech to the Constituent Assembly on 25 November 1949 he warned:

B. R. Ambedkar, Constituent Assembly, 25 November 1949

"On the 26th of January 1950, we are going to enter into a life of contradictions. In politics we will have equality and in social and economic life we will have inequality."

In the same speech he gave three warnings: that once constitutional methods were available, methods such as civil disobedience and satyagraha should be abandoned as the "grammar of anarchy"; that citizens should not lay their liberties at the feet of even a great man, since in politics hero-worship is a sure road to degradation and eventual dictatorship; and that political democracy must be made a social democracy.

Ambedkar also stressed constitutional morality, a phrase he took from the historian George Grote: a paramount reverence for the forms of the constitution, combined with freedom of criticism and restraint in the use of power. Constitutional morality, he observed, is not a natural sentiment; it has to be cultivated. He argued that a constitution's success depends on the spirit of those who work it.

docs.title: State socialism and rights
docs.text: In States and Minorities (1947), a memorandum submitted to the Constituent Assembly, Ambedkar proposed state socialism: state ownership of key industries and agricultural land, to be written into the constitution so that it could not be undone by ordinary legislative majorities. Though not adopted in this form, the proposal shows his concern that formal rights mean little without economic security. He favoured strong safeguards for minorities and for Scheduled Castes, including reserved representation, and saw the state and the law as instruments of social transformation.

docs.title: Buddhism
docs.text: After decades of struggle, Ambedkar announced in 1935 that although he had been born a Hindu he would not die one. He studied many religions and chose Buddhism, which he interpreted as a rational, ethical and egalitarian faith centred on human dignity and social justice, in The Buddha and His Dhamma (published 1957). His conversion in 1956 inspired a large Buddhist movement among Dalits.

docs.title: Criticisms and assessment
docs.text:
• Gandhi replied to Annihilation of Caste by defending varṇa, purged of hierarchy, as distinct from caste, and argued that the scriptures should be judged by the conduct of their best exponents; Ambedkar answered that this ideal had never existed in practice.
  • Some critics argued that Ambedkar's emphasis on separate political safeguards for the depressed classes risked dividing the national movement; his defenders reply that the national movement had too often subordinated the interests of the oppressed to those of caste elites.
  • His warning against the "grammar of anarchy" is debated by those who think non-violent protest remains important in a constitutional democracy.
  • Others have asked whether his reliance on the state and law to transform society underestimates the persistence of social prejudice, a concern he himself shared.

Ambedkar is now widely recognised as one of the most important political thinkers of modern India, whose analysis of the relation between political, social and economic democracy has influence far beyond India.

docs.title: Life and writings
docs.text: Jawaharlal Nehru, educated at Harrow, Cambridge and the Inner Temple, became one of the leaders of the national movement and a close associate of Gandhi, and served as the first Prime Minister of India from 1947 until his death in 1964. His major writings, mostly composed in prison, include Glimpses of World History (1934), An Autobiography (1936) and The Discovery of India (1946). His speech on the eve of independence, on the night of 14–15 August 1947, is remembered for the phrase "tryst with destiny".

docs.title: Main ideas
docs.text:
• Democracy. Nehru was committed to parliamentary democracy, universal adult franchise, civil liberties and the rule of law, and to building institutions such as a free press, an independent judiciary and regular elections.
  • Secularism. For Nehru, secularism meant a state that treats all religions equally and does not identify with any, and a public life guided by reason. He saw communalism of all kinds as a threat to Indian unity. The Discovery of India presents India as a palimpsest on which successive cultures had written without erasing what came before: a unity built from diversity.
  • Socialism and planning. Nehru was influenced by Fabian socialism and impressed by Soviet economic planning, while rejecting its authoritarianism. He advocated a mixed economy with a leading role for the public sector in heavy industry and infrastructure, and economic planning through the Planning Commission (1950) and the Five-Year Plans, with the aim of rapid industrialisation and a reduction of poverty and inequality, by democratic means.
  • Scientific temper. Nehru wanted Indians to adopt a scientific temper, an attitude of inquiry, openness to evidence and rejection of dogma and superstition, which he discussed in The Discovery of India. He promoted scientific and technical institutions.
  • Internationalism and non-alignment. Nehru opposed colonialism and racial discrimination worldwide and refused to join either bloc in the Cold War. Non-alignment, which he helped to develop with leaders of other newly independent states, meant independence of judgement in foreign policy, not neutrality on every issue. With China he agreed the Panchsheel (five principles of peaceful coexistence) in 1954.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text:
• Economic policy. Critics argue that the emphasis on central planning and the public sector led to inefficiency and what was later called the "licence raj", slowing growth; defenders reply that it built a base of heavy industry, infrastructure and scientific capacity in a poor country with little private capital.
  • Gandhian critics argued that Nehru's large-scale industrialisation abandoned Gandhi's vision of decentralised village development.
  • Foreign policy. The war with China in 1962 led critics to question the realism of his foreign policy.
  • Secularism. Nehruvian secularism has been criticised from different directions: by some for being imposed by a Westernised elite and insufficiently rooted in Indian religious traditions (Chapter 10), by others for being applied inconsistently.
  • Centralisation. Some argue that his era concentrated power in the central government and in the dominant party.

docs.title: Life
docs.text: Rabindranath Tagore, poet, novelist, composer, painter and educator, was the first non-European to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature (1913), largely for the English version of Gitanjali. He composed the songs that became the national anthems of India and Bangladesh. He took part in the protests against the partition of Bengal in 1905 but withdrew when the Swadeshi movement turned to violence and coercion. He renounced his British knighthood in protest against the massacre at Jallianwala Bagh in 1919.

docs.title: Humanism and the critique of nationalism
docs.text:
Tagore's political thought centres on universal humanism: the belief that the highest truth is the unity of all humanity, and that cultures should meet in mutual respect and learning. His critique of the Nation as an organisation of power and commerce (Chapter 9) followed from this: aggressive nationalism divides humanity and makes people instruments of the state. His novel Ghare Baire (The Home and the World, 1916) dramatises the dangers of a nationalism that becomes intolerant and coercive.

One of his best-known poems, from Gitanjali, expresses his vision of freedom:

Rabindranath Tagore, Gitanjali (English version, 1912), poem 35

"Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls ... Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake."

docs.title: Education
docs.text: Tagore believed that education should develop the whole person in freedom and in harmony with nature and with other cultures, not drill pupils in rote learning for examinations. He founded a school at Santiniketan in 1901 and the university Visva-Bharati in 1921, whose motto (from a Sanskrit text) expresses the ideal of a place where the whole world meets in a single nest.

docs.title: Tagore and Gandhi
docs.text: Tagore and Gandhi admired each other (Tagore is often credited with popularising the title Mahatma for Gandhi), but they disagreed openly. In 1921 Tagore questioned the Non-Cooperation Movement, the burning of foreign cloth and the cult of the charkha, warning that they appealed to emotion rather than reason, encouraged a narrow rejection of the West and demanded uniform obedience. Gandhi replied that non-cooperation was not hostility to the West but refusal to cooperate with evil, and that the spinning wheel was a means of livelihood and self-reliance for the poor. The exchange is a classic debate about nationalism, reason and mass politics.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text:
Critics, including some contemporaries in the national movement, regarded Tagore's universalism as idealistic and politically ineffective in the face of colonial rule, and his aristocratic background as distancing him from mass politics. Admirers reply that his warnings against intolerant nationalism, and his insistence on freedom of mind, have lasting value.

docs.title: 13.9 Other voices
docs.text:
Modern Indian political thought is much wider than these four thinkers. A brief map, stated neutrally:

  • Aurobindo Ghose (1872–1950) moved from revolutionary nationalism to a spiritual philosophy of human evolution.
  • V. D. Savarkar (1883–1966) formulated the idea of Hindutva in Essentials of Hindutva (1923), defining Indian nationhood in terms of a shared Hindu cultural identity; supporters see it as cultural nationalism, critics as exclusive of religious minorities.
  • Muhammad Iqbal (1877–1938), poet and philosopher, developed ideas of Muslim selfhood and community that influenced the demand for a separate homeland.
  • E. V. Ramasamy "Periyar" (1879–1973) led the Self-Respect Movement from 1925 against caste, brahmanical dominance and religious orthodoxy, and for rationalism and women's rights.
  • M. N. Roy (1887–1954) moved from communism to radical humanism, emphasising individual freedom and rationalism.
  • Ram Manohar Lohia (1910–1967) developed a socialism attentive to caste and gender, and Jayaprakash Narayan (1902–1979) called in the 1970s for "total revolution", a moral, social and political transformation.

Worked example 13.1: Four thinkers, one question

Question. How should a newly independent India deal with the poverty of its villages?

Gandhi would answer: rebuild village self-reliance through handicrafts, khadi, local self-government and trusteeship, and limit large-scale industry that displaces labour.

Nehru would answer: plan for rapid industrialisation, build dams, steel plants and scientific institutions, and use a mixed economy to raise national income and reduce poverty.

Ambedkar would answer: poverty in villages is bound up with caste; the village, which he described in the Constituent Assembly as a sink of localism and a den of ignorance, is not a model to be idealised. Secure legal rights, land reform, state ownership of key resources, education and urban opportunity for the oppressed.

Tagore would answer: revive village life through education, cooperation and the creative participation of villagers themselves, as he attempted in his rural reconstruction work at Sriniketan.

The disagreement shows how different values (self-reliance, development, equality, creative freedom) lead to different policies, and why the Constitution of India contains elements of several visions, such as panchayats, planning, Fundamental Rights and the abolition of untouchability.

Summary

  • Ancient Indian thought developed the concepts of dharma, daṇḍa and rājadharma, the fear of mātsya-nyāya, assemblies and gaṇa-saṅghas, and the Buddhist story of Mahāsammata, a ruler chosen by agreement.
  • The Arthaśāstra, attributed to Kauṭilya and probably compiled over several centuries, describes the state's seven limbs, the science of daṇḍanīti, the maṇḍala theory of foreign relations, six policies and four means (sāma, dāna, bheda, daṇḍa), with a strong concern for the welfare of subjects.
  • Gandhi's thought centres on swaraj as self-rule, satyagraha founded on ahiṃsā, the unity of means and ends, sarvodaya, trusteeship and decentralised village self-government, together with a critique of modern civilisation; he was criticised by Ambedkar, modernisers and Marxists.
  • Ambedkar argued for the annihilation of caste, for liberty, equality and fraternity, for social and economic democracy as the base of political democracy, and for constitutional morality; he converted to Buddhism in 1956.
  • Nehru stood for parliamentary democracy, secularism, a planned mixed economy, scientific temper and non-alignment; critics question his economic and foreign policies.
  • Tagore's universal humanism led him to criticise aggressive nationalism and rote education; his debate with Gandhi in 1921 is a classic exchange on nationalism and reason.

docs.title: 13.10 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

What is mātsya-nyāya, and how does it compare with Hobbes's state of nature?

Answer

Mātsya-nyāya, "the law of the fishes", is the condition in which, without daṇḍa (coercive authority), the strong devour the weak as big fish eat small ones. Like Hobbes's state of nature, it describes the disorder that would exist without government and justifies coercive authority as the remedy. Unlike Hobbes's account, it appears within a framework where the ruler remains bound by dharma.

Exercise 2

Name the seven limbs of the state in the Arthaśāstra and give a modern equivalent for any three.

Answer

Svāmin (ruler), amātya (ministers), janapada (territory and people), durga (fort), kośa (treasury), daṇḍa (army, coercive force), mitra (ally). Modern equivalents: svāmin = executive government; amātya = bureaucracy; janapada = territory and population; kośa = public finance; daṇḍa = armed forces and police; mitra = foreign relations.

Exercise 3

Explain the maṇḍala theory and the four upāya.

Answer

The maṇḍala theory places the expanding king (vijigīṣu) at the centre of circles of states: his neighbour is a natural enemy, the state beyond the neighbour a natural ally, and so on, with middle and neutral kings also considered. The four upāya for dealing with others are sāma (conciliation), dāna (gifts), bheda (sowing dissension) and daṇḍa (force).

Exercise 4

Why did Gandhi say that Indians might gain "English rule without the Englishman"? What did he mean by swaraj instead?

Answer

He meant that if Indians merely replaced British rulers while keeping the same institutions and values of modern industrial civilisation, India would not be truly free. Swaraj for Gandhi meant self-rule in two senses: individual self-control over one's desires, and collective self-government by self-reliant, decentralised communities, a moral as well as political freedom.

Exercise 5

How did Ambedkar distinguish political democracy from social democracy, and why did he think the first depended on the second?

Answer

Political democracy is one person, one vote, one value; social democracy is a way of life that recognises liberty, equality and fraternity in social relations. Ambedkar argued that political equality could not last amid social and economic inequality, the "life of contradictions" he described on 25 November 1949: those denied equality would eventually blow up the structure of political democracy.

Exercise 6

What did Ambedkar mean by "constitutional morality"?

Answer

Borrowing from George Grote, he meant a paramount reverence for the forms of the constitution, combined with freedom to criticise those in power and restraint in the use of power. He stressed that it is not natural but must be cultivated, and that a constitution's success depends on those who work it.

Exercise 7

Summarise the debate between Tagore and Gandhi in 1921.

Answer

Tagore questioned the Non-Cooperation Movement, the burning of foreign cloth and the cult of the charkha, arguing that they appealed to emotion over reason, encouraged a narrow rejection of the West and demanded uniform obedience. Gandhi replied that non-cooperation was refusal to cooperate with evil, not hostility to the West, and that the spinning wheel offered livelihood and self-reliance to the poor.

Exercise 8

State two features of Nehru's political thought and one criticism of each.

Answer

Any two: (1) Planning and a mixed economy: criticised for inefficiency and the "licence raj". (2) Secularism: criticised as elite-driven or inconsistently applied. (3) Non-alignment: criticised for lack of realism, especially after 1962. (4) Scientific temper and industrialisation: criticised by Gandhians for abandoning village-based development.

docs.title: Chapter 6: Justice
docs.text:
From Plato to Rawls, Nozick and Sen: what a just society owes its members

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • distinguish distributive, corrective, procedural and social justice;
  • outline the classical ideas of justice of Plato and Aristotle and the utilitarian approach, with its main criticisms;
  • explain Rawls's original position, the veil of ignorance and his two principles of justice, and apply the difference principle;
  • explain Nozick's entitlement theory, the Wilt Chamberlain argument and his defence of the minimal state;
  • explain Sen's capability approach and his distinction between transcendental and comparative theories of justice;
  • state the communitarian and feminist criticisms of liberal theories of justice.

docs.title: 6.1 What is justice about?
docs.text:
Justice is often called the first virtue of social institutions. When we call a law, a policy or a social arrangement unjust, we mean more than that it is unwise or unkind: we mean that it wrongs someone, that it fails to give people what they are due. The ancient Roman jurists defined justice as the constant and perpetual will to render to each his due. The difficulty, of course, is to say what each person is due.

It helps to distinguish several kinds of justice.

Kind Question Example Distributive justice How should benefits and burdens be shared among members of a society? Who should pay how much tax; who should receive health care Corrective (rectificatory) justice How should a wrong be put right? Compensation for damage; restitution of stolen property Retributive justice What punishment does wrongdoing deserve? Sentencing criminals Procedural justice Are the procedures by which decisions are made fair? A fair trial; a fair election; a fair competition Social justice Is the overall structure of society, including its distribution of wealth, status and opportunity, fair? Policies against poverty, caste and gender discrimination

Table 6.1. Kinds of justice.

This chapter is mainly about distributive and social justice: the justice of the basic arrangements of society that shape people's prospects from birth.

docs.title: Procedural and outcome-based justice
docs.text: Rawls drew a helpful distinction. In perfect procedural justice, there is an independent standard of a fair outcome and a procedure guaranteed to reach it: to divide a cake equally, let the person who cuts it take the last piece. In imperfect procedural justice, there is an independent standard but no procedure guaranteed to reach it: a criminal trial aims to convict all and only the guilty, but sometimes fails. In pure procedural justice, there is no independent standard; whatever results from a fair procedure is fair, as in a fair lottery or a fair bet. Theories of justice differ in how far they treat justice as a matter of fair procedure (Nozick) or of fair outcomes.

docs.title: Plato
docs.text: In the Republic, Plato rejected the view that justice is simply the interest of the stronger (argued by the character Thrasymachus) or a convenient agreement among the weak. He argued that justice in the city, as in the soul, is a kind of harmony: each part does its own proper work. The ideal city has three classes (rulers, auxiliaries who defend it, and producers), corresponding to reason, spirit and appetite in the soul. The city is just when each class performs its function and does not interfere with the others, and when the wise rule. Critics, most famously Karl Popper in The Open Society and Its Enemies (1945), saw in this a blueprint for a rigid, authoritarian society.

docs.title: Aristotle
docs.text: Aristotle distinguished distributive justice, which concerns the division of honours, wealth and other goods among members of a community, from corrective justice, which concerns transactions between individuals and the rectification of wrongs. Distributive justice is proportional: goods should be shared in proportion to merit or desert. Equals should receive equal shares, unequals unequal shares. The difficulty, Aristotle saw, is that people disagree about what counts as merit: democrats say free birth, oligarchs say wealth, aristocrats say virtue. Corrective justice, by contrast, is arithmetical: it restores the balance between the parties whatever their merit.

docs.title: 6.3 Utilitarianism
docs.text:
Utilitarianism holds that the right action or policy is the one that produces the greatest total happiness (or well-being, or preference satisfaction). Its founder, Jeremy Bentham (1748–1832), opened his Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789) with the claim that nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure. J. S. Mill refined the theory, distinguishing higher and lower pleasures. For utilitarians, justice is not a separate value but a name for those rules (such as respecting property and keeping promises) that generally promote utility.

Utilitarianism was a reforming doctrine. It judged laws by their effects on human welfare rather than by tradition or religion, it counted everyone's happiness equally ("everybody to count for one, nobody for more than one", a principle attributed to Bentham), and it supported reforms of the criminal law, the franchise and the treatment of animals.

Its critics raise three main objections.

  • It ignores the separateness of persons. Maximising the total allows great sacrifices by some for larger gains to others. A policy that made a minority very miserable would be justified if it made the majority a little happier, by enough in total. Rawls argued that utilitarianism treats society as if it were one person balancing present against future satisfactions, and so does not take seriously the distinction between persons.
  • It does not protect rights. In principle utilitarianism could justify punishing an innocent person or suppressing an unpopular minority, if that produced more total happiness (Chapter 1, Worked example 1.2).
  • It is indifferent to distribution. Two distributions with the same total are equally good, however unequally the total is shared.

Utilitarians have replies. Rule utilitarians argue that we should follow the rules (including rules protecting rights) whose general acceptance would maximise utility, which would rarely permit punishing the innocent. Utilitarians also point out that money matters less to the rich than to the poor (diminishing marginal utility), so maximising total welfare usually favours redistribution. But the basic objection, that the theory does not treat individuals as having claims that cannot be outweighed by others' gains, motivated the theory that dominated late twentieth-century discussion.

docs.title: 6.4 Rawls: justice as fairness
docs.text: John Rawls (1921–2002) set out his theory in A Theory of Justice (1971) and revised it in later works, including Political Liberalism (1993) and Justice as Fairness: A Restatement (2001). He called it justice as fairness. Its subject is the basic structure of society: the main political, economic and social institutions (the constitution, the legal system, the economy, the family) that distribute rights and duties and shape people's life prospects from the start.

docs.title: Society as a fair system of cooperation
docs.text: Rawls saw society as a cooperative venture for mutual advantage among free and equal citizens. Cooperation produces benefits that no one could achieve alone, and the question is how to divide them. Since people's starting positions in society are largely a matter of luck (the family, class and country into which they are born, and the natural talents they happen to have), Rawls argued that these factors, which are "arbitrary from a moral point of view", should not determine people's shares.

docs.title: The original position and the veil of ignorance
docs.text:
To find fair principles, Rawls used a thought experiment in the social contract tradition. Imagine representatives of citizens meeting in an original position to choose the principles that will govern their society. They are rational and mutually disinterested (each wants to do well for the person they represent). Crucially, they choose behind a veil of ignorance: they do not know their own place in society, class or social status, their natural talents and strength, their sex, race or religion, or even their particular idea of what makes a life good. They know general facts about society, economics and psychology.

The veil removes the influence of bias. If you do not know whether you will be rich or poor, a member of the majority religion or of a minority, able-bodied or disabled, you cannot choose principles that favour your own position. The principles chosen will therefore be fair to everyone. The original position is hypothetical: it is a device for testing principles, not a story about how societies began.

The parties choose among primary goods: things that any rational person is presumed to want, whatever else they want, because they are useful for any plan of life. Rawls listed basic rights and liberties, freedom of movement and choice of occupation, powers and prerogatives of offices, income and wealth, and the social bases of self-respect.

Figure 6.1 The original position. A diagram of the original position. On the left, representatives stand behind a curtain labelled the veil of ignorance, which hides their class, talents, sex, race, religion and idea of the good life. They know general facts about society. Arrows lead to the principles they choose: equal basic liberties, fair equality of opportunity and the difference principle.

docs.title: The two principles
docs.text:
Rawls argued that the parties would choose two principles. In plain words, following his later formulation:

  1. The liberty principle. Everyone has an equal right to the most extensive and adequate set of basic liberties that can be secured for all alike. (The basic liberties include political liberty, freedom of speech and assembly, liberty of conscience and freedom of thought, freedom of the person, the right to hold personal property, and freedom from arbitrary arrest.)
  2. Social and economic inequalities are permissible only if they meet two conditions:
    • (a) fair equality of opportunity: the positions and offices to which they are attached are open to all, with genuinely equal chances for people of similar talent and effort; and
    • (b) the difference principle: they work to the greatest benefit of the least advantaged members of society.

The principles are in lexical order: the first principle has priority over the second, and within the second, fair equality of opportunity has priority over the difference principle. Basic liberties may not be traded for economic gains. A society may not deny some citizens the vote or freedom of religion, even if this would make everyone richer.

docs.title: The difference principle
docs.text:
The difference principle is the most distinctive and controversial part of the theory. It does not require equality. It permits inequalities, but only if they work to the advantage of the worst-off group. If paying doctors or entrepreneurs more gives them incentives to work harder or innovate, producing more wealth that raises the position of the least advantaged, the inequality is just. If an inequality benefits the better-off without improving the position of the worst-off, it is unjust.

Why would the parties choose it? Rawls argued that, facing a choice of such importance under deep uncertainty, with no basis for estimating probabilities, and with some possible outcomes intolerable, rational parties would follow the maximin rule: choose the option whose worst outcome is best. Since any of them might turn out to be among the least advantaged, they would want the worst position to be as good as possible.

System Least advantaged Middle Most advantaged Total Strict equality 10 10 10 30 Incentive scheme 14 20 35 69 Laissez-faire 8 25 60 93

Table 6.2. Three economic systems: index of primary goods for three equal social groups.

Worked example 6.1: Applying the difference principle

Situation. A society can adopt one of the three economic systems of Table 6.2. The numbers are the average primary goods (an index) of three social groups of equal size.

Analysis. Utilitarianism (maximising the total) chooses laissez-faire (93). Strict equality chooses equality, though everyone could be better off. The difference principle chooses the incentive scheme: its least advantaged group (14) is better off than in either alternative. The inequality in the incentive scheme is justified because it raises the position of the worst off; the larger inequality of laissez-faire is not, because the worst off do worse (8) than under strict equality.

docs.title: Political liberalism
docs.text: In Political Liberalism (1993) Rawls addressed a problem he had underplayed: modern societies are marked by reasonable pluralism, a diversity of religious, philosophical and moral doctrines held by reasonable people. A just and stable society cannot be founded on any one of them. Rawls argued that justice as fairness should be presented as a political conception that citizens holding different comprehensive doctrines can endorse from within their own views, forming an overlapping consensus. When citizens debate fundamental political questions, they should offer reasons that others could reasonably accept (public reason), not reasons that depend on their own religion alone. Critics ask whether this asks religious citizens to leave their deepest convictions out of politics (Chapter 10).

docs.title: Criticisms of Rawls
docs.text:
• From the libertarian right, Nozick argued that Rawls ignores how holdings came about and violates people's rights over themselves and their property (section 6.5).
  • From the egalitarian left, G. A. Cohen argued that the incentive argument is suspect: if talented people would work just as hard for less pay but demand more, inequality reflects their bargaining power, not a necessity. A just society would require an egalitarian ethos in personal choices, not only just institutions.
  • Communitarians argued that the parties behind the veil are abstract selves without the attachments that make up real people (section 6.7).
  • Feminists argued that Rawls did not apply his principles fully to the family (section 6.7).
  • Sen argued that Rawls's focus on perfectly just institutions and on primary goods is misplaced (section 6.6).
  • Some question maximin itself: rational people might accept a small risk of being slightly worse off for a high chance of being much better off.

Key idea

Rawls asks what principles free and equal people would choose if they did not know their place in society. His answer: equal basic liberties first, then fair equality of opportunity, then the difference principle, which permits inequalities only when they benefit the least advantaged.

docs.title: 6.5 Nozick: entitlement and the minimal state
docs.text: Robert Nozick (1938–2002) replied to Rawls in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974), a defence of libertarianism. He began from the claim that individuals have rights, and that there are things no person or group may do to them without violating their rights. Rights are side constraints: they limit what others, including the state, may do in pursuit of any goal, however good. Each person owns himself: his body, talents and labour. From this Nozick argued that only a minimal state, limited to protecting people against force, theft and fraud and enforcing contracts, can be justified. Any more extensive state violates people's rights.

docs.title: The entitlement theory
docs.text:
Nozick's theory of justice in holdings has three parts.

  1. Justice in acquisition: how people may justly come to own previously unowned things. Nozick followed Locke, who argued that a person who mixes his labour with unowned land makes it his property, provided that "enough, and as good" is left for others (the Lockean proviso). Nozick accepted a weakened version: an acquisition is unjust if it makes others worse off than they would have been if the thing had remained unowned.
  2. Justice in transfer: how people may justly transfer holdings to others, by voluntary exchange, gift or bequest.
  3. Rectification of injustice: how past injustices in acquisition or transfer (theft, fraud, conquest, enslavement) should be corrected.

A distribution is just if everyone is entitled to what they hold under these principles, whatever the resulting pattern. If it arose by just steps from a just situation, it is just, however unequal.

docs.title: Historical and patterned principles
docs.text: Nozick distinguished historical principles, which judge a distribution by how it came about, from end-state or patterned principles, which judge it by its shape at a given moment ("to each according to need", "to each according to merit", "maximise the position of the worst off"). Rawls's difference principle, utilitarianism and most egalitarian principles are patterned. Nozick argued that any patterned principle can be maintained only by continual interference in people's lives.

docs.title: The Wilt Chamberlain argument
docs.text: To illustrate, Nozick asked us to start from any distribution we regard as just; call it D1. Wilt Chamberlain, a famous basketball player of the time, signs a contract under which each spectator at his games drops a small sum into a box for him. Over a season a million people freely do so, and Chamberlain ends up much richer than anyone else, producing a new, unequal distribution D2. Is D2 unjust? Everyone was entitled to their holdings under D1; they chose freely to transfer some of it to Chamberlain; no one else's holdings were affected. Nozick concluded that liberty upsets patterns: to keep any pattern, the state would have to forbid "capitalist acts between consenting adults" or continually take from people what others have freely given them.

docs.title: Taxation
docs.text: Nozick argued that taxation of earnings from labour to fund redistribution is on a par with forced labour. If the state takes the earnings of so many hours of a person's work, it is in effect forcing him to work those hours for others; it makes others partial owners of him. Taxation to fund the minimal state's protective functions is legitimate; taxation for welfare is not.

docs.title: Criticisms of Nozick
docs.text:
• The starting point. The theory needs just original acquisition, but almost all present holdings descend from conquest, enslavement, colonial seizure or fraud somewhere in their history. Nozick admitted that rectification might, in practice, justify substantial redistribution, perhaps even something like the difference principle as a rough rule of thumb, but gave no detailed account.
  • Self-ownership. Critics question whether self-ownership implies full ownership of external resources. G. A. Cohen, in Self-Ownership, Freedom, and Equality (1995), argued that even if people own themselves, the world's resources were originally owned in common or by no one, and appropriating them limits others' freedom.
  • Freedom. A poor person in a libertarian society may have formal rights but few real options. If freedom matters, critics say, it matters for everyone, and a minimal state may leave many people with very little of it.
  • The Chamberlain example. Critics argue that the transfers have effects beyond the parties: Chamberlain's wealth may give him power over others, and spectators did not consent to the resulting inequality of power. Others note that a tax system known in advance is part of the background against which contracts are made.

docs.title: 6.6 Sen: capabilities and realisations
docs.text: Amartya Sen (born 1933), an economist and philosopher who received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1998, developed the capability approach in a series of works, including Commodities and Capabilities (1985), Inequality Reexamined (1992), Development as Freedom (1999) and The Idea of Justice (2009).

docs.title: Functionings and capabilities
docs.text:
• A functioning is something a person does or is: being adequately nourished, being in good health, being literate, taking part in the life of the community, appearing in public without shame.
  • A capability is the real freedom to achieve a combination of functionings: the set of lives a person could actually choose to live.

Sen argued that justice and development should be judged by people's capabilities, not by their income or resources (as in Rawls's primary goods) or by their happiness (as in utilitarianism). Two reasons are central.

  • Conversion factors. People differ greatly in their ability to convert resources into functionings because of personal features (age, disability, pregnancy), environment (climate, disease) and social circumstances (discrimination, public services). Equal incomes can mean very unequal capabilities.
  • Adaptive preferences. People who have lived with deprivation may learn to want little and report contentment. Measuring happiness would then hide their deprivation.

The capability approach influenced the Human Development Index published by the United Nations Development Programme since 1990, which combines indicators of life expectancy, education and income instead of relying on income alone. The philosopher Martha Nussbaum developed a version that lists ten central capabilities (including life, bodily health, bodily integrity, practical reason, affiliation, and control over one's environment) which, she argued, every just constitution should guarantee to every citizen up to a threshold. Sen himself declined to fix a single list, arguing that the selection and weighting of capabilities should be a matter for public reasoning in each society.

docs.title: Transcendental and comparative justice
docs.text:
In The Idea of Justice Sen criticised what he called transcendental institutionalism: the approach of Hobbes, Rousseau, Rawls and others that seeks to identify perfectly just institutions. He favoured a comparative, realisation-focused approach, in the tradition of thinkers such as Adam Smith, Condorcet, Mary Wollstonecraft and Mill, which asks how to make the world less unjust by comparing feasible alternatives and attending to the lives people actually lead. Sen used an analogy from art: knowing which painting is the best in the world does not tell us how to rank two other paintings against each other, and we can compare two paintings without first identifying a perfect one. In the same way, we do not need a theory of perfect justice to know that abolishing slavery or ending famine reduces injustice.

Sen drew on two Sanskrit words from Indian jurisprudence: nīti, organisational propriety and correct rules and institutions, and nyāya, the realised justice of the lives people actually live. He argued that justice must be concerned with nyāya, not only nīti.

Worked example 6.2: Sen's three children and a flute

Situation. Sen's own illustration in The Idea of Justice. Three children, Anne, Bob and Carla, quarrel over a flute. Anne says it should be hers because she is the only one who knows how to play it. Bob says it should be his because he is so poor that he has no toys at all. Carla says it should be hers because she made it, with months of labour.

Analysis. Each claim reflects a serious approach to justice. A utilitarian might give the flute to Anne, who will get the most enjoyment from it. An economic egalitarian might give it to Bob, the worst off. A libertarian, emphasising entitlement to the fruits of one's labour, would give it to Carla. Sen's point is that there may be no single impartial answer that all reasonable people must accept; several principles survive critical scrutiny. Public reasoning may still rank some alternatives, and we can agree on removing obvious injustices without settling every such dispute.

docs.title: Criticisms of Sen
docs.text:
Critics ask how capabilities are to be measured and compared, since they are freedoms rather than observed achievements. Others argue that without a list (like Nussbaum's) the approach is too indeterminate to guide policy, while with a list it risks imposing one view of the good life. Some Rawlsians reply that primary goods are used precisely because they are publicly measurable, and that Rawls's theory can accommodate many of Sen's concerns.

docs.title: Communitarians
docs.text: In the 1980s several philosophers, later grouped together as communitarians, criticised liberal theories of justice. Michael Sandel (Liberalism and the Limits of Justice, 1982) argued that Rawls's parties behind the veil are unencumbered selves, imagined apart from the attachments, loyalties and shared purposes that actually constitute persons; we cannot coherently think of ourselves that way. Alasdair MacIntyre (After Virtue, 1981) argued that moral reasoning makes sense only within traditions and practices. Michael Walzer (Spheres of Justice, 1983) argued that different goods (health care, education, political office, money, love) have different social meanings and should be distributed by different principles; injustice occurs when success in one sphere, typically money, is converted into domination in others. Communitarians do not usually reject liberal rights, but they argue that justice must be rooted in a community's shared understandings and that the common good deserves more weight.

docs.title: Feminists
docs.text:
Susan Moller Okin, in Justice, Gender, and the Family (1989), argued that theories of justice had largely ignored the family, assuming that it is just or that it lies outside the scope of justice. Yet the family is where children first learn (or fail to learn) a sense of justice, and the gendered division of labour within it shapes women's opportunities throughout life: women's greater share of unpaid care work makes them economically vulnerable. Okin argued that Rawls's theory, applied consistently with sex hidden behind the veil, would require a radical transformation of the family. Other feminists, drawing on an ethics of care (associated with Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice, 1982), argued that the language of rights and impartial principles neglects the moral importance of relationships, care and responsibility.

Summary

  • Justice concerns giving people their due; distributive, corrective, retributive, procedural and social justice address different questions.
  • Plato saw justice as each part doing its proper work; Aristotle distinguished proportional distributive justice from arithmetical corrective justice.
  • Utilitarianism maximises total happiness; it is criticised for ignoring the separateness of persons, rights and distribution.
  • Rawls's original position and veil of ignorance lead to two principles in lexical order: equal basic liberties; fair equality of opportunity and the difference principle (inequalities must benefit the least advantaged). Later he developed political liberalism, overlapping consensus and public reason.
  • Nozick's entitlement theory is historical: holdings justly acquired and transferred are just whatever the pattern. Liberty upsets patterns (Wilt Chamberlain); redistributive taxation is on a par with forced labour; only a minimal state is justified.
  • Sen's capability approach judges justice by people's real freedoms to achieve valued functionings, and favours comparative, realisation-focused reasoning (nyāya over nīti). Nussbaum proposed a list of ten central capabilities.
  • Communitarians criticise the unencumbered self and abstract universal principles; feminists criticise the neglect of the family and of care.

docs.title: 6.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Explain the difference between pure and imperfect procedural justice, with an example of each.

Answer

In pure procedural justice there is no independent standard of the right outcome; any outcome of a fair procedure is fair, as in a fair lottery. In imperfect procedural justice there is an independent standard but no procedure guaranteed to achieve it, as in a criminal trial, which aims to convict all and only the guilty but can make mistakes.

Exercise 2

Why does Rawls say that utilitarianism does not take seriously the distinction between persons?

Answer

Utilitarianism adds up everyone's happiness and maximises the total, so one person's loss can be outweighed by others' gains, as if society were a single person trading off present against future satisfactions. But persons are separate: a loss to one is not compensated by a gain to another. Rawls's principles give each person claims (basic liberties, a position as good as possible for the worst off) that cannot be sacrificed for the greater total.

Exercise 3

List four things the parties in the original position do not know, and explain why the veil of ignorance is meant to produce fair principles.

Answer

They do not know (any four): their class or social status, their natural talents and strength, their sex, their race, their religion, their conception of the good. Because they cannot tell which principles would favour themselves, they cannot tailor principles to their own advantage; principles chosen under these conditions are therefore impartial between all positions in society.

Exercise 4

A society can choose between system X (groups have 12, 18 and 30) and system Y (groups have 11, 30 and 50). Which would the difference principle choose? Which would a utilitarian choose?

Answer

The difference principle chooses X, because its least advantaged group (12) is better off than Y's (11). A utilitarian maximising the total chooses Y (total 91, against 60 for X).

Exercise 5

Summarise the Wilt Chamberlain argument and give one objection to it.

Answer

Start from any distribution regarded as just. Many people freely pay a small sum to watch Chamberlain play, and he becomes much richer than others. Since each person was entitled to their holdings and transferred them freely, the new unequal distribution seems just too. So liberty upsets patterns, and maintaining any pattern requires continual interference. Objection: the transfers have effects on third parties, such as the concentration of wealth and power that may disadvantage others who did not consent; also, a tax system known in advance is part of the fair background of all transactions, so taxing Chamberlain does not upset legitimate expectations.

Exercise 6

Explain the difference between a functioning and a capability, and why Sen preferred capabilities to income as a measure of well-being.

Answer

A functioning is an achieved state of doing or being (being nourished, being literate). A capability is the real freedom to achieve such functionings. Sen preferred capabilities because people differ in converting income into functionings (a disabled person needs more income for the same mobility; a person in a disease-prone area needs more for the same health), and because focusing on capabilities respects freedom of choice: a person who fasts by choice is not deprived like one who starves.

Exercise 7

State the communitarian criticism of the "unencumbered self" and Okin's feminist criticism of theories of justice.

Answer

Communitarians (Sandel) argue that Rawls imagines persons as unencumbered selves who choose principles prior to and apart from their attachments, but real persons are partly constituted by their communities, loyalties and shared purposes. Okin argues that theories of justice ignored the family, though it is the first school of justice and its gendered division of labour shapes women's opportunities; a consistent theory of justice must apply to the family.
