docs.title: Chapter 11: Liberalism, Conservatism, Socialism and Marxism
docs.text:
The great ideologies of the modern age: their core ideas, varieties and critics

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • define ideology and explain the origins and limits of the left–right spectrum;
  • state the core values of liberalism and distinguish classical, social and neo-liberalism;
  • state the core ideas of conservatism and distinguish traditional, one-nation and New Right conservatism;
  • explain the main ideas of socialism and its varieties: utopian, Marxist, democratic socialist and social democratic;
  • explain the key concepts of Marxism: historical materialism, class struggle, exploitation, alienation, the state and revolution;
  • state the main criticisms of each ideology fairly.

docs.title: 11.1 What is an ideology?
docs.text:
An ideology is a more or less coherent set of ideas that provides a basis for organised political action. Most ideologies contain three elements:

  • a description of the existing order, its problems and their causes;
  • a vision of a better society;
  • a programme for getting from one to the other.

The word was coined in the 1790s by the French philosopher Antoine Destutt de Tracy, who meant by it a "science of ideas". Marx and Engels gave it a critical meaning: ideology is the set of ideas that serves the interests of the ruling class while presenting them as universal truths, producing what later Marxists called false consciousness. Others have used the word for any closed, dogmatic system of thought, contrasted with pragmatic, open-minded politics. Most political scientists now use it in a neutral sense: every political outlook is an ideology, and the study of ideologies examines how they combine concepts such as liberty, equality and community. The political theorist Michael Freeden described ideologies as distinctive arrangements of political concepts, each giving priority to some and interpreting all of them in its own way.

docs.title: Left and right
docs.text:
The terms "left" and "right" come from the seating of the French National Assembly in 1789: supporters of the king sat on the president's right, supporters of revolution on his left. Today the spectrum is often described like this:

Figure 11.1 The left–right spectrum and a second axis. A horizontal left–right spectrum. On the left are communism and socialism, emphasising equality and collective action; in the centre are social democracy and liberalism; on the right are conservatism and the New Right, emphasising tradition, order or free markets. Below, a second axis from libertarian to authoritarian shows that the left–right line leaves out attitudes to personal freedom and authority.

The single line is a crude simplification. It mixes economic questions (how much should the state redistribute?) with social questions (how much should it enforce traditional values?), and some ideologies, such as anarchism, environmentalism and feminism, do not fit on it at all. Many political scientists add a second axis from libertarian (maximising personal freedom) to authoritarian (emphasising order and authority). Totalitarian regimes of the far left and far right resembled each other in their authoritarianism while differing in economic doctrine.

docs.title: 11.2 Liberalism
docs.text: Liberalism is the ideology of the modern West and has spread far beyond it. It emerged in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries in opposition to absolute monarchy, feudal privilege and religious intolerance.

docs.title: Core values
docs.text:
• The individual. Society consists of individuals, each of equal moral worth, each with his or her own interests and conception of the good. Liberals are suspicious of claims that a community, class or nation has interests superior to those of its members.
  • Liberty. Individuals should be as free as possible, consistent with a like freedom for others. Liberals differ on whether liberty is mainly negative or also positive (Chapter 4).
  • Reason. Human beings are rational and capable of running their own lives. Liberals have faith in progress through reason, debate and education.
  • Equality. Liberals believe in legal and political equality and in equality of opportunity; most do not seek equality of outcome.
  • Toleration and pluralism. A free society contains many beliefs and ways of life, which should be tolerated (Chapter 10).
  • Consent and constitutionalism. Government rests on the consent of the governed and should be limited by a constitution, the rule of law, the separation of powers and protected rights.

docs.title: Classical liberalism
docs.text: Classical liberalism, dominant in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, saw the state as a necessary evil to be kept small. Locke defended natural rights to life, liberty and property; Adam Smith, in The Wealth of Nations (1776), argued that free markets, guided as if by an "invisible hand", tend to promote general prosperity better than state regulation; utilitarians such as Bentham supported free trade and limited government. Classical liberals favoured free trade, free markets, minimal taxation and a state confined to defence, order and a few public works.

docs.title: Social (modern) liberalism
docs.text: By the late nineteenth century industrial capitalism had produced great wealth alongside poverty, slums and insecurity. Social liberals argued that freedom requires more than the absence of interference. T. H. Green defended positive freedom (Chapter 4); L. T. Hobhouse (Liberalism, 1911) argued that the state should secure the conditions for each person's self-development. The economist J. M. Keynes argued in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) that governments could and should manage overall demand to prevent mass unemployment, and William Beveridge's report of 1942 laid the plans for the British welfare state. Social liberalism supported progressive taxation, social insurance, public education and health care, and regulation of markets. Rawls's theory of justice (Chapter 6) is a philosophical statement of this tradition.

docs.title: Neo-liberalism
docs.text: From the 1970s, faced with economic problems in many welfare states, neo-liberals revived classical liberal ideas. Friedrich Hayek (The Road to Serfdom, 1944) argued that central economic planning threatens freedom and that markets coordinate dispersed knowledge better than any planner; Milton Friedman (Capitalism and Freedom, 1962) argued that economic freedom is a condition of political freedom. Neo-liberal policies included privatisation, deregulation, lower taxes, control of inflation and reduced welfare spending. Libertarians such as Nozick (Chapter 6) took the argument further.

docs.title: Criticisms of liberalism
docs.text:
• Conservatives argue that liberalism's abstract individualism and faith in reason neglect tradition, community and human imperfection.
  • Socialists and Marxists argue that liberal freedoms are formal and that liberalism defends capitalist inequality.
  • Communitarians criticise the "unencumbered self" (Chapter 6).
  • Feminists argue that liberalism's division between public and private has shielded injustice within the family (Chapter 12).
  • Critics from postcolonial perspectives note that leading liberals, including Locke and Mill, justified colonial rule, and ask whether liberal universalism has been tied to Western domination.

docs.title: 11.3 Conservatism
docs.text: Conservatism arose as a reaction to the French Revolution and to the rationalism of the Enlightenment. Its founding text is Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790).

docs.title: Core ideas
docs.text:
• Tradition. Institutions and customs that have survived for generations embody accumulated wisdom, tested by experience, that no individual reason could reproduce. Burke described society as a partnership not only among the living, but between those who are living, those who are dead and those who are to be born.
  • Human imperfection. Human beings are limited in their reason and morally fallible. Grand schemes to remake society by abstract principles are likely to fail and to cause great harm.
  • Pragmatism and gradual change. Conservatives are not opposed to all change; Burke wrote that a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. But change should be gradual, organic and responsive to circumstances, like the repair of an old building rather than its demolition.
  • Organic society. Society is like a living organism, not a machine assembled by individuals. Institutions such as the family, the church, local communities and voluntary associations (Burke's "little platoons") bind people together.
  • Authority and hierarchy. Social order requires authority, and some hierarchy is natural and beneficial. Traditional conservatives believed in leadership by those with experience and responsibility.
  • Property. Property gives people security, a stake in society and a link between generations.

docs.title: Varieties
docs.text:
• Traditional or paternalistic conservatism emphasises duty, hierarchy and social responsibility. One-nation conservatism, associated with the nineteenth-century British prime minister Benjamin Disraeli, held that the privileged have obligations to the less fortunate, and accepted social reform to prevent society splitting into "two nations", rich and poor.
  • Philosophical conservatism: the English philosopher Michael Oakeshott (Rationalism in Politics, 1962) criticised "rationalism" in politics, the belief that politics can be guided by abstract technical knowledge, and defended practical knowledge gained from experience. The conservative disposition, he suggested, is a preference for what is present, familiar and tested over what is merely possible and untested.
  • The New Right, influential from the 1970s, combined two strands that sit uneasily together: neo-liberal economics (free markets, a smaller state) and neo-conservative social policy (strong government, law and order, traditional morality, national identity).

docs.title: Criticisms of conservatism
docs.text:
• Defence of privilege. Critics argue that conservatism has often been a defence of the interests of those who benefit from existing hierarchies, and that "tradition" has included slavery, caste and the subordination of women.
  • Vagueness. If conservatism means preserving what exists, it seems to have no content of its own and to defend whatever happens to be established.
  • Internal tension. The New Right's free-market economics can undermine the communities and traditions that its social conservatism wants to protect.

Conservatives reply that their ideology is a disposition, not a blueprint, and that its value lies precisely in its scepticism about blueprints. They point to the destruction caused by twentieth-century attempts to remake society from scratch.

docs.title: 11.4 Socialism
docs.text: Socialism emerged in the early nineteenth century in reaction to industrial capitalism. It is a broad family of ideologies sharing a set of values.

docs.title: Core values
docs.text:
• Community and cooperation. Human beings are social creatures, shaped by society, and capable of cooperating for the common good. Competition and individualism set people against one another.
  • Equality. Socialists favour social and economic equality, not only legal and political equality. Inequality reflects unequal social conditions more than unequal talents.
  • Need. Goods should be distributed at least partly according to need.
  • Class. Society is divided into classes based on economic position, and politics is shaped by conflict between them.
  • Common ownership. Many socialists have favoured collective ownership of productive resources, by the state, cooperatives or communities, in place of private ownership.

docs.title: Utopian socialism
docs.text: The early socialists, later called utopian by Marx and Engels, believed that a cooperative society could be created by example and persuasion. Robert Owen set up model factory communities in Scotland and the United States; Charles Fourier proposed cooperative communities called phalanxes; Henri de Saint-Simon envisaged a society organised by scientists and industrialists for the benefit of the poorest.

docs.title: Democratic socialism and social democracy
docs.text:
In the late nineteenth century many socialists came to believe that socialism could be achieved gradually through elections and reform rather than revolution. Eduard Bernstein, a German Social Democrat, argued in Evolutionary Socialism (1899) that capitalism was not collapsing as Marx predicted, that workers' conditions were improving, and that socialism should be pursued by democratic reform; this was called revisionism. In Britain the Fabian Society (founded 1884), including Sidney and Beatrice Webb and George Bernard Shaw, advocated the gradual extension of public ownership and welfare.

Over the twentieth century much of the democratic left moved from seeking to replace capitalism to seeking to reform it. Social democracy accepts a market economy but aims to make it fairer through a mixed economy, progressive taxation, a comprehensive welfare state, strong trade unions and economic management. The welfare states of the Scandinavian countries are often cited as examples. In the 1990s some centre-left parties adopted what was called the "Third Way", which sought to combine market efficiency with social justice; critics on the left saw this as an accommodation with neo-liberalism.

docs.title: Criticisms of socialism
docs.text:
• Economic calculation. The economists Ludwig von Mises and Hayek argued that without market prices a central planner cannot know the relative scarcity of goods and so cannot allocate resources efficiently.
  • Incentives. Common ownership and equal rewards may weaken incentives to work, save and innovate.
  • Freedom. Concentrating economic power in the state threatens political freedom (Hayek's Road to Serfdom).
  • Historical experience. Critics point to the economic failures and political repression of states that abolished private ownership in the name of socialism. Democratic socialists reply that these were authoritarian distortions, not democratic socialism.

docs.title: 11.5 Marxism
docs.text: Marxism is the body of thought developed by Karl Marx (1818–1883) and Friedrich Engels (1820–1895), and elaborated by many later thinkers. It is both a theory of history and society and a programme for revolution. Its main works include the Communist Manifesto (1848) and Marx's Capital (volume 1, 1867).

docs.title: Historical materialism
docs.text:
Marx's theory of history is called historical materialism (Engels's term was the "materialist conception of history"). Its central claim is that the way people produce the material means of life shapes the rest of society.

  • The forces of production are the means by which people produce: tools, machines, technology, raw materials and human labour power.
  • The relations of production are the social relations in production, above all relations of ownership: who owns the means of production and who must work for the owners.
  • Together they form the economic base (or mode of production). On the base rises a superstructure of law, politics, religion, art and philosophy, which broadly reflects and supports the base.

History, on this view, moves through a series of modes of production: primitive communism, ancient slavery, feudalism and capitalism, with socialism and communism expected to follow. Change occurs when the developing forces of production come into conflict with existing relations of production, which become fetters on further development; an era of social revolution follows.

Figure 11.2 Base and superstructure in Marx's theory. A diagram of base and superstructure. At the bottom, the economic base consists of forces of production and relations of production. Above it, the superstructure consists of law, the state, religion, ideas and culture. A thick arrow points upward from the base, showing that the base shapes the superstructure, and a thinner arrow points down, showing that the superstructure also reinforces the base.

docs.title: Class struggle
docs.text: "The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles," the Communist Manifesto begins. In each mode of production one class owns the means of production and another does not: masters and slaves, lords and serfs, capitalists (the bourgeoisie) and wage-workers (the proletariat). Under capitalism, society tends to split into these two great classes.

docs.title: Exploitation and surplus value
docs.text:
Marx argued that capitalism is exploitative even when workers are paid the full market value of their labour power. Workers sell their labour power (their capacity to work) for a wage that equals the cost of maintaining them. But in a working day they produce more value than this. The difference, surplus value, is appropriated by the capitalist as profit. Exploitation is thus built into the wage relation itself, not a matter of unusually low wages.

Worked example 11.1: Surplus value in a simple model

Situation. In Marx's labour theory of value, suppose a worker works a 10-hour day. The goods needed to maintain the worker for a day take 6 hours of social labour to produce, so the day's wage is equivalent to 6 hours of value.

Analysis. In the first 6 hours (necessary labour) the worker produces value equal to the wage. In the remaining 4 hours (surplus labour) the worker produces surplus value that goes to the capitalist. Marx's rate of surplus value (or rate of exploitation) is surplus labour divided by necessary labour:

\[ \frac{4 \text{ hours}}{6 \text{ hours}} \approx 0.67, \text{ or about } 67\%. \]

The capitalist can raise it by lengthening the working day (absolute surplus value) or by raising productivity so that the wage goods take less time to produce (relative surplus value). Critics reject the labour theory of value on which this analysis rests (see below); most modern economists explain prices by supply, demand and marginal productivity instead.

docs.title: Alienation
docs.text: In his early writings, especially the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, Marx described workers under capitalism as alienated (estranged) in four ways: from the product of their labour, which belongs to another and confronts them as an alien power; from the activity of labour, which is forced and not an expression of themselves; from their species-being, their distinctively human capacity for free, creative, conscious activity; and from other people, who confront them as competitors or exploiters.

docs.title: The state, revolution and communism
docs.text: For Marx the state in class society is an instrument of class rule (Chapter 2). Capitalism, he predicted, would be undermined by its own contradictions: competition would concentrate capital in fewer hands, crises would recur, and the proletariat, growing in numbers and organisation, would become conscious of itself as a class and overthrow the bourgeoisie. After the revolution a transitional period, which Marx called the dictatorship of the proletariat, would abolish private ownership of the means of production. Eventually, with classes abolished, the state as an instrument of coercion would wither away, and a communist society would emerge, governed by the principle that Marx stated in his Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875): "From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs!"

docs.title: Later Marxism
docs.text:
• Lenin argued that a disciplined vanguard party of professional revolutionaries must lead the working class, and that imperialism was the highest stage of capitalism. After the Russian Revolution of 1917, the Soviet state under Lenin and later Stalin became a one-party dictatorship.
  • Western Marxists such as Gramsci (hegemony, Chapter 3), and the Frankfurt School (Theodor Adorno, Max Horkheimer, Herbert Marcuse) turned attention to culture, ideology and the ways capitalism secures consent.
  • Mao Zedong adapted Marxism to a largely peasant society, making the peasantry a revolutionary force.
  • Analytical Marxists such as G. A. Cohen reconstructed Marx's ideas with the tools of analytical philosophy, and in later work turned to the moral case for equality.

docs.title: Criticisms of Marxism
docs.text:
• Failed predictions. Capitalism did not collapse in the most advanced countries; workers' living standards rose; revolutions occurred instead in largely agrarian societies. Classes became more complex, with a large middle class.
  • The labour theory of value is rejected by most economists.
  • Economic determinism. Critics argue that Marx underestimated the independent role of ideas, religion, nationalism and politics. (Engels himself insisted that the economic factor was decisive only "in the last instance".)
  • Authoritarianism. States governed by Marxist-Leninist parties in the twentieth century suppressed political freedom, and some caused mass deaths through repression and famine. Critics argue that the idea of a dictatorship of the proletariat and a vanguard party invited this; defenders argue that it betrayed Marx's democratic and humanist aims.
  • Neglect of other forms of oppression. Feminists and others argue that class is not the only or always the most important form of domination (Chapter 12).

Defenders reply that Marx's analysis of capitalism's tendency to concentrate wealth, generate crises and commodify human life remains illuminating, and that his critique of alienation and exploitation raises questions any theory of justice must answer.

Liberalism Conservatism Socialism Marxism Human nature Rational, self-interested individuals Imperfect, limited in reason, social Social, cooperative Shaped by social and economic conditions Key value Liberty Order and tradition Equality and community Human emancipation View of the state Necessary, but limited (classical) or enabling (social) Source of order and authority Instrument for social reform (democratic socialism) Instrument of class rule; to wither away Economy Market economy, with more or less regulation Private property; varies from paternalistic to free-market Mixed or collectively owned Common ownership; communism Change Reform through reason and debate Gradual and organic Reform or revolution Revolution

Table 11.1. Four ideologies compared.

Key idea

Liberalism puts the free individual first, conservatism the wisdom of tradition and the limits of reason, socialism equality and community, and Marxism the abolition of class exploitation through a transformation of the economic base.

Summary

  • An ideology combines a description of society, a vision of a better one and a programme for change. The left–right spectrum originated in 1789 and is a crude simplification; a second libertarian–authoritarian axis helps.
  • Liberalism values the individual, liberty, reason, equality, toleration and consent. Classical liberals (Locke, Smith) favour a limited state; social liberals (Green, Hobhouse, Keynes) an enabling welfare state; neo-liberals (Hayek, Friedman) a return to markets.
  • Conservatism (Burke, Oakeshott) values tradition, organic society, gradual change, authority and property, and is sceptical of abstract reason; varieties include one-nation conservatism and the New Right.
  • Socialism values community, equality, need and common ownership; its varieties include utopian socialism, revisionism (Bernstein), Fabianism and social democracy; it is criticised on grounds of calculation, incentives and freedom.
  • Marxism explains history by the base (forces and relations of production) and class struggle; capitalism exploits workers through surplus value and alienates them; revolution and a transitional dictatorship of the proletariat would lead to classless communism. Its predictions, economics and political record have been heavily criticised.

docs.title: 11.6 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Give the three elements of an ideology and explain why the left–right spectrum is a simplification.

Answer

An ideology offers (1) a description of the existing order, (2) a vision of a better society and (3) a programme of action. The left–right line is a simplification because it merges economic questions (redistribution, ownership) with social questions (tradition, personal freedom), and cannot place ideologies such as anarchism, feminism or environmentalism; a second libertarian–authoritarian axis is often added.

Exercise 2

Distinguish classical from social liberalism on (a) the meaning of freedom and (b) the role of the state.

Answer

(a) Classical liberals understand freedom mainly as negative liberty, the absence of interference; social liberals add a positive conception, the real capacity to develop oneself. (b) Classical liberals favour a minimal state limited to order, defence and contracts; social liberals favour an enabling state that provides education, health care, social insurance and economic management.

Exercise 3

Explain Burke's view of society as a partnership across generations, and what it implies for political change.

Answer

Burke saw society as a partnership not only among the living but between the dead, the living and those yet to be born. Present generations inherit institutions embodying accumulated wisdom and hold them in trust for the future. Change should therefore be gradual and organic, repairing rather than demolishing, and abstract schemes that tear up inherited institutions are both arrogant and dangerous.

Exercise 4

What was Bernstein's revisionism, and how does social democracy differ from Marxism?

Answer

Bernstein argued (1899) that capitalism was not collapsing, workers' conditions were improving, and socialism should be pursued through democratic reform, not revolution. Social democracy accepts a market economy and seeks to make it fair through a mixed economy, welfare and progressive taxation, while Marxism seeks to abolish capitalism and private ownership of the means of production, by revolution.

Exercise 5

In Marx's terms, a worker works 8 hours; the value of the wage is produced in 5 hours. Calculate the surplus labour and the rate of surplus value.

Answer

Surplus labour = 8 − 5 = 3 hours. Rate of surplus value = surplus labour ÷ necessary labour = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6, or 60 per cent.

Exercise 6

Name the four forms of alienation Marx described in 1844.

Answer

Alienation from (1) the product of labour, (2) the activity of labour, (3) species-being (human creative nature) and (4) other people.

Exercise 7

Give three criticisms of Marxism and one reply a Marxist might make.

Answer

Any three: (1) failed predictions (no collapse of advanced capitalism; rising living standards; revolutions in agrarian countries); (2) the labour theory of value is rejected by most economists; (3) economic determinism underrates ideas, religion and nationalism; (4) Marxist-Leninist states were authoritarian and repressive; (5) neglect of non-class oppression. Reply: Marx's analysis of capitalism's tendencies to concentrate wealth, generate crises and commodify life remains illuminating, and twentieth-century dictatorships betrayed rather than fulfilled his emancipatory aims.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Liberty
docs.text:
Freedom from, freedom to, and freedom as not being dominated

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • explain why liberty is a contested concept and use MacCallum's triadic formula to clarify claims about it;
  • distinguish negative and positive liberty as Berlin described them, and state the main worries about each;
  • explain the republican idea of liberty as non-domination;
  • state Mill's harm principle and his arguments for freedom of thought and expression;
  • analyse paternalism, the offence principle and hate speech as limits on liberty;
  • apply these ideas to concrete cases of state restriction.

docs.title: 4.1 Why liberty is contested
docs.text:
Almost everyone says they value freedom. Defenders of free markets and critics of them, conservatives and revolutionaries, all claim to stand for liberty. This is not simply hypocrisy. "Liberty" (or "freedom"; the two words are used interchangeably in this book) has several meanings, and people who use the word may be pointing at quite different things.

Consider three people who all say "I am not free".

  • A journalist whose articles are censored by the government.
  • A worker who is legally free to take any job, but is so poor that she must accept whatever is offered.
  • A man addicted to gambling, who keeps betting although he wishes he could stop.

The journalist is prevented by another person's deliberate act. The worker faces no legal barrier but lacks the means to act. The gambler faces no external obstacle at all; his obstacle is inside him. Whether all three are really unfree, and whether the state should do anything about it, depends on which conception of liberty we adopt.

docs.title: MacCallum's formula
docs.text:
In 1967 the philosopher Gerald MacCallum suggested a way to cut through much of the confusion. Every claim about freedom, he argued, has three parts, even if some are left unstated: an agent (X) is free from some constraint (Y) to do or become something (Z).

\[ \text{X is (or is not) free from Y to do or become Z.} \]

Disagreements about freedom are then disagreements about what counts as X (the individual? the "true self"? the community?), what counts as a constraint Y (only deliberate interference by others? also poverty, ignorance or inner compulsion?), and what counts as Z (any action at all? only worthwhile ones?). Using the formula, the journalist's case is "the journalist is not free from censorship to publish"; the worker's is "the worker is not free from poverty to choose her job"; the gambler's is "the gambler is not free from compulsion to live as he wishes".

Key idea

Any claim about freedom can be written as "X is free from Y to do or become Z". Rival theories of liberty disagree mainly about what counts as a constraint (Y) and who the free agent (X) is.

docs.title: 4.2 Negative liberty
docs.text:
In his lecture "Two Concepts of Liberty" (1958), the philosopher Isaiah Berlin distinguished two ideas that had dominated the history of political thought.

Negative liberty answers the question: what is the area within which a person is, or should be, left to do or be what he is able to do or be, without interference by other persons? I am free in the negative sense to the extent that no other person or group deliberately interferes with my actions. The wider the area of non-interference, the wider my freedom.

Negative liberty has a long history. Hobbes defined liberty as the absence of external impediments to motion; a free man is one who is not hindered from doing what he has the will to do. The classical liberal tradition (Locke, Benjamin Constant, Mill) saw the core of freedom as a protected private sphere where the individual may live as he chooses.

Three features are important.

  • Only human interference counts. If I cannot fly, I lack the ability, not the freedom. If I am too poor to buy a book, the negative theorist says I lack the means to use my freedom, not the freedom itself. Berlin was clear that poverty is a great evil, but he insisted on calling it by its own name rather than "unfreedom", to avoid confusing different values.
  • Freedom is a matter of opportunity, not exercise. I am free to vote whether or not I actually vote.
  • Freedom can be traded against other values. Laws restrict freedom, but some restriction is necessary for security, justice or equality. The negative theorist asks only that we be honest that a loss of freedom is a loss, even when it is worth it.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text:
• Formal freedom may be empty. Critics on the left argue that a freedom one cannot use is worth little. To tell a homeless person that she is free to rent a house is, they say, a mockery. Socialists and social liberals therefore argue that real freedom requires resources. Some negative theorists reply that poverty does involve interference: if I try to take food I cannot pay for, I will be stopped by the police, so lack of money is itself a lack of negative freedom (an argument made by G. A. Cohen).
  • It may ignore domination. A slave whose master happens to be kind and never interferes has, on a strict negative view, a great deal of liberty. Yet the slave lives at the master's mercy. This criticism leads to the republican theory of section 4.4.

docs.title: 4.3 Positive liberty
docs.text:
Positive liberty answers a different question: what, or who, is the source of control or interference that can determine someone to do, or be, this rather than that? It is the freedom of self-mastery: being one's own master, governed by one's own reason and choices rather than by others or by one's passions. I am free in the positive sense when I am the author of my own life.

Positive liberty has been understood in several ways.

  • Self-government by reason. For Rousseau and the German philosopher Immanuel Kant, to be free is to obey a law one has given oneself, not to follow every impulse. The gambler in section 4.1 lacks this kind of freedom.
  • Collective self-government. A people is free when it governs itself, through democratic participation. This links positive liberty to democracy and to national independence.
  • Capacity or power. The English idealist T. H. Green argued in 1881 that freedom is a positive power or capacity of doing or enjoying something worth doing or enjoying, in common with others. On this view the state promotes freedom when it provides education, regulates working hours and improves public health, because it gives people real capacities they would otherwise lack. Green's view helped to inspire the social liberalism of the early twentieth century (Chapter 11).

docs.title: Berlin's warning
docs.text:
Berlin did not reject positive liberty, but he warned of its dangers. The idea of self-mastery invites a division of the self into a "higher", rational self and a "lower", empirical self of desires. It then becomes possible to say that people are not really free when they do what they want, but only when they do what their higher self, or reason, would choose. And if some authority (a party, a church, a state) claims to know what reason requires, it may coerce people in the name of their own freedom. Berlin pointed to Rousseau's phrase about forcing people to be free, and to the twentieth-century totalitarian regimes that claimed to liberate people while imprisoning them.

Defenders of positive liberty reply that Berlin described a perversion of the idea, not the idea itself. Valuing people's capacity to lead self-directed lives, they say, gives the state reason to provide education and resources, not to impose a doctrine. And negative liberty can be abused too: the freedom of the strong from regulation can mean the domination of the weak.

Negative liberty Positive liberty Central question How large is the area in which I am left alone? Who governs me, and am I my own master? Constraint Deliberate interference by other people Interference, but also lack of capacity, ignorance, inner compulsion Typical defenders Hobbes, Constant, Mill (mainly), Berlin, Hayek Rousseau, Kant, Hegel, Green, many socialists Implication for the state Protect a private sphere; limit state action Enable self-development and self-government; may require state action Main worry Formal freedoms may be empty for the poor Others may coerce people in the name of their "true" freedom

Table 4.1. Berlin's two concepts of liberty.

Figure 4.1 Negative and positive liberty. Two panels. On the left, negative liberty is shown as a person standing inside a circle of protected space, with other people and the state kept outside by the boundary. On the right, positive liberty is shown as a person steering their own course, with arrows from capacities such as education and health feeding into the person's ability to act.

docs.title: 4.4 Liberty as non-domination
docs.text:
A third view, revived from the Roman and early modern republican tradition by historians and philosophers such as Quentin Skinner and Philip Pettit (Republicanism, 1997), holds that freedom means not being subject to the arbitrary will of another. What makes a slave unfree is not that the master interferes, but that the master could interfere at will, without having to answer to anyone. The slave of a kind master is still unfree; he must flatter, anticipate and appease.

On this view:

  • Domination without interference is possible (the kind master, an employer who could fire a worker at whim but chooses not to, a husband who in law controls his wife's property but does not use the power).
  • Interference without domination is also possible: a law that is made through fair democratic processes and that tracks the interests of those it governs interferes with people but does not dominate them, because it is not arbitrary.

Republicans therefore emphasise the rule of law, the dispersal of power, the contestability of decisions (people must be able to challenge them), and the protection of vulnerable people from dependence on others' goodwill. Critics ask whether "arbitrary" can be defined without relying on a prior theory of justice, and whether non-domination is really a distinct idea of freedom or a combination of negative liberty with other values.

Worked example 4.1: Three views of one case

Situation. A domestic worker lives in her employer's house. She is paid, is not mistreated, and is allowed to go out on Sundays. But the employer holds her passport, and she could be dismissed and deported at any moment without reason or appeal.

Negative view. Her day-to-day freedom is restricted (limited time out), but on many days there is little active interference. The holding of her passport is a clear interference with her freedom to leave.

Positive view. Her capacity to direct her own life, develop her abilities and take part in her community is very limited.

Republican view. Even on days when nothing bad happens, she is dominated: she lives at the mercy of the employer's will, which is subject to no check. Republicans would recommend legal protections (the right to keep one's own documents, protection against arbitrary dismissal) that reduce domination, even if they add some regulation.

docs.title: 4.5 Mill and the harm principle
docs.text:
The most famous defence of individual liberty in English is John Stuart Mill's On Liberty (1859). Mill was worried less about tyrannical kings than about the tyranny of the majority, and especially the social tyranny of prevailing opinion and custom, which could crush individuality more thoroughly than any law. He proposed what he called one very simple principle, now known as the harm principle:

Mill, On Liberty (1859), Chapter 1

"The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others. His own good, either physical or moral, is not a sufficient warrant."

docs.title: Self-regarding and other-regarding conduct
docs.text:
Mill distinguished conduct that concerns only oneself (or others only with their free consent) from conduct that affects the interests of others. Over the first, the individual is sovereign: society may advise, persuade or avoid him, but may not compel him. Over the second, society may intervene if it would do more good than harm. Mill applied the principle only to adults in a mature society; it did not, he said, apply to children or, in a notorious passage reflecting the imperial assumptions of his time, to what he called backward societies.

Critics have long asked whether any conduct is purely self-regarding. If I ruin my health, my family suffers and public health services bear the cost. Mill's answer was that such harms are indirect and contingent; society should punish the definite breach of a duty to others (a father who fails to support his children because he drinks), not the self-regarding vice itself.

docs.title: Why Mill valued liberty
docs.text: Mill was a utilitarian, but he grounded liberty in utility "in the largest sense, grounded on the permanent interests of man as a progressive being". Liberty allows individuality to flourish: people develop their faculties by making their own choices, and a society with varied "experiments of living" discovers better ways of life. He valued originality and feared a society of conformity in which people ask only what is suitable to their position.

docs.title: The argument for freedom of thought and discussion
docs.text:
Mill's second chapter gives a powerful argument for near-absolute freedom of opinion. Silencing an opinion is wrong in every case.

  1. The opinion may be true. To suppress it assumes our own infallibility.
  2. It may be partly true. Prevailing opinion is rarely the whole truth; only the collision of opinions supplies the rest.
  3. Even if it is false, challenge keeps the truth alive. Unchallenged, true beliefs are held as dead dogma, as prejudice, without understanding of their grounds.
  4. The meaning of the doctrine itself will be lost or weakened if it is never defended.

Mill distinguished opinion from incitement. The opinion that corn dealers starve the poor may be freely published in the press, he wrote, but may justly be punished when delivered orally to an excited mob assembled before a corn dealer's house.

Worked example 4.2: Applying the harm principle

Cases. (a) A law requiring motorcyclists to wear helmets. (b) A law banning the sale of alcohol to under-eighteens. (c) A law punishing a newspaper for publishing an article arguing that the country's economic policy is disastrous.

Analysis. (a) The main harm prevented is to the rider, so a strict Millian would object: it is paternalistic (section 4.6). Some argue that crashes impose costs on others (medical services, family), but Mill would call these indirect. (b) Mill's principle does not apply to children, so restricting their access is consistent with it. (c) This punishes the expression of an opinion and is precisely what Mill's argument for free discussion condemns; there is no harm to others in the relevant sense, only disagreement.

docs.title: 4.6 Limits of liberty: paternalism, offence and hate speech
Paternalism
docs.text:
Paternalism is interference with a person's liberty for his or her own good. Mill rejected it for adults, with a famous exception: if someone is about to cross a bridge known to be unsafe and there is no time to warn him, an official may seize him and turn him back, since liberty consists in doing what one desires, and he does not desire to fall into the river. Philosophers distinguish:

  • soft paternalism, which intervenes only to check that conduct is voluntary and informed (the bridge case), and is compatible with respect for autonomy; and
  • hard paternalism, which overrides fully informed, voluntary choices for the person's good (banning a dangerous sport for willing adults).

More recently, behavioural economists Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein have proposed libertarian paternalism or "nudging": arranging choices (for example, making pension saving the default option, which people can opt out of) so that people tend to choose what benefits them, without forbidding anything. Critics worry that nudges manipulate people and bypass their reason.

docs.title: The offence principle
docs.text: Should the law prevent conduct that does not harm others but deeply offends them, such as public nudity or obscene displays? The American philosopher Joel Feinberg, in a four-volume study The Moral Limits of the Criminal Law (1984–1988), proposed an offence principle alongside the harm principle, but hedged it carefully: the offence must be serious, widespread and hard to avoid, and must be weighed against the value of the conduct and the ease with which offended people can avoid it. Offence caused by the mere knowledge that others are doing something in private would not count.

docs.title: Legal moralism
docs.text: Legal moralism holds that the law may prohibit conduct simply because it is immoral, even if no one is harmed. In a famous debate in the late 1950s and 1960s, the English judge Lord Devlin argued that a society is held together by a shared morality and may protect it by law; H. L. A. Hart replied, in Mill's spirit, that private conduct between consenting adults that harms no one is not the law's business, and that shared morality can change without society collapsing. The debate arose from proposals to decriminalise homosexual conduct in Britain.

docs.title: Hate speech
docs.text:
Many democracies restrict hate speech: expression that attacks or demeans people on the basis of characteristics such as religion, race, caste, ethnicity or sexuality. Arguments for restriction hold that such speech harms its targets (by intimidating them, damaging their standing as equal members of society and silencing them) and can incite discrimination or violence. Arguments against warn that vague laws can be used to silence unpopular political or religious views, that the best answer to bad speech is more speech, and that the state is not a trustworthy judge of what is offensive. Constitutions strike different balances. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution is interpreted to protect most hateful speech unless it incites imminent lawless action; many European countries and India permit wider restrictions. Article 19(2) of the Constitution of India allows "reasonable restrictions" on freedom of speech and expression on grounds that include public order, decency or morality, and incitement to an offence.

Table 4.2. Principles for limiting liberty.

Worked example 4.3: A ban on a protest march

Situation. A city bans a march by a group that wants to protest against the presence of a religious minority in the area, on the ground that the march will pass through the minority's neighbourhood and is likely to lead to violence.

Analysis. A strict negative-liberty view sees a serious restriction of freedom of assembly and expression that requires strong justification. Applying Mill's distinction between opinion and incitement, the decisive questions are whether the march would amount to incitement in a volatile setting (like the speech before the corn dealer's house) and whether lesser measures, such as a different route, would prevent harm. A republican might stress that the march aims to intimidate a vulnerable group and so threatens its members with domination. A defender of hate-speech laws would ask whether the march attacks the minority's standing as equal citizens. Many legal systems would allow the authorities to change the route or impose conditions rather than ban the march outright, since a narrower restriction protects others while limiting liberty less.

docs.title: 4.7 Liberty and other values
docs.text:
Berlin ended "Two Concepts of Liberty" with a defence of value pluralism: the view that human values are many, that they can genuinely conflict, and that there is no single master value by which all conflicts can be settled. Liberty may conflict with equality, security, justice or community, and sometimes we must sacrifice some of one value for another. What we should not do, he argued, is pretend that nothing is lost, for example by redefining liberty so that whatever the state demands becomes "true freedom".

Others argue that the conflicts are less deep than they look. Ronald Dworkin argued that liberty, properly understood as the freedom to use one's fair share of resources as one chooses, cannot really conflict with equality properly understood. Republicans argue that well-designed laws increase freedom by reducing domination. The relation between liberty and equality is a central theme of the next two chapters.

Summary

  • Liberty is contested; MacCallum's formula, "X is free from Y to do or become Z", shows that rival views disagree about the agent, the constraints and the goals.
  • Berlin's negative liberty is the absence of deliberate interference by others; positive liberty is self-mastery or self-government. Berlin warned that positive liberty can be used to justify coercion in the name of people's "true" selves; critics reply that negative liberty can leave freedoms empty for those without means.
  • Republicans (Skinner, Pettit) define liberty as non-domination: not being subject to the arbitrary will of another.
  • Mill's harm principle permits interference with adults only to prevent harm to others; he defended individuality and near-absolute freedom of opinion on four grounds, while distinguishing opinion from incitement.
  • Other possible grounds for limiting liberty are paternalism (soft or hard), the offence principle (Feinberg) and legal moralism (Devlin, opposed by Hart). Hate speech raises hard questions on which democracies differ.
  • Berlin's value pluralism holds that liberty can conflict with other values; others argue the conflicts are less deep.

docs.title: 4.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Use MacCallum's formula to express each claim: (a) "Under the old regime, people were not free to travel abroad." (b) "Without free schooling, poor children are not really free."

Answer

(a) People (X) were not free from state prohibition (Y) to travel abroad (Z). (b) Poor children (X) are not free from lack of education and resources (Y) to develop their abilities and choose their path in life (Z). The second claim treats lack of resources as a constraint, which a strict negative theorist would call a lack of means rather than of freedom.

Exercise 2

Why did Berlin think positive liberty could be dangerous? How might a defender of positive liberty reply?

Answer

Positive liberty as self-mastery divides the self into a higher, rational self and a lower self of desires. An authority that claims to know what the higher self wants may then coerce people while claiming to free them, as Rousseau's "forced to be free" suggests and totalitarian regimes practised. A defender can reply that this is an abuse, not a consequence, of the idea: valuing people's capacity to direct their own lives supports providing education and resources and respecting their choices, not imposing a doctrine.

Exercise 3

Explain why a republican would say that the slave of a kind master is unfree, although the master never interferes.

Answer

For republicans freedom is non-domination. The slave lives under the master's arbitrary power: the master could interfere at any time, without answering to anyone. The slave must therefore watch, flatter and appease, and his good fortune depends wholly on the master's goodwill. Absence of actual interference does not remove the domination.

Exercise 4

State Mill's four reasons for allowing freedom of opinion even when the opinion seems false.

Answer

(1) The opinion may be true, and to suppress it assumes infallibility. (2) It may be partly true, and only collision of opinions supplies the whole truth. (3) Even a true received opinion, unchallenged, will be held as dead dogma, without understanding of its grounds. (4) The meaning of the doctrine will be weakened or lost if it is never defended.

Exercise 5

Distinguish soft from hard paternalism and give an example of each.

Answer

Soft paternalism interferes only to ensure that a choice is voluntary and informed, for example stopping someone who is about to step onto an unsafe bridge without knowing it, or requiring a cooling-off period before a risky contract. Hard paternalism overrides choices that are fully voluntary and informed, for the person's own good, for example banning adults from a dangerous sport they understand and want to take part in.

Exercise 6

What was the Hart–Devlin debate about, and what position did each take?

Answer

It concerned whether the law may enforce morality as such, arising from proposals to decriminalise private homosexual conduct in Britain. Devlin argued that a society is held together by shared morality and may use law to protect it. Hart argued, following Mill, that private conduct between consenting adults that harms no one is not the law's business, and that a society's morality can change without the society disintegrating.

Exercise 7

Give one argument for and one against laws restricting hate speech.

Answer

For: hate speech harms its targets: it intimidates them, undermines their standing as equal citizens, can silence them, and may incite discrimination or violence. Against: such laws can be vague and abused to silence unpopular political or religious opinions; the state is not a neutral judge of offence; and counter-speech may be a better remedy.
