docs.title: Chapter 3: Power, Authority and Legitimacy
docs.text:
Who gets their way, who has the right to rule, and why we obey

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • define power and distinguish it from influence, force, authority and legitimacy;
  • explain the three dimensions of power (Dahl, Bachrach and Baratz, Lukes) and apply them to a case;
  • outline the ideas of power of Gramsci, Arendt and Foucault;
  • describe Weber's three types of authority and the distinction between being in authority and an authority;
  • compare sociological and normative ideas of legitimacy, including Beetham's three criteria;
  • evaluate the main theories of political obligation and the case for and against civil disobedience.

docs.title: 3.1 Three questions
docs.text:
A traffic police officer signals you to stop, and you stop. Why? Perhaps because you fear a fine (the officer has power over you). Perhaps because you accept that police officers have the right to direct traffic (the officer has authority). And perhaps because you believe the whole system of traffic law is rightly made and serves a good purpose (the system has legitimacy). These three ideas are closely related but different, and political theory has spent much effort separating them.

Concept Rough meaning Example Power The capacity to bring about outcomes, especially to make others act as one wishes An employer can make workers stay late by threatening dismissal Influence The ability to affect others' choices by persuasion, example or reputation, without threats A respected scientist changes public opinion on vaccines Force Physical compulsion, or the threat of it A guard physically removes a protester Authority Power that is recognised as rightful by those subject to it; the right to command A judge's sentence is obeyed because judges are entitled to sentence Legitimacy The quality of a regime or rule that makes it rightful and worthy of support A government chosen in free elections under a fair constitution

Table 3.1. Power and related concepts.

A useful slogan is that authority is legitimate power. But the slogan hides a difficulty: does "legitimate" mean that people believe the power is rightful, or that it really is rightful? This chapter returns to that question in section 3.5.

docs.title: 3.2 What is power?
docs.text: Power is perhaps the most central concept in political science, and also one of the most disputed. In the most general sense, power is the capacity to produce effects. In politics we are mainly interested in power over others: the capacity of some people to get others to do what they would not otherwise do. Some theorists, especially feminists, also stress power to: the capacity to act, often together with others, as when a community gains the power to run its own school.

docs.title: The first dimension: decision-making
docs.text: The American political scientist Robert Dahl gave an influential definition in 1957: A has power over B to the extent that A can get B to do something that B would not otherwise do. To find out who has power in a community, Dahl argued, we should study observable conflicts over key decisions and see whose preferences prevail. In Who Governs? (1961), a study of the city of New Haven in the United States, he found that different groups won on different issues (urban renewal, education, party nominations), and concluded that power was dispersed rather than held by a single elite. This is the pluralist view of power.

docs.title: The second dimension: agenda-setting
docs.text: In 1962 Peter Bachrach and Morton Baratz published "Two Faces of Power". They argued that Dahl had seen only one face. Power is also exercised when A shapes the political agenda so that issues threatening A's interests are never raised for decision at all. They called this non-decision-making. A council that never discusses pollution from the town's largest factory, because everyone knows the owner would object and the matter would go nowhere, displays power even though no visible conflict occurs.

docs.title: The third dimension: shaping wants
docs.text:
In Power: A Radical View (1974) Steven Lukes added a third dimension. The most effective power, he argued, is the power to shape people's very preferences and beliefs, so that they do not even want what would be in their interests. If workers come to believe that their low wages are natural and deserved, or members of a subordinate group accept a doctrine that justifies their subordination, there is no conflict at all, observable or hidden, yet power is at work. Lukes defined power as A affecting B in a manner contrary to B's interests.

Figure 3.1 The three dimensions of power. Three nested circles. The inner circle is the first dimension of power, decision-making, where conflicts are visible and we ask who wins. The middle circle is the second dimension, agenda-setting or non-decision-making, where some issues are kept off the agenda. The outer circle is the third dimension, shaping preferences, where people are led not to want what is in their interests.

Caution: the difficulty of 'real interests'

Lukes's third dimension is powerful but contested. To say that people are mistaken about their own interests, we need some standard of what their real interests are, and critics ask who is entitled to decide this. Lukes answered that real interests are what people would choose if they could make choices under conditions of relative autonomy, with full information. Even so, the claim must be made carefully, with evidence, and with respect for the views of the people concerned.

Worked example 3.1: Three dimensions in one town

Situation. A town has a large chemical plant that employs a third of the workforce and pollutes the river. Residents suffer health problems.

First dimension. A proposal to fine the plant comes before the council and is defeated after the company lobbies hard. We can see a conflict and who won.

Second dimension. No proposal is ever made, because council members know the company would threaten to close the plant. The issue never reaches a decision.

Third dimension. Residents do not regard pollution as a problem at all: local newspapers, schools and the company's sponsorship of festivals have spread the belief that the plant means prosperity and that health problems have other causes. There is no grievance to suppress.

The example shows why studying only visible decisions may underestimate power.

docs.title: Gramsci: hegemony
docs.text: The Italian Marxist Antonio Gramsci (1891–1937), writing in prison under the fascist regime, asked why workers in Western Europe had not made the revolution Marx expected. His answer was hegemony: the ruling class rules not only by coercion (through the state, police and army) but by consent, winning the acceptance of subordinate groups through culture, religion, education, the media and common sense. Ideas that serve the interests of the dominant class come to seem natural to everyone. Changing society therefore requires a struggle over ideas within civil society, not only a seizure of the state.

docs.title: Arendt: power as acting together
docs.text: The political theorist Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) sharply distinguished power from violence. Power, she argued in On Violence (1970), corresponds to the human ability not just to act but to act in concert. It belongs to a group and exists only as long as the group stays together. Violence is instrumental: it can destroy power but never create it. A government that must rely on violence alone has already lost power. On this view a peaceful mass movement that brings down a regime displays power in its purest form.

docs.title: Foucault: power everywhere
docs.text:
The French philosopher Michel Foucault (1926–1984) argued that modern power is not mainly something held by a sovereign and exercised from the top down. It is diffused through institutions such as prisons, schools, hospitals, armies and factories, which discipline bodies and shape conduct through surveillance, timetables, examinations and the classification of people as normal or abnormal. In Discipline and Punish (1975) he took as a symbol Jeremy Bentham's design for a prison, the Panopticon, in which inmates can always be watched without knowing when, and so come to watch themselves. Foucault also linked power and knowledge: the human sciences, by defining what is normal, both depend on and produce power. Critics ask whether, if power is everywhere, it is still possible to distinguish just from unjust power, or to resist on principle.

Thinker Where power is found What power mainly is Dahl Observable decisions Getting others to do what they would not otherwise do Bachrach and Baratz Decisions and non-decisions Also keeping issues off the agenda Lukes Decisions, agendas and preferences Affecting others contrary to their interests, including by shaping wants Gramsci State and civil society Coercion plus consent (hegemony) Arendt Groups acting together The ability to act in concert; opposed to violence Foucault Everywhere, in institutions and knowledge Disciplinary shaping of conduct

Table 3.2. Theories of power compared.

docs.title: 3.4 Authority
docs.text: Authority is the right to command and to be obeyed. Someone who has authority can expect compliance not because of the threat of force but because those subject to it accept that the command is rightful. Authority therefore economises on force: a state whose laws are accepted as authoritative needs far fewer police.

docs.title: Weber's three types of authority
docs.text:
Max Weber, interested in why people accept domination, distinguished three ideal types of legitimate authority, by the ground on which it is accepted.

  1. Traditional authority rests on belief in the sanctity of long-standing customs and the status of those who rule by them: "it has always been so". Hereditary monarchs, tribal chiefs and patriarchal heads of families are examples. Its weakness is that it struggles to adapt to change.
  2. Charismatic authority rests on devotion to the exceptional personal qualities of a leader: heroism, holiness or extraordinary vision. Prophets, revolutionary leaders and the founders of movements are examples. It is unstable, since it depends on one person, and after the leader's death it must be routinised into traditional or legal forms.
  3. Legal-rational authority rests on belief in the legality of rules and the right of those appointed under them to issue commands. Obedience is owed to the office, not the person. Modern bureaucracies and constitutional governments are the leading examples. Weber saw it as the characteristic form of modern authority, efficient but potentially an "iron cage" of impersonal rules.
Figure 3.2 Weber's three types of authority. A triangle with the three Weberian types of authority at its corners: traditional authority based on custom, charismatic authority based on personal qualities, and legal-rational authority based on rules and offices. Arrows show that charismatic authority is routinised into the other two over time.

These are ideal types: real cases mix them. A constitutional monarch combines traditional and legal authority; a popular elected leader adds charisma to a legal office.

docs.title: In authority and an authority
docs.text:
Philosophers distinguish two senses of authority.

  • A person is in authority when they occupy a position in a system of rules that entitles them to command: a police officer, a judge, a minister. Their authority is de jure (by right under the rules).
  • A person is an authority when their knowledge or expertise gives us reason to defer to their judgement: a doctor on medicine, a historian on the past. This is epistemic authority.

A third distinction is between de jure authority (the right to rule, according to some rules or principles) and de facto authority (actually being obeyed, and being widely believed to have the right). A government that has seized power in a coup may have de facto authority without de jure authority; a government in exile may claim de jure authority without being obeyed.

Key idea

Power is the capacity to get others to act as one wishes; authority is power accepted as rightful. Weber's three grounds of acceptance are tradition, charisma and legal rules.

docs.title: 3.5 Legitimacy
docs.text: Legitimacy comes from the Latin legitimare, to declare lawful. In political theory it means the rightfulness of a political order, the quality that gives it a claim to obedience and support.

docs.title: Sociological and normative legitimacy
docs.text:
There are two quite different ways of thinking about legitimacy.

  • Sociological (or empirical) legitimacy, in Weber's tradition, is a matter of belief: a regime is legitimate to the extent that the people subject to it believe it rightful. This can be studied by surveys and observation. On this view even an unjust regime can be legitimate if people accept it.
  • Normative legitimacy is a matter of justification: a regime is legitimate if it really does have the right to rule, according to sound moral principles, whatever people believe. On this view the question is not whether people accept the regime but whether they ought to.

docs.title: Beetham's three criteria
docs.text:
The British political theorist David Beetham, in The Legitimation of Power (1991), criticised Weber for reducing legitimacy to belief. Power is legitimate, he argued, to the extent that three conditions hold:

  1. it is acquired and exercised according to established rules (legal validity);
  2. the rules can be justified by beliefs shared by both rulers and ruled, for example that authority should come from the people and serve the common interest;
  3. there is evidence of consent by the subordinate, through actions such as voting, swearing allegiance or signing agreements.

When the first fails, power is illegitimate; when the second fails, there is a "legitimacy deficit"; when the third fails, power is "delegitimated" (as when mass protests withdraw consent).

docs.title: Sources of legitimacy
docs.text: Different traditions have located the source of legitimacy in different places: divine will, tradition, the consent of the governed, democratic procedure, the protection of rights, good outcomes such as prosperity and security, or conformity to a constitution. Most modern democratic theory combines procedural legitimacy (power is acquired and exercised fairly, through free elections under the rule of law) with substantive legitimacy (power respects basic rights and serves the common good).

docs.title: Legitimation crisis
docs.text:
The German philosopher Jürgen Habermas, in Legitimation Crisis (1973), argued that modern welfare states face a recurring problem. They must manage the economy and promise welfare, so they are blamed when the economy fails; but if they cannot meet rising expectations, citizens lose faith in the system. Whether or not one accepts Habermas's particular analysis, the idea that regimes can lose legitimacy through failure to deliver what they promise has been widely used.

Worked example 3.2: Assessing legitimacy

Situation. A military group overthrows an elected government, citing corruption. It promises elections within two years. Many citizens, tired of corruption, welcome the change; others protest and are arrested.

Analysis. By Beetham's first criterion, power was not acquired according to established rules: the constitution was overthrown. By the second, the justification offered (ending corruption) may be widely shared, but the rule that authority should come from the people is violated. By the third, consent is mixed: some welcome the coup, but arrests suggest consent is being forced. Sociologically, the regime may enjoy some legitimacy in the short run; normatively, most democratic theories would judge it illegitimate unless and until power is returned through fair procedures.

docs.title: 3.6 Political obligation
docs.text:
If a state is legitimate, do its citizens have a moral duty to obey its laws? The problem of political obligation asks why, and when, people ought to obey the law simply because it is the law, even when they disagree with it and could disobey without being caught. Several answers have been offered.

  • Consent. We are obliged because we have agreed to obey. This is the social contract answer (Chapter 2). Its difficulty is that few people have ever consented expressly, and tacit consent, by staying in the country or voting, seems too weak, as Hume argued.
  • Gratitude. We owe obedience to the state as we owe gratitude to parents, for the benefits it has given us. In Plato's dialogue Crito, Socrates refuses to escape from prison before his execution partly on this ground: the laws of Athens had raised and educated him. Critics reply that benefits we did not request do not create strict duties.
  • Fair play. H. L. A. Hart (1955) and later Rawls argued that when people take part in a mutually beneficial cooperative scheme, accepting its benefits, they are obliged to do their share and not free-ride on others' compliance. Robert Nozick objected that benefits pressed on us without our choice cannot bind us: if neighbours set up a public address system and take turns entertaining the street, do I have to take my turn because I sometimes hear the music?
  • Natural duty. Rawls also argued that we have a natural duty of justice to support and comply with just institutions that apply to us, whether or not we consented. The difficulty is to explain why the duty attaches to our state in particular.
  • Utility. Utilitarians argue that general obedience to law produces better consequences than disobedience. This supports obedience in general, but seems to allow disobedience whenever breaking a particular law would produce better results.
  • Philosophical anarchism. Some theorists, such as A. John Simmons and Robert Paul Wolff, conclude that none of these arguments succeeds, so that there is no general obligation to obey the law as such. This does not mean we should break laws: we usually have independent moral reasons not to steal or assault. It means that the fact that something is the law does not by itself create a duty.

docs.title: 3.7 Civil disobedience
docs.text:
Even where there is a general obligation to obey, there may be laws so unjust that disobedience is justified. Civil disobedience is a public, non-violent, conscientious breach of law, undertaken to bring about a change in laws or policies, by people who accept the legal penalty. Rawls, in A Theory of Justice, gave a classic definition along these lines and argued that in a nearly just society civil disobedience can be justified when it addresses serious and clear injustice, when normal legal means have been tried and failed, and when it does not threaten the stability of the constitutional order.

The American writer Henry David Thoreau refused to pay a tax in protest against slavery and the war against Mexico, and spent a night in jail in 1846; his essay of 1849, later known as "Civil Disobedience", argued that individuals should not let governments override their consciences. Mohandas Gandhi developed civil disobedience into a mass method of struggle, satyagraha, in South Africa and India, most famously in the Salt March of 1930 (Chapter 13). Martin Luther King Jr. led campaigns of non-violent civil disobedience against racial segregation in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s, arguing in his letter from Birmingham jail (1963) that one has a moral responsibility to disobey unjust laws, openly and lovingly, accepting the penalty.

Feature Why it matters Public Done openly, often with advance notice, to appeal to the community's sense of justice Non-violent Respects others' rights and shows the act is a form of address, not coercion Conscientious Motivated by moral conviction, not personal gain Aimed at change Seeks to change a law or policy, not to overthrow the whole system Accepting the penalty Shows fidelity to law in general and sincerity of conviction

Table 3.3. Features usually ascribed to civil disobedience.

Critics on one side argue that civil disobedience undermines the rule of law and invites anyone to disobey any law they dislike; in a democracy, they say, one should use the vote and the courts. Critics on the other side argue that the classic definition is too restrictive: requiring disobedients to accept punishment and avoid all coercion may make resistance to serious injustice ineffective, and the line between civil disobedience and other forms of protest is not always clear.

Worked example 3.3: Is it civil disobedience?

Cases. (a) Students sit in at a restaurant that refuses to serve them because of their caste, and wait to be arrested. (b) A person secretly avoids paying taxes because he thinks taxation is theft. (c) Protesters block a road for an hour to draw attention to a factory's pollution, announce the action in advance and accept arrest.

Answer. (a) Yes: public, non-violent, conscientious, aimed at ending unjust discrimination, penalty accepted. (b) No: it is covert and the penalty is evaded; it is conscientious evasion, not civil disobedience. (c) Probably yes on most definitions, though it imposes costs on uninvolved road users; whether it is justified depends on the seriousness of the issue, whether legal means were tried and whether the disruption is proportionate.

Summary

  • Power is the capacity to make others act as one wishes; influence works by persuasion; force by compulsion; authority is power recognised as rightful; legitimacy is the rightfulness of a political order.
  • Dahl studied power in observable decisions; Bachrach and Baratz added non-decision-making; Lukes added the shaping of preferences against people's interests.
  • Gramsci explained rule by hegemony (consent as well as coercion), Arendt saw power as acting together and opposed to violence, and Foucault saw disciplinary power diffused through institutions and knowledge.
  • Weber distinguished traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority. One can be in authority (by office) or an authority (by expertise); authority may be de jure or de facto.
  • Legitimacy may be understood sociologically (belief) or normatively (justification). Beetham's criteria are legal validity, justifiability by shared beliefs and evidence of consent.
  • Theories of political obligation rest on consent, gratitude, fair play, natural duty or utility; philosophical anarchists deny a general obligation. Civil disobedience is public, non-violent, conscientious law-breaking aimed at change, with acceptance of the penalty.

docs.title: 3.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Explain the difference between power and authority, with an example of power without authority and of authority without much power.

Answer

Power is the capacity to get others to act as one wishes, whether or not it is accepted as rightful; authority is the recognised right to command. Power without authority: an armed robber who makes you hand over your wallet. Authority without much power: a lawfully elected government that has been driven from its capital by rebels still has de jure authority but little power to enforce its commands.

Exercise 2

How did Bachrach and Baratz criticise Dahl? Give an example of non-decision-making.

Answer

They argued that Dahl studied only the first face of power (visible decisions) and missed the second face: the power to keep issues off the agenda, so that some grievances never reach the point of decision. Example: a city council never discusses the poor condition of housing in a particular neighbourhood because its residents are unorganised and powerful landlords sit on the council's committees; the issue is screened out before any vote.

Exercise 3

Classify each as traditional, charismatic or legal-rational authority: (a) a tax officer who demands a return because the law requires it; (b) the head of a religious order chosen by inheritance according to ancient custom; (c) the founder of a new mass movement whose followers believe he has a unique mission.

Answer

(a) Legal-rational: obedience is owed to the office under rules. (b) Traditional: authority rests on custom and hereditary status. (c) Charismatic: authority rests on devotion to extraordinary personal qualities.

Exercise 4

What is the difference between sociological and normative legitimacy? Can a regime be legitimate in one sense and not the other?

Answer

Sociological legitimacy is the belief of those subject to a regime that it is rightful; normative legitimacy is whether it really is rightful by sound principles. Yes: a regime that has convinced its population by propaganda that it is divinely ordained may be sociologically legitimate but normatively illegitimate; a just government facing a hostile, misinformed population may be normatively legitimate but lack sociological legitimacy.

Exercise 5

Explain the fair-play theory of political obligation and Nozick's objection to it.

Answer

The fair-play theory (Hart, Rawls) holds that those who accept the benefits of a just cooperative scheme, such as a legal order, are obliged to do their part and not free-ride on others' compliance. Nozick objected that benefits imposed on people without their choice do not create obligations: a neighbourhood entertainment system that I happen to enjoy does not oblige me to take my turn running it. Defenders reply that some benefits (security, the rule of law) are so important that anyone would accept them, so receiving them can still create obligations.

Exercise 6

List the features of civil disobedience and give one argument for and one against its use in a democracy.

Answer

Civil disobedience is public, non-violent, conscientious, aimed at changing a law or policy, and accepts the penalty. For: democratic majorities can commit serious injustice, especially against minorities who cannot win votes; civil disobedience appeals to the majority's sense of justice and has helped end injustices such as racial segregation. Against: in a democracy there are legal channels for change, and breaking laws one disagrees with may encourage others to do the same, weakening the rule of law.

Exercise 7

How does Arendt distinguish power from violence, and what does her view imply about a government that rules only by force?

Answer

For Arendt, power is the ability of people to act together in concert; it belongs to a group and depends on its cohesion and support. Violence is instrumental, relying on implements, and can destroy power but not create it. A government that rules only by violence has, in her sense, lost its power: violence appears where power is failing.

docs.title: Preface
docs.text: What political theory is for, and how to read this book

docs.title: About this book
docs.text:
Every society has to answer the same few questions. Who should rule, and why should anyone obey them? How much may the state tell us what to do? What do we owe one another, and what may we keep for ourselves? Who belongs to the community, and on what terms? Political theory is the careful, reasoned study of such questions. It does not ask only how political life works; it also asks how it ought to work, and it tests the answers by argument.

This book is an introduction to that study. It explains the central concepts of politics (the state, sovereignty, power, authority, liberty, equality, justice, rights, democracy, citizenship, nationalism and secularism), the great families of political ideas (liberalism, conservatism, socialism and Marxism, feminism, environmentalism and others), the political thought of modern India, and the questions of justice and human rights that cross national borders.

The book tries hard to be fair. Political theory is a field of disagreement: thoughtful people reach opposite conclusions about liberty, equality or the proper role of religion in public life. For every major view the book sets out what it says, the reasons offered for it, and the main criticisms made of it. It does not tell you which view to hold. Its aim is to help you understand each position well enough to state it in a way its own defenders would accept, and then to judge it for yourself. The book makes no claims about present-day politicians or political parties; where it discusses events, they are historical.

docs.title: Who it is for
docs.text:
The book is written for a reader meeting the subject for the first time:

  • a student in a first university course in political science, philosophy, law, sociology or public policy;
  • a candidate preparing for a competitive examination with a paper on political theory or political thought;
  • a teacher, a journalist or any citizen who wants to think more clearly about the arguments heard in public life.

No background is needed beyond school. Technical words are explained when they first appear, and the glossary at the end collects them.

docs.title: How the book is organised
docs.text:
The fourteen chapters are grouped in five parts.

Part Chapters What it covers I. Foundations 1–3 What political theory is; the state and sovereignty; power, authority and legitimacy II. Core values 4–7 Liberty; equality; justice (including Rawls, Nozick and Sen); rights III. Democracy and belonging 8–10 Democracy; citizenship and nationalism; secularism IV. Ideologies and traditions 11–13 Liberalism, conservatism, socialism and Marxism; feminism, environmentalism and other ideologies; Indian political thought V. Beyond the state 14 Global justice and human rights

Table P.1. The plan of the book.

The order is deliberate. The first part explains the basic setting of politics: an organised community with a state that claims the right to rule. The second part examines the values by which that rule is judged. The third asks who governs and who belongs. The fourth shows how values are combined into larger outlooks, and how Indian thinkers worked on the same questions in their own circumstances. The last part asks whether the ideas of justice and rights stop at the borders of the state.

docs.title: How each chapter is built
docs.text:
Every chapter has the same parts, so that you always know where you are.

  • Learning outcomes at the top say what you should be able to do when you have finished the chapter.
  • Numbered sections move from an everyday puzzle to a precise statement of the concept and the main theories about it.
  • Boxes pick out what matters. A key idea box states the one thing in a section not to forget. A note adds a detail, a piece of history or a link to another chapter. A caution marks a common confusion.
  • Worked examples take a concrete case (a ban on a protest march, a scholarship scheme, a dispute about a school uniform) and show how the theories in the chapter would analyse it.
  • Figures and tables show comparisons and structures that are hard to hold in words.
  • A summary collects the chapter in a few points.
  • Exercises come with answers folded under them. Try each one before you open the answer. Many exercises have no single right answer; the folded text then shows what a good answer would contain.
  • A short quiz at the end lets you check yourself; it remembers your answers in your browser.

docs.title: How to use it
docs.text:
Read the chapters in order the first time. Later chapters lean on earlier ones: justice (Chapter 6) uses the ideas of liberty and equality from Chapters 4 and 5, and the ideologies of Chapters 11 and 12 combine almost every concept in the book.

Four habits will help you more than any amount of memorising.

  1. Define before you argue. Many political quarrels are really disagreements about the meaning of a word. Before you ask whether a law restricts liberty, ask which idea of liberty you have in mind.
  2. Look for the reasons. A position in political theory is only as good as the arguments for it. When you meet a claim, ask what reasons support it and what would count against it.
  3. State the other side at its strongest. You do not understand a view until you can present it as well as its best defender would. Then criticise it.
  4. Test theories against cases. A principle that sounds attractive in general may give a strange answer in a particular case. Use the worked examples, and invent your own.

docs.title: A note on sources and quotations
docs.text: The thinkers discussed in this book wrote over more than two thousand years, in many languages. Their ideas are explained here in plain words. Short quotations are given only from works that are long out of copyright (such as those of Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Mill, Wollstonecraft and Tagore), from public records, or where a phrase has become a well-known part of the language of politics. Everything else is paraphrase. Dates given for books are the dates of first publication. The list of further reading at the end names standard editions and textbooks for going deeper; reading at least one primary text in full, such as Mill's On Liberty, is the best next step after this book.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Rights
docs.text:
What rights are, where they come from, and what they demand of others

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • define a right and distinguish moral from legal rights;
  • use Hohfeld's four categories (claims, liberties, powers and immunities) to analyse a right;
  • compare the will (choice) theory and the interest theory of rights;
  • trace the idea of natural rights from Locke to the declarations of the eighteenth century, and state the criticisms of Bentham, Burke and Marx;
  • distinguish negative and positive rights and the three "generations" of rights;
  • discuss the relation between rights and duties, conflicts of rights, and group rights.

docs.title: 7.1 The language of rights
docs.text:
Modern politics is full of rights: the right to life, to free speech, to vote, to education, to food, to a clean environment, to privacy. Many political demands are made in this language. A group that wants something from the state does not usually say "it would be good if we had it"; it says "we have a right to it". Why is the language of rights so powerful, and what exactly is being claimed?

A right is a justified claim or entitlement that a person holds, which others are required to respect. To have a right is to be in a position to demand something as one's due, not merely to hope for it as a favour. If I have a right to something, others who fail to respect it do not merely act badly; they wrong me. Rights thus have three features that distinguish them from other moral considerations.

  • They belong to someone. A right has a holder, who is wronged when it is violated.
  • They correspond to duties of others. If I have a right to life, others have a duty not to kill me.
  • They carry special weight. Rights cannot be overridden simply because overriding them would produce slightly better results overall. Ronald Dworkin captured this with the phrase rights as trumps: in a card game a trump beats any card of an ordinary suit, and a right beats ordinary considerations of general welfare.

docs.title: Moral and legal rights
docs.text:
• A legal right is one recognised and enforced by a legal system. Whether someone has a legal right is a question of fact about the law: what the statute, constitution or court decision says.
  • A moral right is one that a person has according to sound moral principles, whether or not the law recognises it. Slaves had a moral right to freedom even when the law denied it.

Much political argument is about turning moral rights into legal ones. Many rights now in constitutions, such as equal citizenship for women or the abolition of untouchability, began as moral claims made against the law of the time.

docs.title: 7.2 The structure of rights: Hohfeld
docs.text:
The American legal theorist Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld, in work published in 1913 and 1917, showed that the word "right" is used for four quite different relations. His analysis is still the standard tool for clarifying what a right involves.

Hohfeldian element Meaning Correlative (what others have) Example Claim (claim-right) A is owed something by B B has a duty to A A has a claim that B repay the loan Liberty (privilege) A is free to do something; A has no duty not to B has no claim that A not do it A is at liberty to wear a red shirt Power A can change legal relations B has a liability to have them changed A can sell her house, transferring ownership Immunity B cannot change A's legal relations B has a disability Parliament cannot by ordinary law abolish a constitutional right

Table 7.1. Hohfeld's four elements of rights.

Most important rights are bundles of these elements. The right of ownership of a book includes a liberty to read it, a claim that others not take it, a power to sell or give it away, and an immunity from having it taken without due process. The right to free speech includes a liberty to speak, a claim that the state not punish one for speaking, and (in a constitutional democracy) an immunity against ordinary legislation abolishing it.

Worked example 7.1: Analysing a right

Right. "Every citizen has the right to vote."

Analysis. The citizen has a liberty to vote or not (no duty to vote, unless voting is compulsory); a claim against election officials that they register her, give her a ballot and count her vote, with corresponding duties on them; a power, together with other voters, to change who holds office; and, in a constitutional system, an immunity: the legislature cannot remove the right by ordinary law. Saying exactly which elements are meant clarifies disputes. For example, an argument that compulsory voting violates the right to vote is really a claim that the right includes a liberty not to vote.

docs.title: 7.3 Two theories of what rights do
docs.text: Why do people have rights at all? Two theories dominate.

docs.title: The will (choice) theory
docs.text:
The will theory, defended by H. L. A. Hart and others, holds that the function of a right is to give the right-holder control over another's duty. To have a right is to be a "small-scale sovereign": you may demand that the duty be performed, waive it, or enforce it. If B promises to help A move house, A has a right because A can release B from the promise or insist on it.

Strength: it explains why rights are bound up with freedom and choice, and why right-holders can waive their rights.

Weakness: it seems to deny rights to beings who cannot exercise choice, such as infants, people in a coma or animals; yet we think infants have a right not to be tortured. It also has difficulty with rights that cannot be waived: most legal systems do not let people sell themselves into slavery.

docs.title: The interest (benefit) theory
docs.text:
The interest theory, defended by Joseph Raz, Neil MacCormick and others, holds that the function of a right is to protect an interest of the right-holder. On Raz's definition, X has a right if an aspect of X's well-being (interest) is a sufficient reason for holding some other person to be under a duty.

Strength: it explains the rights of infants and others who cannot choose, and inalienable rights.

Weakness: it may be too broad, since many people benefit from duties without having rights (if A promises B to look after B's elderly mother, the mother benefits, but it is B who seems to hold the right). Will theorists also say it loses the special connection between rights and autonomy.

Key idea

A right is a justified entitlement that imposes duties on others and carries special weight. The will theory says rights give holders control over others' duties; the interest theory says rights protect holders' important interests.

docs.title: Natural rights
docs.text:
The idea that people have rights simply by virtue of being human, independently of any law or government, is the idea of natural rights. It grew from the medieval tradition of natural law and became central in the seventeenth century. John Locke argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty and property that exist in the state of nature and that government is instituted to protect (Chapter 2).

These ideas inspired two famous declarations. The American Declaration of Independence (1776) held it self-evident that all men are created equal and endowed with certain unalienable rights, among them life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments are instituted to secure these rights. The French Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) declared that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, and named the natural and imprescriptible rights of man as liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression.

The universal language of these declarations contrasted sharply with practice: the American republic kept slavery, and neither declaration extended equal rights to women. Critics used the declarations' own principles against these exclusions. In France, Olympe de Gouges wrote a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen (1791); in England, Mary Wollstonecraft wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792).

docs.title: Three classic criticisms
docs.text:
Bentham. The utilitarian Jeremy Bentham rejected natural rights altogether. Real rights, he argued, are created by law; a "natural right" is a right without a law, a contradiction. In a pamphlet written in the 1790s against the French declaration (published later as Anarchical Fallacies), he called natural rights "simple nonsense" and natural and imprescriptible rights "rhetorical nonsense, nonsense upon stilts". He also feared that absolute natural rights would encourage people to resist any law they disliked.

Burke. The conservative Edmund Burke, in Reflections on the Revolution in France (1790), did not deny that people have rights, but he preferred the concrete, inherited rights of Englishmen, built up over centuries, to abstract rights derived from reason. Abstract rights, he argued, ignore circumstances, invite endless claims and justify the destruction of institutions that actually protect liberty.

Marx. In On the Jewish Question (1844), Karl Marx argued that the rights of man proclaimed in the French declarations were the rights of egoistic man, separated from other men and from the community. The right of property is the right to use one's possessions without regard to others; liberty is the liberty of man as an isolated monad. Such rights achieved political emancipation (freeing the state from religion and privilege) but not human emancipation, which would require overcoming the division between the political citizen and the self-interested member of market society.

docs.title: Rights without "nature"
docs.text: Many modern theorists defend human rights without relying on a contested metaphysics of nature. Some ground them in human dignity or basic human needs; some in the conditions of agency (what any agent needs in order to act purposefully); some in the requirements of a decent political order. Others treat human rights as a practical, political agreement among people of different traditions, as the drafters of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights did in 1948 (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 7.5 Negative and positive rights; generations of rights
Negative and positive rights
docs.text:
• A negative right is a right that others refrain from doing something to the holder: not to kill, torture, imprison arbitrarily or censor. It imposes duties of non-interference.
  • A positive right is a right that others provide something: education, health care, a minimum income, legal aid. It imposes duties of assistance.

Some libertarians argue that only negative rights are genuine rights, because they can always be satisfied together (everyone can refrain from killing everyone else at once), cost nothing and do not require taking from some to give to others. Positive rights, they say, depend on resources, conflict with each other and involve coercing some to serve others.

Critics answer that the distinction is less sharp than it seems. Henry Shue, in Basic Rights (1980), argued that every right involves several kinds of duty: to avoid depriving, to protect from deprivation, and to aid the deprived. Protecting even "negative" rights, such as the right not to be assaulted, requires police, courts and prisons, all paid for by taxes. And security and subsistence, Shue argued, are equally basic, because without them no other right can be enjoyed.

docs.title: Generations of rights
docs.text:
In 1977 the jurist Karel Vasak proposed dividing human rights into three "generations", loosely matching the French revolutionary ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity.

Figure 7.1 Three generations of rights. Three columns showing the generations of rights. First generation: civil and political rights, associated with liberty, such as life, free speech, fair trial and the vote. Second generation: economic, social and cultural rights, associated with equality, such as work, education, health and social security. Third generation: solidarity or collective rights, associated with fraternity, such as development, peace, a healthy environment and self-determination.
  1. First generation: civil and political rights. Life, liberty, security of the person, freedom from torture and slavery, fair trial, freedom of thought, religion, expression and assembly, and the right to vote. Many are negative rights. They are set out in the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (1966).
  2. Second generation: economic, social and cultural rights. Work, fair wages, social security, an adequate standard of living, health, education and participation in cultural life. Many are positive rights. They are set out in the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (1966), which asks states to realise them progressively to the maximum of their available resources.
  3. Third generation: solidarity rights. Rights to development, peace, a healthy environment and self-determination of peoples. Many are held collectively.

The scheme is a useful teaching device, but it should not be taken too literally. The "generations" did not arise in strict order, and international human rights law since the World Conference on Human Rights in Vienna (1993) has insisted that all human rights are universal, indivisible, interdependent and interrelated. The right to vote means little to someone without education; the right to food is easier to secure where there is a free press to expose famine. Sen famously argued that no substantial famine has ever occurred in a functioning democracy with a relatively free press.

Rights in the Constitution of India

The Constitution of India reflects the distinction between kinds of rights. Part III (Fundamental Rights) lists mainly civil and political rights, which are justiciable: they can be enforced in the courts. Part IV (Directive Principles of State Policy) lists many economic and social goals, such as the right to work, to education and to public assistance, which are declared fundamental in the governance of the country but are not enforceable by any court. Over time the Supreme Court has read some of these goals into the right to life under Article 21, and the right to education for children aged six to fourteen was made a Fundamental Right in Article 21A by the 86th Amendment (2002).

docs.title: 7.6 Rights and duties
docs.text:
Rights and duties are closely linked, in two different ways.

  • Correlativity. Every claim-right of one person corresponds to a duty of another (Hohfeld). My right not to be assaulted is your duty not to assault me.
  • Reciprocity. Some argue that those who claim rights must also accept duties: to obey just laws, to pay taxes, to respect others' rights, to contribute to the community. On this view rights are part of a social relationship of mutual obligation.

The second idea is contested. If rights depended on performing duties, then people who fail in their duties (prisoners, the idle) might lose their rights, including basic human rights. Most theorists hold that human rights are not conditional on good behaviour, while some civic rights may reasonably be linked to responsibilities.

Indian thought has often emphasised duty (dharma) more than rights. Gandhi argued that rights flow from duties well performed: the true source of rights is duty, and if we all discharge our duties, rights will not be far to seek. The Constitution of India added a list of Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Critics of duty-centred approaches worry that they can be used to make people's rights depend on the state's judgement of their conduct; defenders reply that a society of rights-claimers without a sense of obligation cannot sustain itself.

docs.title: 7.7 Conflicts of rights and group rights
Conflicts
docs.text:
Rights can conflict. A newspaper's right to free expression may conflict with a person's right to privacy; a religious group's freedom of religion may conflict with the right of its members to equal treatment; a property owner's rights may conflict with tenants' right to housing. Theories handle conflicts in different ways.

  • Some rank rights in a hierarchy (Rawls gives basic liberties priority over economic advantages).
  • Some argue that apparent conflicts disappear when rights are properly specified: the right to free speech never included a right to defame.
  • Many courts use balancing or proportionality: a restriction of one right is permissible if it pursues a legitimate aim, is suitable and necessary to achieve it, and does not impose a burden disproportionate to the benefit.

Worked example 7.2: A conflict of rights

Situation. A magazine plans to publish photographs of a well-known film actor taken secretly inside his home. The actor seeks to stop publication.

Analysis. The magazine invokes freedom of the press; the actor invokes privacy. A proportionality approach asks: does publication serve a legitimate public interest (such as exposing wrongdoing by a public official) or merely satisfy curiosity? Is there a less intrusive way of serving any public interest? Most legal systems would protect the actor here, because the intrusion is serious and the public interest weak. If the photographs showed him committing a crime relevant to public safety, the balance might shift.

docs.title: Group rights
docs.text:
Are there rights held by groups rather than individuals? Examples include the right of peoples to self-determination, the rights of indigenous peoples to their lands, and the right of religious or linguistic minorities to run their own educational institutions (protected in India by Article 30).

  • Defenders, such as Will Kymlicka (Multicultural Citizenship, 1995), argue that some goods, such as a living culture or language, are inherently shared and can be protected only collectively, and that minority cultures need protection against assimilation by the majority. Kymlicka distinguished external protections (which protect a group against pressure from the wider society, and which he supported) from internal restrictions (which limit the freedom of the group's own members, and which he opposed).
  • Critics argue that only individuals have moral standing, so that "group rights" are best understood as individual rights exercised together; and they worry that group rights can empower traditional leaders to oppress dissenters, women or other vulnerable members within the group.

Summary

  • A right is a justified entitlement that belongs to a holder, imposes duties on others and carries special weight (Dworkin's "rights as trumps"). Rights may be moral or legal.
  • Hohfeld distinguished claims (with correlative duties), liberties, powers and immunities; most rights are bundles of these.
  • The will theory says rights give their holders control over others' duties; the interest theory says rights protect important interests.
  • Natural rights (Locke) inspired the American (1776) and French (1789) declarations. Bentham called natural rights "nonsense upon stilts"; Burke preferred inherited rights; Marx saw them as the rights of egoistic man.
  • Negative rights require non-interference, positive rights require provision; Shue argued that all rights involve both kinds of duty. Vasak's three generations are civil and political, economic and social, and solidarity rights, but human rights are indivisible.
  • Rights correlate with duties; whether they depend on performing duties is contested. Conflicts of rights are often resolved by proportionality. Group rights protect shared goods but raise concerns about internal restrictions.

docs.title: 7.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Distinguish moral from legal rights and give an example of a moral right that was once not a legal right.

Answer

A legal right is recognised and enforced by a legal system; a moral right is held according to sound moral principles whether or not the law recognises it. Example: the right of women to vote was a moral right before it was recognised in law (in many countries only in the twentieth century); so was the right of enslaved people to freedom.

Exercise 2

Using Hohfeld's categories, analyse a person's right to make a will leaving her property to whomever she chooses.

Answer

It is mainly a power: she can change legal relations by creating new ownership rights for her beneficiaries, who have a corresponding liability to have their legal position changed. It includes a liberty to choose any beneficiary (no duty to choose a particular one, subject to the law of the land), a claim that courts and executors respect the will, and possibly an immunity against others altering it.

Exercise 3

Why does the will theory have difficulty with the rights of infants? How does the interest theory deal with them?

Answer

On the will theory a right gives its holder control (to waive or enforce) over another's duty. Infants cannot exercise such choices, so the theory seems to imply that they have no rights, which is counter-intuitive. The interest theory says a right exists where a person's interest is sufficient reason to impose a duty on others; infants have strong interests (in not being harmed, in being fed), so they have rights, which others may enforce on their behalf.

Exercise 4

State Bentham's, Burke's and Marx's criticisms of natural rights in one sentence each.

Answer

Bentham: rights are created by law, so "natural rights" are nonsense, and natural and imprescriptible rights "nonsense upon stilts". Burke: abstract rights derived from reason ignore circumstances and are inferior to concrete rights inherited through tradition. Marx: the rights of man are the rights of egoistic man separated from community, giving political but not human emancipation.

Exercise 5

Explain Shue's argument against a sharp distinction between negative and positive rights.

Answer

Shue argued that every right involves three kinds of duty: to avoid depriving, to protect against deprivation and to aid the deprived. Even "negative" rights such as security require positive action and resources (police, courts), while "positive" rights such as subsistence also involve duties not to deprive. Security and subsistence are both basic rights, since without them no other right can be enjoyed.

Exercise 6

What does it mean to say that human rights are "indivisible"? Give an example of how one kind of right depends on another.

Answer

It means that civil and political rights and economic, social and cultural rights form a single whole: none can be fully enjoyed without the others, and none should be ranked as optional. Example: the right to vote is hard to use meaningfully without education; conversely, the right to food is better protected where free speech and a free press expose hunger and press governments to act.

Exercise 7

Distinguish Kymlicka's external protections from internal restrictions, with an example of each.

Answer

External protections protect a minority group against pressure from the wider society, for example guaranteed funding for schools teaching in a minority language. Internal restrictions limit the liberty of the group's own members in the name of tradition, for example a rule preventing members from leaving the group or women from inheriting property. Kymlicka supported the first, under conditions, and opposed the second.
