docs.title: Chapter 10: Secularism
docs.text:
Religion, the state and equal citizenship: models, debates and the Indian case

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • distinguish secularism as a political doctrine from secularisation as a social process;
  • explain the historical origins of secularism and the argument for religious toleration;
  • compare the main models of the relation between state and religion: established religion, strict separation, laïcité and the Indian model of principled distance;
  • describe the constitutional provisions on religion in India and the main judicial statements on secularism;
  • state the main criticisms of secularism, including those made in the Indian debate, fairly;
  • apply different models to concrete cases such as religious dress, funding of religious schools and personal laws.

docs.title: 10.1 The problem
docs.text:
Every society with more than one religion, or with religious and non-religious citizens, faces a basic question: how should the state relate to religion? Should it support one religion, all religions or none? Should it stay out of religious matters entirely, or intervene to reform religious practices that harm people? Should religious arguments have a place in public debate? These questions have produced wars, persecutions and revolutions, and they remain among the most contested in politics.

Secularism is a family of answers to these questions. In its most general sense it is the political doctrine that the state should not be governed by or identified with any religion, and that citizens' rights and status should not depend on their religious beliefs. But, as this chapter shows, secular states differ greatly in how they put the doctrine into practice.

docs.title: Secularism and secularisation
docs.text:
Two words are often confused.

  • Secularisation is a social process: the declining influence of religion over social institutions and individual belief, which sociologists once expected to accompany modernisation. Whether it is happening, and where, is an empirical question; the expectation of universal secularisation has been widely questioned since the late twentieth century.
  • Secularism is a political doctrine about the proper relation between state and religion. A deeply religious society can have a secular state, and a largely non-religious society can have an established church. The United Kingdom has an established Church of England while being one of the less religious societies in Europe; the United States has strict constitutional separation and a comparatively religious population.

The word "secularism" was coined in English in 1851 by George Jacob Holyoake, as a name for an ethics based on reason and concern for this world, independent of religion.

docs.title: 10.2 Origins: from toleration to secularism
docs.text:
Modern secularism in Europe grew from the wars of religion of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, which followed the Protestant Reformation. When Catholics and Protestants fought for control of states, and each regarded the other as heretics, peace required some way of living together.

The first answer was the principle cuius regio, eius religio ("whose realm, his religion") of the Peace of Augsburg (1555): each prince chose the religion of his territory. This ended some wars but not persecution of minorities.

A deeper answer was toleration. John Locke, in A Letter Concerning Toleration (1689), argued that the business of civil government is limited to protecting life, liberty, health and possessions; the care of souls does not belong to the magistrate. Coercion cannot produce genuine belief, since true religion consists in inward persuasion of the mind; so persecution is both wrong and futile. Locke's toleration was limited by the standards of later times: he did not extend it to atheists, whose oaths he thought could not be trusted, or to Catholics, whom he suspected of allegiance to a foreign power.

Toleration means putting up with beliefs and practices one disapproves of. Secularism goes further: it seeks a state that does not take sides among religions at all, treating all citizens as equals regardless of belief. This idea was expressed in the First Amendment to the United States Constitution (1791), which forbids Congress to make any law respecting an establishment of religion or prohibiting its free exercise, and in the French Revolution's attack on the privileges of the Catholic Church.

Toleration in Indian history

Ideas of tolerance and coexistence also have deep roots in Indian history. The edicts of the Mauryan emperor Aśoka (third century BCE) urged respect for all religious sects and restraint in speech about other faiths. The Mughal emperor Akbar (reigned 1556–1605) held discussions among scholars of many religions and promoted a policy of sulh-i kul (peace with all). Historians debate how far such examples anticipate modern secularism, which rests on equal citizenship rather than the benevolence of a ruler, but they show that the problem of religious diversity was addressed in many traditions.

docs.title: 10.3 Models of state and religion
docs.text:
States can be placed along a range, from full identification with a religion to strict exclusion of religion from public life.

Figure 10.1 Models of the relation between state and religion. A spectrum of models of the relation between state and religion. At one end, a theocracy in which religious authorities rule. Then a state with an established religion, which gives one religion official status but grants freedom to others. Then the Indian model of principled distance, in which the state keeps a flexible distance from all religions and may intervene to protect equality. Then strict separation on the American model, with a wall of separation. At the other end, French laïcité, which keeps religion out of public institutions.

docs.title: Theocracy and established religion
docs.text: In a theocracy religious authorities rule, and religious law is state law. In a state with an established religion one religion has official status and privileges (for example in the head of state's role, in education or in state funding), while others may be tolerated or enjoy full freedom. Many democratic states have mild forms of establishment, such as the Church of England, or state churches in some Scandinavian countries, combined with complete religious freedom.

docs.title: Strict separation: the American model
docs.text: The American model is often summed up in Thomas Jefferson's phrase, in a letter of 1802 to the Danbury Baptists, describing a "wall of separation between church and state". The state may neither establish nor favour any religion, nor interfere in religious affairs. Religion is treated mainly as a private matter of individual conscience and voluntary association. In practice the wall has many gaps and has been interpreted differently over time by the courts, for example on prayer in public schools and public funding for religious schools. A distinctive feature of the American model is mutual protection: separation protects the state from religion and religion from the state.

docs.title: Laïcité: the French model
docs.text: French laïcité, established by the law of 1905 separating the churches and the state, emerged from a long struggle against the political power of the Catholic Church. The Republic neither recognises, pays nor subsidises any religion. More than the American model, laïcité seeks to keep religion out of public institutions and public space, in the name of a shared civic identity and the freedom of individuals from religious pressure. A law of 2004 bans the wearing of conspicuous religious symbols (such as headscarves, large crosses, turbans and skullcaps) by pupils in state schools. Supporters see this as protecting the neutrality of the school and the freedom of children; critics argue that it restricts religious freedom and in practice falls hardest on religious minorities.

docs.title: The Indian model: principled distance
docs.text:
The framers of the Constitution of India faced a society of deep and pervasive religious diversity, a history of communal conflict culminating in the violence of Partition, and religious practices (such as untouchability) that denied equality. They did not adopt either strict separation or laïcité. The political theorist Rajeev Bhargava has described the resulting model as principled distance. Its main features are:

  • No established religion. The state does not identify with any religion.
  • Equal respect, not equal indifference. The state may engage with all religions, for example by funding educational institutions run by religious communities on a non-discriminatory basis, or by managing religious endowments.
  • Intervention for equality. The state may intervene in religious practices to promote social reform, equality and dignity. The Constitution itself abolishes untouchability and allows the state to throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.
  • Context-sensitive distance. The state decides when to engage with or keep away from religion, not by a fixed rule of separation, but by asking what the values of liberty and equality require in each case. It may treat different religions differently if that serves those values.

A related idea is sarva dharma samabhāva, "equal regard for all religions", often associated with Gandhi. Supporters of the Indian model argue that it is better suited to deeply religious, diverse societies than models developed in largely Christian Western countries. Its critics argue that the flexibility of principled distance makes it inconsistent and open to political manipulation (section 10.5).

Strict separation (USA) Laïcité (France) Principled distance (India) Established religion None None None State funding of religious institutions Generally not for religious activities; contested for schools Not for worship; some support for private schools under contract Permitted on a non-discriminatory basis, e.g. aid to minority educational institutions Religion in public institutions Limited; no state-led prayer in public schools Strongly excluded; ban on conspicuous symbols in state schools Accommodated; religious symbols generally allowed State intervention in religion Avoided Limited Permitted for social reform and equality Main aim Freedom of conscience; mutual protection Civic unity and individual freedom from religious pressure Equality and freedom in a deeply plural society

Table 10.1. Three models of secularism compared.

Key idea

Secular states share a refusal to establish or be governed by any religion, but they differ in how they relate to religion: the American model builds a wall, laïcité keeps religion out of public institutions, and the Indian model keeps a principled, flexible distance that allows engagement and intervention for the sake of equality.

docs.title: 10.4 Secularism in the Constitution of India
docs.text:
The original Constitution of 1950 did not use the word "secular", though its provisions embodied a secular state. The word was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976), which describes India as a "sovereign socialist secular democratic republic". The main provisions are these.

  • Article 14 (equality before the law) and Article 15 (no discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth).
  • Article 16: equality of opportunity in public employment, without discrimination on grounds of religion.
  • Article 25: freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality and health and to the other Fundamental Rights. The state may regulate secular activities associated with religious practice and provide for social welfare and reform.
  • Article 26: the right of every religious denomination to manage its own affairs in matters of religion.
  • Article 27: no person may be compelled to pay taxes the proceeds of which are specifically used for promoting any particular religion.
  • Article 28: no religious instruction in educational institutions wholly maintained out of state funds.
  • Articles 29 and 30: the right of minorities to conserve their language, script or culture, and to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice.
  • Article 44 (a Directive Principle): the state shall endeavour to secure for citizens a uniform civil code throughout the territory of India.

In S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994) the Supreme Court held that secularism is part of the basic structure of the Constitution, which cannot be destroyed even by constitutional amendment. The Court has also developed the essential religious practices test: the protection of Article 25 extends to practices that are essential or integral to a religion, which the courts decide. This test has been criticised by scholars for requiring judges to decide questions of theology.

docs.title: Personal laws and the uniform civil code
docs.text:
In India, matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption are governed largely by personal laws that differ by religious community. The Hindu personal law was codified and reformed by Parliament in the 1950s (the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, and related acts); the personal laws of other communities have been changed less by legislation. Article 44 sets the goal of a uniform civil code.

The debate is long-standing and has thoughtful participants on several sides.

  • For a uniform code: equal citizenship and gender justice require the same civil laws for all; differing personal laws may disadvantage women; a uniform code would strengthen national integration and secularism.
  • Against imposing a uniform code, or for caution: personal laws are part of the cultural and religious identity protected by the Constitution; reform should come from within communities and with their consent; a uniform code might in practice reflect the customs of the majority; gender justice can be pursued by reforming each personal law.
  • Middle positions include an optional uniform code (as in the Special Marriage Act, 1954, which allows any couple to marry under a common civil law), and reform of personal laws to remove gender discrimination one by one.

docs.title: 10.5 Criticisms of secularism
docs.text: Secularism is criticised from several directions, and each criticism deserves to be stated at its strongest.

docs.title: Religious criticisms
docs.text: Some religious believers argue that secularism privatises religion, treating faith as a matter of personal preference rather than truth, and so marginalises believers in public life. Requiring citizens to give only secular reasons in political debate (Rawls's public reason, Chapter 6) may, they argue, ask believers to leave their deepest convictions at the door. Defenders of secularism reply that a secular state protects all religions, including minority ones, from domination by any one of them, and that many religious citizens support secularism for exactly this reason. Some theorists, such as Jürgen Habermas in later work, have proposed that religious citizens may use religious language in public debate, provided that formal state decisions are justified in terms all can share.

docs.title: Critiques of Western secularism
docs.text: Scholars such as Talal Asad and Charles Taylor (A Secular Age, 2007) have argued that secularism is not a neutral framework but a product of the particular history of Christian Europe, carrying assumptions (for example that religion is essentially a matter of private belief) that may not fit other traditions. Applied elsewhere, it may be experienced as alien.

docs.title: The Indian debate
docs.text:
In the Indian context secularism has been criticised from quite different directions, and the debate is politically sensitive. The criticisms commonly made in scholarly and public debate include the following.

  • Secularism as alien to Indian society. The sociologist T. N. Madan argued in the 1980s that secularism, as a doctrine that confines religion to private life, is a product of the history of Western Christianity that cannot easily be transplanted to South Asia, where religion pervades social life. For the great majority of South Asians, who are active adherents of a faith, he held that it is unworkable as a way of life and impracticable as a basis for state action. The psychologist and social theorist Ashis Nandy argued that the modern state's secularism, imposed from above by elites, can provoke rather than prevent religious conflict, and drew instead on traditions of everyday religious tolerance.
  • Secularism as inconsistent. Critics argue that the state's flexibility in engaging with religions has led to unequal treatment, for example in the different degrees to which various personal laws have been reformed, or in state management of the religious institutions of some communities but not others. Some describe this as favouring minorities; others argue that the state has in practice favoured the majority.
  • Secularism as insufficiently defended. Other critics argue that the secular state has failed to protect minorities against communal violence and discrimination, and that secular principles have been weakened in practice.

Defenders of the Indian model, such as Bhargava, reply that the model's flexibility is a principled response to deep diversity, that inconsistency in practice is a failure to apply the principle, not a defect in it, and that the alternatives (an established religion, or strict separation that would forbid needed reforms) would be worse for both equality and freedom.

docs.title: 10.6 Hard cases
docs.text:
Secularism is tested by concrete cases in which the freedom of religion, the equality of citizens and the authority of the state pull in different directions.

Worked example 10.1: Religious dress in schools

Situation. A government school prescribes a uniform. Some pupils wish to wear a religious head covering with it.

Analysis. Under laïcité (as in the French law of 2004), conspicuous religious symbols are banned in state schools to keep the school a neutral space; the pupils would not be allowed to wear the covering. Under strict separation, the state would generally accommodate individual religious expression, as long as the school does not itself endorse religion. Under principled distance, the question would be whether accommodation respects the pupils' freedom and equal dignity without undermining any important educational purpose or the rights of others. The essential practices test used by Indian courts would ask whether the practice is essential to the religion, a question critics say courts are ill-equipped to answer. The case shows how the same principle, a secular state, can yield opposite conclusions under different models.

Worked example 10.2: Funding religious schools

Situation. A state offers grants to private schools that meet educational standards. Some applicants are run by religious organisations and include religious instruction for pupils who choose it.

Analysis. Strict separation has historically been wary of public funds supporting religious education, though courts in the United States have increasingly allowed neutral programmes that include religious schools. Laïcité forbids funding of worship but allows funding of private (including religious) schools that teach the national curriculum under contract with the state. Principled distance permits non-discriminatory aid: in India, Article 30 protects the right of minorities to establish educational institutions, Article 30(2) forbids the state to discriminate against them in giving aid, and Article 28(3) provides that no one attending a state-aided institution may be required to take part in religious instruction without consent. The key secular requirement in each model is non-discrimination among religions and freedom of the individual pupil.

Summary

  • Secularism is a political doctrine about the relation between state and religion; secularisation is a social process of declining religious influence.
  • Secularism grew from the European wars of religion and the argument for toleration (Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration, 1689); Indian history also contains traditions of tolerance (Aśoka, Akbar).
  • Models range from theocracy and established religion to strict separation (the American "wall of separation"), laïcité (France, 1905) and India's principled distance (Bhargava), which allows engagement with all religions and intervention for equality.
  • The Constitution of India protects religious freedom (Articles 25–28) and minority rights (29–30), forbids religious discrimination, and sets the goal of a uniform civil code (Article 44); "secular" was added to the Preamble in 1976, and S. R. Bommai (1994) made secularism part of the basic structure.
  • Secularism is criticised by some religious thinkers, by critics of its Western origins (Asad, Taylor) and in the Indian debate by Madan and Nandy, and by those who see it as inconsistently or insufficiently applied; defenders argue that principled distance suits deep diversity.

docs.title: 10.7 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Distinguish secularism from secularisation, and give an example showing that the two can come apart.

Answer

Secularism is a political doctrine about the state's relation to religion; secularisation is a social process in which religion's influence declines. They can come apart: the United Kingdom has an established church but a relatively non-religious population; the United States has strict constitutional separation but a comparatively religious population.

Exercise 2

State Locke's main arguments for toleration and two limits of his view.

Answer

Locke argued that (1) the civil government's business is limited to life, liberty, health and possessions, not the care of souls; and (2) coercion cannot produce genuine belief, which depends on inward persuasion, so persecution is futile as well as wrong. Limits: he excluded atheists, whose oaths he thought untrustworthy, and Catholics, whom he suspected of allegiance to a foreign power.

Exercise 3

Compare the American, French and Indian models of secularism on (a) state funding for religious schools and (b) religious symbols in state schools.

Answer

(a) USA: historically wary of funding religious education, though neutral programmes including religious schools have increasingly been allowed. France: no funding of worship, but contract funding for private schools teaching the national curriculum. India: non-discriminatory aid permitted, and minority institutions protected under Article 30. (b) USA: individual religious expression generally accommodated. France: conspicuous symbols banned for pupils in state schools (2004). India: religious symbols generally accommodated, subject to case-by-case judgement.

Exercise 4

What does Bhargava mean by "principled distance"? How does it differ from equal indifference to all religions?

Answer

Principled distance means that the state keeps no fixed distance from religion; it decides when to engage with or keep away from religions according to whether this promotes liberty and equality. It may support religious communities on a non-discriminatory basis or intervene to reform practices that deny equality (e.g. untouchability). Equal indifference (strict separation) would forbid both support and intervention; principled distance allows equal respect and active engagement.

Exercise 5

List four articles of the Constitution of India that bear on secularism, with one sentence on each.

Answer

Any four: Article 15 forbids discrimination on grounds of religion. Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion, subject to limits and to social reform. Article 26 lets religious denominations manage their own religious affairs. Article 27 forbids compelling anyone to pay taxes used to promote a particular religion. Article 28 forbids religious instruction in wholly state-funded institutions. Article 30 gives minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions. Article 44 directs the state to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code.

Exercise 6

Set out one argument for and one argument against a uniform civil code, in a way that its supporters would accept.

Answer

For: equal citizenship and gender justice require that all citizens be governed by the same civil laws on marriage, divorce and inheritance, and some personal laws disadvantage women. Against (or for caution): personal laws are part of the religious and cultural identity that the Constitution protects; change should come with the consent and participation of communities, and a uniform code might in practice reflect majority customs; gender justice can be pursued by reforming each personal law.

Exercise 7

Summarise T. N. Madan's criticism of secularism in India and one reply to it.

Answer

Madan argued that secularism, understood as confining religion to private life, is a product of Western Christian history and is unsuited to South Asia, where religion pervades social life; for most people, who are religious, it is unworkable as a way of life and impracticable as a basis for state action. Reply: the Indian model is not privatisation of religion; principled distance accepts religion's public presence and asks only that the state not be identified with any religion and that it protect equal citizenship, which many religious people themselves support.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The State and Sovereignty
docs.text:
What the state is, where it came from, and the idea of supreme authority

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • define the state and distinguish it from government, nation and society;
  • list the elements of a state and apply them to borderline cases;
  • compare the main theories of the origin of the state, especially the social contract theories of Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau;
  • explain the concept of sovereignty and its kinds: internal and external, legal and political, popular;
  • set out Austin's theory of sovereignty and the pluralist criticism of it;
  • compare liberal, Marxist, pluralist and feminist views of the state, and discuss how globalisation affects sovereignty.

docs.title: 2.1 What is the state?
docs.text:
We speak of "the state" constantly: the state builds roads, the state collects taxes, the state should do more for the poor. Yet the state is not a thing you can point to. You can see a police officer, a court building or a tax form, but the state is the organisation that stands behind all of them and gives them their authority.

The most influential modern definition comes from the German sociologist Max Weber (1864–1920). In a lecture of 1919, "Politics as a Vocation", he defined the state as a human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory. Three parts of this definition matter.

  • Force. What is distinctive about the state is not its aims (many organisations seek welfare or order) but its means: in the last resort it can compel.
  • Monopoly. Other people may use force only with the state's permission, as in self-defence or by private security guards licensed by it.
  • Legitimacy. The state claims that its use of force is rightful, and its claim is broadly accepted. A gang that extorts money uses force too, but it does not claim, and is not granted, the right to do so.

Weber's definition describes what all states have in common; it does not say what states should do. That is a normative question taken up later in this chapter and throughout the book.

docs.title: State, government, nation and society
docs.text:
Four words are often confused.

Term Meaning Example of the difference State The permanent political organisation of a people on a territory, with sovereign authority The Indian state continues while governments change Government The people and institutions that exercise the state's authority at a given time A government can be voted out; the state remains Nation A community of people who see themselves as sharing an identity and a political destiny (Chapter 9) One nation may span several states, and one state may contain several nations Society The whole network of social relations among people, including families, markets, religions and associations Society existed before the modern state and includes much that the state does not control

Table 2.1. State, government, nation and society.

The distinction between state and government is especially important in a democracy. Citizens can oppose the government of the day, campaign against it and vote it out, without being disloyal to the state.

Key idea

The state is the political organisation that claims supreme authority, and a monopoly of legitimate force, over a territory and its people. The government is the agency through which the state acts at any moment.

docs.title: 2.2 The elements of the state
docs.text:
Textbooks traditionally list four elements of a state, and international law uses a similar list. The Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States (1933) says that a state should possess a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states.

Figure 2.1 The four elements of the state. Four elements of the state shown as four boxes around a central circle labelled the state: population, territory, government and sovereignty. Sovereignty is divided into internal sovereignty (supreme authority within) and external sovereignty (independence from outside control).
  1. Population. A state needs people. There is no minimum: the population of some small island states is a few thousand, while India's is well over a billion.
  2. Territory. A state has a defined area of land, with its air space and territorial waters. Borders may be disputed without destroying statehood.
  3. Government. There must be an organisation that makes and enforces laws and conducts relations with other states. A territory with no effective government at all is not, in practice, a functioning state.
  4. Sovereignty. The state's authority is supreme within its territory and independent of external control. This is what distinguishes a state from a province or a municipality, which have population, territory and government but are subject to a higher authority.

Some writers add recognition by other states. Whether recognition creates statehood or merely acknowledges it is disputed in international law. The "declaratory" view holds that an entity meeting the criteria is a state whether or not others recognise it; the "constitutive" view holds that recognition is part of what makes it one.

Worked example 2.1: Is it a state?

Cases. (a) A province of a federal country with its own legislature, police and flag. (b) A territory that declares independence, controls its land and people, but is recognised by almost no other states. (c) A small island country with a population of about ten thousand, a parliament and a seat at the United Nations.

Answer. (a) is not a state: it lacks sovereignty, since the federal constitution and federal law bind it. (b) is a contested case: it has population, territory and government, and claims sovereignty, but its capacity to conduct relations with other states is limited by lack of recognition. On the declaratory view it may be a state; on the constitutive view it is not. (c) is a state: size is not one of the criteria.

docs.title: 2.3 Theories of the origin of the state
docs.text:
How did states come into being, and does their origin tell us anything about why we should obey them? Several theories have been offered. Some are historical guesses; others, notably the social contract, are better read as arguments about justification.

  • Divine origin. The state, and the authority of the ruler, were created by God. In seventeenth-century Europe this became the divine right of kings, defended for example by Robert Filmer, whose Patriarcha (published 1680) argued that kings inherited their authority from Adam. Locke's First Treatise was a reply to Filmer. The theory gave rulers great authority but made it hard to criticise them.
  • Force. The state arose when a strong group conquered and subjugated others. There is historical truth in this: many states were founded by conquest. But it explains how power was seized, not why it should be obeyed.
  • Patriarchal and matriarchal theories. The state grew out of the family, with the authority of the father (or mother) extended to the clan, the tribe and the kingdom. Aristotle described the household growing into the village and the village into the polis.
  • Evolutionary or historical theory. The state grew gradually from many factors together: kinship, religion, the need for defence, the rise of agriculture and property, and political consciousness. Most historians and anthropologists today accept a version of this view.
  • Marxist theory. The state arose when society split into classes with the growth of private property, as an instrument by which the owning class keeps the others in subjection. Friedrich Engels set this out in The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884).
  • Social contract. The state was created, or can be justified, by an agreement among individuals who were previously in a "state of nature" without government.

docs.title: 2.4 The social contract: Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau
docs.text: The social contract tradition is the most important of these theories for political theory, because it links the origin of the state to the question of political obligation: why, and when, should we obey? Its three classic versions start from different pictures of human nature and reach different conclusions.

docs.title: Thomas Hobbes
docs.text:
Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) wrote Leviathan (1651) after the English Civil War. He asked what life would be like with no government at all. People are roughly equal in their ability to harm one another, they compete for scarce goods, they fear one another and they seek glory. Without a common power to keep them in awe, the natural condition would be a war of every man against every man. In this condition there would be no industry, agriculture, arts or society, and, in his famous words, the life of man would be "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short".

Rational people would therefore agree to give up their natural liberty to do whatever they judge necessary for their survival, and to authorise a sovereign (one person or an assembly) to act for them all. The sovereign must be absolute and undivided, since a divided or limited authority would lead back to civil war. Subjects keep only the right to defend their own lives: they need not obey a command to kill themselves, and their obligation ends if the sovereign can no longer protect them.

docs.title: John Locke
docs.text:
John Locke (1632–1704), in the Second Treatise of Government (1689), drew a gentler picture. The state of nature is governed by a law of nature, known by reason, which teaches that no one ought to harm another in his life, health, liberty or possessions. People have natural rights to life, liberty and property (which he called, together, their "property" in a broad sense). The trouble with the state of nature is not constant war but inconvenience: there is no settled known law, no impartial judge and no power to enforce judgements, so each person must judge and punish in his own case.

People therefore consent to form a political society and a government to protect their rights better. The government is a trust: it has limited powers, must rule by known laws, may not take property without consent (through representatives), and should separate the legislative from the executive power. If it violates the trust, by attacking the rights it exists to protect, the people may resist it and establish a new government. Locke's ideas influenced the American Declaration of Independence (1776).

docs.title: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
docs.text:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) opened The Social Contract (1762) with a famous line: "Man is born free; and everywhere he is in chains." In his earlier Discourse on the Origin of Inequality (1755) he had argued that natural man was solitary, peaceful and moved by self-love and pity; it was the growth of property and society that bred inequality, vanity and dependence. The problem was not to return to nature, which is impossible, but to find a form of association in which each person, while uniting with all, obeys only himself and remains as free as before.

His answer is that each person gives himself wholly to the community, which then acts by the general will: the will of the citizens directed at the common good, as distinct from the "will of all", which is merely the sum of private interests. Sovereignty belongs inalienably to the people as a whole and cannot be represented; laws must be made by the citizens themselves. Rousseau added a troubling phrase: whoever refuses to obey the general will shall be compelled to do so by the whole body, which means, he said, that he will be forced to be free. Admirers read Rousseau as a founder of democratic self-government; critics, such as Isaiah Berlin and J. L. Talmon, saw in the general will a danger of tyranny in the name of the people (Chapter 4).

Hobbes Locke Rousseau Main work Leviathan (1651) Second Treatise (1689) The Social Contract (1762) Human nature Self-interested, fearful, competitive Rational, guided by natural law Naturally good, corrupted by society State of nature War of all against all Peaceful but insecure; rights unprotected Solitary and free; later corrupted by property Why contract? Security and survival Better protection of life, liberty and property To regain freedom in society Sovereign Absolute ruler or assembly Limited government under the people's trust The people as a whole (general will) Right to resist Only in self-defence Yes, if government breaks its trust Sovereignty stays with the people

Table 2.2. The three classic social contract theories compared.

docs.title: Criticisms of the social contract
docs.text:
• It never happened. David Hume objected that almost all governments were founded on conquest or usurpation, and that people did not consent to them. Most modern contract theorists accept this and treat the contract as hypothetical: a test of what free and rational people would agree to. Rawls's original position (Chapter 6) is a hypothetical contract of this kind.
  • Consent is thin. Locke suggested that living in a country and using its roads amounts to tacit consent. Hume replied that a poor peasant who knows no foreign language and lives from day to day has no real choice to leave, so his staying is not consent.
  • Who is party to it? Feminist critics, notably Carole Pateman in The Sexual Contract (1988), argued that the classic theories presupposed the subordination of women in the family; critics of colonialism, such as Charles Mills in The Racial Contract (1997), argued that the contract in practice included only some people.

docs.title: 2.5 Sovereignty
docs.text: Sovereignty means supreme authority. The modern idea was first set out systematically by the French jurist Jean Bodin in Six Books of the Commonwealth (1576), during the French wars of religion. Bodin defined sovereignty as the absolute and perpetual power of a commonwealth, and its chief mark as the power to give law to all without the consent of any. Hobbes gave the idea its most uncompromising form.

docs.title: Internal and external sovereignty
docs.text:
• Internal sovereignty is the supremacy of the state over all persons and associations within its territory. No church, corporation or local body has authority except under the state's law.
  • External sovereignty is the independence of the state from control by any other state. In international law all sovereign states are formally equal. This principle is often traced to the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which ended the Thirty Years' War, though historians debate how much the treaties themselves established it.

docs.title: Legal, political and popular sovereignty
docs.text:
• Legal sovereignty belongs to the authority that has the final power to make law, recognised by the courts. In the British system this is Parliament: the constitutional lawyer A. V. Dicey described Parliament as able to make or unmake any law.
  • Political sovereignty belongs to the body whose will is ultimately obeyed in practice and to which the legal sovereign must answer. Dicey placed it with the electorate.
  • Popular sovereignty is the principle that ultimate authority rests with the people. It is proclaimed in many constitutions. The Preamble of the Constitution of India begins "We, the people of India" and says the people "do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution".

In a country with a written constitution and judicial review, such as India or the United States, legal sovereignty is not located in any single organ: the legislature, the executive and the courts each act within limits set by the constitution, which can be changed only by a special procedure. Some writers therefore say that the constitution itself, or the people who authorise it, is sovereign.

docs.title: 2.6 Austin's theory and the pluralist attack
docs.text:
The English jurist John Austin, in The Province of Jurisprudence Determined (1832), gave the classic legal theory of sovereignty. Law is a command of the sovereign, backed by a sanction. The sovereign is a determinate person or body that receives habitual obedience from the bulk of a society, and is not in the habit of obeying any other human superior. On this view sovereignty is:

  • absolute: it has no legal limits;
  • indivisible: it cannot be shared, since two supreme authorities would contradict each other;
  • inalienable: it cannot be transferred without destroying the state;
  • permanent and universal: it lasts as long as the state and extends to everyone within it.

docs.title: Criticisms
docs.text:
Austin's theory was criticised from several sides.

  • Legal theorists, such as H. L. A. Hart in The Concept of Law (1961), argued that law is not simply commands backed by threats. Much law confers powers (to make a contract, a will or a marriage) rather than imposing duties, and the authority of a legislature rests on rules that are accepted, not on habits of obedience to a person.
  • Federal and constitutional states divide authority between levels and organs of government, which Austin's indivisible sovereign cannot easily describe.
  • Pluralists, writing in the early twentieth century, attacked the very idea of a monolithic sovereign. F. W. Maitland and J. N. Figgis argued that churches, trade unions, universities and guilds have a real life and authority of their own, not granted by the state. Harold Laski argued that the state is one association among many, whose claim to obedience depends on how well it serves its members; he wrote that it would be good for political science if the whole concept of sovereignty were surrendered. Pluralists wanted a society in which authority is dispersed and the state coordinates rather than commands.

Caution: two senses of pluralism

"Pluralism" has several meanings in political theory. The pluralist theory of sovereignty (Laski, Figgis) denies that the state's authority is absolute. The pluralist theory of democracy (Dahl, Chapter 8) describes politics as competition among many groups. Value pluralism (Berlin, Chapter 4) holds that there are many genuine values that cannot be reduced to one. And cultural pluralism refers to the coexistence of many cultures (Chapter 12). Always ask which is meant.

docs.title: 2.7 What is the state for? Four views
docs.text: Theories of the state answer two linked questions: whose interests does the state actually serve, and what should it do?

docs.title: The liberal view
docs.text: Liberals see the state as a neutral umpire, created by individuals to protect their rights and settle their disputes. Classical liberals favour a limited or "nightwatchman" state confined to defence, police, courts and the enforcement of contracts. Social liberals accept a larger role: public education, health care and social insurance, to give everyone the real capacity to use their freedom. The welfare state of the twentieth century, built in many democracies after the Second World War, reflects this second view. Libertarians such as Nozick defend the minimal state as the most extensive state that can be justified (Chapter 6).

docs.title: The Marxist view
docs.text: Marx and Engels argued that the state is not neutral. In the Communist Manifesto (1848) they wrote that "the executive of the modern State is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie". The state protects private property and the class that owns the means of production. Later Marxists qualified this. Antonio Gramsci emphasised that ruling classes rule mainly by hegemony, winning consent through culture and ideas, and only partly by force (Chapter 3). Others argued that the state has relative autonomy: it must sometimes act against particular capitalists to preserve the system as a whole. Marx expected that after a revolution and a transitional period the state would eventually "wither away", in Engels's phrase, as classes disappeared.

docs.title: The pluralist view
docs.text: Pluralists see the state as an arena in which many groups (business, labour, professions, religious and regional groups) compete for influence, and policy as the outcome of their bargaining. No single group dominates all decisions. Critics reply that groups are very unequal in resources and access, so that the playing field is tilted, especially towards business; Charles Lindblom made this argument in Politics and Markets (1977).

docs.title: The feminist view
docs.text:
Feminists argue that the state has historically reflected and reinforced male power, for example in laws on property, marriage, citizenship and violence, and by treating the family as a private sphere beyond the reach of justice. Liberal feminists seek to reform the state through equal rights; radical feminists see patriarchy as deeply built into it; others see the state as a site of struggle that can be used to advance women's interests (Chapter 12).

Figure 2.2 How much should the state do? A spectrum from a minimal state to a maximal state. At the minimal end is the anarchist position of no state, then the libertarian nightwatchman state, then the classical liberal state, the welfare state of social liberals and social democrats, and at the far end the state that plans the whole economy. Arrows mark that the debate is about how much the state should do.

docs.title: 2.8 Sovereignty in a globalised world
docs.text:
Is the sovereign state still the main unit of politics? Several developments are often said to challenge it.

  • Economic globalisation. Capital, goods and information move across borders quickly, and states compete to attract investment. Some argue that this limits the real choices open to governments; others reply that states still set taxes, regulate markets and spend large shares of national income.
  • International organisations and law. States accept obligations under treaties, trade agreements, human rights conventions and the United Nations Charter. The European Union is the most developed example of states pooling sovereignty, with a court whose rulings bind member states.
  • Human rights and intervention. The idea that sovereignty includes a responsibility to protect one's population (Chapter 14) qualifies the old principle of non-intervention.
  • Global problems. Climate change, pandemics and financial crises cannot be solved by any one state.
  • Non-state actors. Multinational corporations, transnational movements and armed groups act across borders.

Defenders of the sovereign state point out that states created and can leave most international institutions, that they remain the main providers of security, welfare and rights, and that sovereignty protects weaker states and peoples against domination by stronger ones. This last point was central to anti-colonial movements, for which winning sovereignty was the goal. The debate is not whether sovereignty has disappeared, but how far and in what ways it is being shared, limited or transformed.

Worked example 2.2: Does a treaty limit sovereignty?

Situation. A country signs a treaty agreeing to reduce its emissions of greenhouse gases and to accept international review of its progress.

Analysis. On the legal view, the country exercised its sovereignty by choosing to sign, and could in principle withdraw: sovereignty is intact. On a practical view, its freedom of action is now constrained, since withdrawal would be costly, and some decisions are shaped by international review. A pluralist might say this shows that authority is shared among many bodies, and that this is no bad thing. A defender of strong sovereignty might worry that unelected international bodies weaken democratic self-government. Each view captures something; the example shows why sovereignty is better understood today as a matter of degree.

Summary

  • Weber defined the state as a community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a territory. The state is distinct from the government, the nation and society.
  • Its elements are population, territory, government and sovereignty; international law adds the capacity to enter into relations with other states.
  • Theories of origin include divine right, force, patriarchal, evolutionary, Marxist and social contract theories.
  • Hobbes justified an absolute sovereign as the escape from a war of all against all; Locke a limited government holding power in trust to protect natural rights; Rousseau the sovereignty of the people expressed in the general will.
  • Sovereignty is supreme authority: internal and external; legal, political and popular. Austin saw it as absolute and indivisible; pluralists such as Laski rejected this.
  • Liberals, Marxists, pluralists and feminists give different accounts of whose interests the state serves. Globalisation and international law have made sovereignty more shared and limited, but the state remains central.

docs.title: 2.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Explain each part of Weber's definition of the state, and say why a criminal gang that controls a neighbourhood is not a state.

Answer

The state is a human community that (i) uses physical force as its distinctive means, (ii) holds a monopoly of it, permitting others to use force only by its leave, (iii) claims legitimacy for that use, (iv) within a given territory, and does so successfully. A gang uses force and may control an area, but it neither claims nor is generally granted the right to do so: its force is not regarded as legitimate, and it does not hold a monopoly against the state's own police.

Exercise 2

Distinguish the state from the government. Why does the distinction matter in a democracy?

Answer

The state is the permanent political organisation with sovereign authority; the government is the set of people and institutions exercising that authority at a given time. In a democracy citizens may oppose, criticise and remove the government without being disloyal to the state; treating opposition to a government as hostility to the state would undermine democratic competition.

Exercise 3

Compare Hobbes and Locke on (a) the state of nature, (b) the powers of the sovereign and (c) the right of resistance.

Answer

(a) Hobbes: a war of all against all, with life "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short". Locke: a condition governed by natural law, peaceful but insecure because there is no impartial judge or enforcer. (b) Hobbes: the sovereign is absolute and undivided. Locke: government is limited, a trust bound to protect life, liberty and property and to rule by known laws. (c) Hobbes: subjects may resist only to save their own lives. Locke: the people may resist and replace a government that violates its trust.

Exercise 4

What is the difference between the general will and the will of all in Rousseau? Why have some critics found the idea of the general will dangerous?

Answer

The will of all is the sum of private wills, each aiming at a person's own interest. The general will is the will of citizens directed at the common good. Critics fear that anyone claiming to know the general will may override what people actually want, in the name of their "true" interest; Rousseau's phrase that a person who disobeys may be "forced to be free" seems to license this. Defenders reply that for Rousseau the general will is expressed only through laws that all citizens make together and that apply equally to all.

Exercise 5

State four characteristics of sovereignty according to Austin, and give two criticisms of his theory.

Answer

Austin's sovereign is absolute, indivisible, inalienable and permanent (and universal). Criticisms: (1) Hart: law is not just commands backed by threats; power-conferring rules and accepted rules of recognition are central. (2) Federal and constitutional states divide authority, and sovereignty seems to lie with the constitution or the people rather than a determinate person. (3) Pluralists (Laski, Figgis) argue that associations have authority of their own and the state is not absolute.

Exercise 6

A student says: "Globalisation has made the sovereign state obsolete." Give one argument for and one against.

Answer

For: capital mobility, international law, supranational bodies such as the European Union and global problems such as climate change limit what any state can do alone, so supreme and independent authority is increasingly fictional. Against: states created and can leave international institutions, still raise taxes, make law and provide security, and sovereignty remains the main protection of weaker peoples against domination. Many scholars conclude that sovereignty has been transformed and shared rather than made obsolete.

docs.title: Chapter 1: What Is Political Theory?
docs.text:
Politics, the questions it raises, and the ways of answering them

Learning outcomes

When you have finished this chapter you should be able to:

  • give and compare several definitions of politics;
  • explain what political theory studies and how it differs from empirical political science;
  • distinguish descriptive, explanatory and normative claims, and recognise each in an argument;
  • describe the main methods of political theory: conceptual analysis, normative argument, historical interpretation and reflective equilibrium;
  • outline the history of the subject from ancient Greece and India to its modern revival;
  • explain why political theory matters for citizens and not only for scholars.

docs.title: 1.1 What is politics?
docs.text:
Imagine a village that must decide how to share water from a single well during a dry summer. Some families have large fields, some small ones; some have been in the village for generations, some arrived last year. One family says the water should be shared equally per household; another says per person; a third says it should go first to those whose crops will die without it; a fourth says the families who dug the well should decide. Someone suggests a vote. Someone else asks who may vote, and whether a majority may take the water of a minority.

Nothing in this story involves a government building, a party or an election campaign, yet it is plainly political. It contains the elements that make an activity political:

  • a shared problem that affects many people and cannot be left wholly to each one;
  • disagreement about what should be done, rooted partly in interests and partly in different ideas of what is fair;
  • a need for a decision that will bind everyone, including those who disagreed;
  • questions of power and authority: who decides, by what right, and what happens to those who refuse to comply.

Political scientists have offered several definitions of politics, each catching part of this picture.

Definition Associated with What it emphasises Politics as the art of government The traditional view, going back to the Greek word polis (city-state) The activities of the state and those who run it Politics as public affairs Aristotle; later liberal thinkers The public sphere of common concerns, as opposed to private life Politics as the authoritative allocation of values for a society David Easton, The Political System (1953) Binding decisions about who gets what goods, rights and burdens Politics as who gets what, when, how Harold Lasswell, Politics: Who Gets What, When, How (1936) Competition for scarce resources and influence Politics as compromise and consensus Bernard Crick, In Defence of Politics (1962) Peaceful resolution of conflict by discussion rather than force Politics as power Many writers, including Marxists and feminists Power relations wherever they occur, including the family and the workplace

Table 1.1. Six definitions of politics.

The definitions differ mainly in how wide they draw the boundary. The narrowest confines politics to the state. The widest finds politics wherever power is exercised, which led the feminist movement of the 1960s and 1970s to the slogan "the personal is political": relations within the household, it argued, are shaped by power and can be just or unjust (Chapter 12). Neither boundary is simply correct. Where you draw it is itself a theoretical choice with consequences, because what counts as "political" is what we think may properly be debated and changed by collective action.

Key idea

Politics arises wherever people who disagree must reach decisions that bind them all. It always involves both interests (what people want) and values (what they think is right), and it always raises the question of who has the power and the right to decide.

docs.title: 1.2 What is political theory?
docs.text:
Political theory is the systematic study of the ideas, values and arguments that underlie political life. It asks three kinds of question.

  1. What do our political concepts mean? What is liberty? Is power the same as authority? What makes a group of people a nation?
  2. How should political life be organised? Should the state redistribute wealth? Is democracy the best form of government, and if so, which kind? When, if ever, is it right to break the law?
  3. How have thinkers answered these questions, and why? What did Plato, Kautilya, Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau, Marx, Gandhi or Ambedkar argue, and what problems were they trying to solve?

Political theory is closely related to political philosophy. Some writers use the two terms interchangeably. Others use "political philosophy" for the most abstract and normative work (what justice is, whether the state is legitimate), and "political theory" for a broader field that also includes the history of political ideas, the analysis of ideologies and theories that explain political behaviour. This book uses "political theory" in the broad sense.

It is also related to, and different from, political science in the empirical sense: the study of how political institutions and actors actually behave, using observation, comparison, surveys and statistics. An empirical political scientist might ask why turnout at elections is lower among young voters. A political theorist might ask whether voting should be compulsory, or whether a democracy whose young citizens rarely vote is fully legitimate. The two need each other. Normative arguments that ignore facts are idle, and empirical research always rests on concepts (such as "democracy" or "power") whose meaning has to be worked out.

docs.title: 1.3 Three kinds of claim
docs.text:
The single most useful skill in political theory is the ability to tell what kind of claim is being made. There are three main kinds.

  • A descriptive claim says how things are: "Women won the right to vote in national elections in New Zealand in 1893." It is true or false as a matter of fact.
  • An explanatory claim says why things are as they are: "Countries with higher average incomes are more likely to remain democracies." It is tested by evidence and by reasoning about causes.
  • A normative claim says how things ought to be: "Every adult should have an equal vote." It cannot be settled by facts alone; it needs an argument about values.

Many real arguments mix the three. Consider: "Rent control reduces the supply of housing, so it should be abolished." This contains an explanatory claim (rent control reduces supply) and a normative conclusion (it should be abolished). The conclusion follows only with a hidden normative premise, for example that the goal of housing policy should be to maximise supply, or that the benefits to existing tenants are outweighed by the harm to future ones. Bringing such hidden premises into the open is a basic task of political theory.

Figure 1.1 Three kinds of claim. A diagram with three columns. Descriptive claims ask what is the case and are tested by observation. Explanatory claims ask why it is the case and are tested by evidence about causes. Normative claims ask what ought to be the case and are tested by argument about values. Arrows show that a policy conclusion combines facts with at least one normative premise.

Caution: you cannot get an ought from an is alone

The Scottish philosopher David Hume observed in A Treatise of Human Nature (1739–40) that writers often slide from statements about what is to statements about what ought to be, without explaining how. Facts matter to every political argument, but a conclusion about what should be done always needs at least one premise about what is valuable or right. When an argument seems to move straight from facts to a recommendation, look for the missing value premise.

Worked example 1.1: Taking an argument apart

Argument. "Most citizens in this country follow one religion. Therefore the state should give that religion a special official status."

Analysis. The first sentence is descriptive. The conclusion is normative. To connect them we need a value premise such as "the state should reflect the religion of the majority". Once stated, the premise can be examined. Is it consistent with equal citizenship for members of other religions or of none? Would its defenders accept it if they were in the minority? Chapter 10 discusses the arguments on each side. The point here is that the original argument was incomplete; the real debate is about the hidden premise.

docs.title: 1.4 The methods of political theory
docs.text: Political theory has no laboratory, but it does have methods. Four are especially important.

docs.title: Conceptual analysis
docs.text: Conceptual analysis asks what a concept means and how it is related to others. It often proceeds by drawing distinctions. Is "freedom" the absence of interference, or the ability to act, or not being under another's arbitrary power (Chapter 4)? Is "equality" about treating people the same or about giving them what they need (Chapter 5)? Some concepts are essentially contested, a term introduced by the philosopher W. B. Gallie in 1956: they are evaluative, complex, and open to rival interpretations, and disputes about their proper use cannot be ended by definition alone. "Democracy", "justice" and "freedom" are standard examples. Recognising that a concept is contested does not mean that all interpretations are equally good. It means that choosing between them requires argument rather than a dictionary.

docs.title: Normative argument
docs.text: Normative argument starts from premises about values and reasons towards conclusions about what should be done. It uses the ordinary tools of logic: an argument is valid if the conclusion follows from the premises, and sound if it is valid and the premises are true. Political theorists often test principles by thought experiments, imagined situations designed to isolate one feature of a problem. The state of nature in Hobbes and Locke (Chapter 2) and the veil of ignorance in Rawls (Chapter 6) are famous examples.

docs.title: Historical and contextual interpretation
docs.text: Much political theory consists of reading the great texts of the past. One approach treats them as contributions to a timeless conversation about perennial questions. Another, associated with historians of ideas such as Quentin Skinner and J. G. A. Pocock (the "Cambridge school"), insists that a text must be read in its context: to understand what Machiavelli or Locke meant, we must ask what they were doing in writing, which debates they were entering and which opponents they were answering. The two approaches can be combined: knowing the context guards against reading our own concerns into old texts, while the questions the texts raise often remain alive.

docs.title: Reflective equilibrium
docs.text:
How do we test a moral principle? John Rawls described a method he called reflective equilibrium. We start with our considered judgements about particular cases (slavery is wrong; a fair trial is owed to everyone) and with general principles that seem plausible. Where they conflict, we adjust one or the other, sometimes giving up a principle that yields an unacceptable verdict, sometimes revising a judgement in the light of a principle we find compelling, until principles and judgements fit together. The method is widely used, even by theorists who reject Rawls's conclusions.

Figure 1.2 Reflective equilibrium. A cycle diagram for reflective equilibrium. Considered judgements about cases and general principles are compared. Where they conflict, either the principle is revised or the judgement is revised, and the comparison is repeated until they fit together.

Worked example 1.2: Reflective equilibrium in action

Principle. "The government should always do whatever produces the greatest total happiness."

Test case. A town could prevent a riot that would kill several people by framing and punishing one innocent person. The principle seems to require it.

Adjustment. Most people judge firmly that punishing the innocent is wrong. We might give up the principle, or add a constraint to it (for example, that certain rights of individuals may not be violated even to increase total happiness), or argue that the principle, properly applied, would not recommend framing the innocent because of the long-run damage to trust in the courts. Each option is a move towards equilibrium. This is exactly the debate between utilitarianism and its critics in Chapter 6.

docs.title: 1.5 A short history of political thought
docs.text: Systematic thinking about politics is very old and appears in many civilisations. A brief map helps to place the thinkers who appear later in the book.

docs.title: Ancient Greece
docs.text: The word "politics" comes from the Greek polis, the self-governing city-state. In the fifth and fourth centuries BCE, Athens was a direct democracy in which adult male citizens met in an assembly to decide on laws, war and peace (women, slaves and resident foreigners were excluded). Plato (c. 427–347 BCE), in the Republic, asked what justice is and argued that the ideal city would be ruled by philosophers who understood the good. He was deeply critical of democracy, which had condemned his teacher Socrates to death in 399 BCE. Aristotle (384–322 BCE), in the Politics, described the human being as by nature a political animal, one who can live fully only in a political community. He classified constitutions by who rules (one, few or many) and whether they rule for the common good or for themselves, and he favoured a mixed constitution.

docs.title: Ancient India
docs.text: Indian thought about kingship, law and statecraft is equally ancient. The texts of dharmaśāstra set out the duties (rājadharma) of rulers. The Arthaśāstra attributed to Kauṭilya is a detailed treatise on governing a kingdom: its administration, revenue, law, diplomacy and war. Buddhist texts contain stories of a ruler chosen by the people to keep order. Chapter 13 discusses Kauṭilya at length. Political thought in China (Confucius, Mencius and the Legalists) and in the Islamic world (al-Fārābī, Ibn Khaldūn) also developed rich traditions which this book mentions only in passing.

docs.title: Medieval and early modern Europe
docs.text: In medieval Europe political thought was framed by Christianity: thinkers such as Augustine and Thomas Aquinas asked how earthly government related to divine law. The early modern period brought a decisive change. Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), in The Prince (written in 1513), analysed how rulers actually gain and keep power, separating political skill from conventional morality. The religious wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries prompted new theories of sovereignty and of the state. Thomas Hobbes (Leviathan, 1651), John Locke (Two Treatises of Government, 1689) and Jean-Jacques Rousseau (The Social Contract, 1762) developed versions of the social contract: the idea that political authority is justified by the agreement, actual or hypothetical, of those subject to it (Chapter 2).

docs.title: The modern age
docs.text: The American and French Revolutions of the late eighteenth century turned ideas of rights and popular sovereignty into constitutions. The nineteenth century produced the great ideologies: liberalism (J. S. Mill), conservatism (whose founding text is Edmund Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790), socialism and Karl Marx's critique of capitalism (Chapter 11). The twentieth century saw the struggle between democracy and the totalitarian regimes of fascism and Soviet communism, the end of the European empires and the rise of anti-colonial thought, of which Gandhi, Ambedkar, Nehru and Tagore are major Indian examples (Chapter 13), and the spread of feminist and environmental thought (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 1.6 Decline and revival
docs.text:
In the middle of the twentieth century some scholars believed that political theory was dying. Two pressures seemed to threaten it. The philosophical movement of logical positivism held that only statements that can be verified by observation, or are true by definition, are meaningful; moral and political claims, on this view, merely express feelings. At the same time the behavioural revolution in political science, especially in the United States in the 1950s and 1960s, emphasised measurable behaviour (voting, opinion, group activity) and treated normative questions as unscientific. In 1956 the historian Peter Laslett wrote that, for the moment at least, political philosophy was dead.

The obituary was premature. Isaiah Berlin answered in an essay of 1962 that political theory would survive as long as people disagreed about the ends of life, which is to say as long as there was politics. The civil rights movement, the Vietnam War and decolonisation raised urgent questions about civil disobedience, just war and self-determination. Then in 1971 John Rawls published A Theory of Justice, a large and rigorous argument about the principles of a just society. It provoked replies from libertarians such as Robert Nozick (Anarchy, State, and Utopia, 1974), from communitarians, feminists and Marxists, and from Amartya Sen, whose capability approach (Chapter 6) reshaped thinking about equality and development. Political theory today is a lively and varied field, connected to economics, law, history and philosophy.

Is political theory Western?

Textbooks have often presented political theory as a conversation among European thinkers from Plato onwards. This is too narrow. Thinkers in India, China, the Islamic world, Africa and the Americas have asked the same basic questions about rule, justice and community, and modern anti-colonial and feminist writers have shown how the European canon was shaped by the experience of the societies that produced it. The growing field of comparative political theory studies these traditions side by side. This book draws on Indian thought throughout and devotes Chapter 13 to it.

docs.title: 1.7 Why political theory matters
docs.text:
Political theory might seem remote from real politics. In fact, it is everywhere in it.

  • Every policy rests on values. A tax system embodies a view about fairness; a law on speech embodies a view about liberty and harm; an immigration policy embodies a view about membership. Political theory makes these views explicit so that they can be examined.
  • Political language is theory in disguise. Words such as "rights", "the people", "secular" and "equal opportunity" carry theories with them. Citizens who understand the theories are harder to manipulate with slogans.
  • Constitutions are applied political theory. The framers of the Constitution of India argued about sovereignty, rights, federalism, secularism and social justice. Reading those debates without political theory is like reading a mathematical proof without knowing what the symbols mean.
  • It teaches a way of thinking. Political theory trains the habits of defining terms, looking for reasons, considering objections and treating opponents fairly. These habits are valuable in any profession and indispensable in a democracy.

Summary

  • Politics arises wherever people who disagree must make binding collective decisions; definitions differ in how widely they draw its boundary, from the state alone to all relations of power.
  • Political theory studies the concepts, values and arguments of political life: what concepts mean, how political life should be organised, and how past thinkers answered these questions.
  • Descriptive claims say what is, explanatory claims say why, normative claims say what ought to be. A normative conclusion always needs at least one normative premise.
  • The main methods are conceptual analysis (including the recognition of essentially contested concepts), normative argument and thought experiments, historical and contextual interpretation, and reflective equilibrium.
  • Political thought has a long history in Greece, India, China, the Islamic world and Europe; the social contract theorists, the nineteenth-century ideologies and anti-colonial thought are milestones.
  • After a mid-century decline under positivism and behaviouralism, political theory revived, especially after Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971).

docs.title: 1.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 1

Classify each claim as descriptive, explanatory or normative. (a) "The Constitution of India came into force on 26 January 1950." (b) "Proportional representation tends to produce more political parties than first-past-the-post." (c) "Voting at sixteen would make democracy more representative and should be introduced."

Answer

(a) Descriptive. (b) Explanatory: it makes a general claim about cause and effect, to be tested by evidence. (c) Mixed: it contains an explanatory or predictive claim (it would make democracy more representative) and a normative conclusion (it should be introduced), which also depends on the value premise that a more representative democracy is better.

Exercise 2

Explain the difference between Easton's and Crick's definitions of politics. Which activities would count as political under one but not the other?

Answer

Easton defines politics as the authoritative allocation of values for a society: any binding decision about who gets what, whoever makes it and however it is made. Crick defines politics more narrowly as the peaceful reconciliation of different interests by discussion and compromise. A dictator who allocates land by decree, with no discussion, engages in politics on Easton's definition but not on Crick's; for Crick, rule by pure force is the opposite of politics.

Exercise 3

What does it mean to call a concept "essentially contested"? Give an example and explain why the dispute about it cannot be settled by a dictionary.

Answer

An essentially contested concept (W. B. Gallie, 1956) is one that is evaluative, complex and open to rival interpretations, so that disputes about its proper use are part of using it. "Democracy" is an example: some take it to mean free elections and majority rule, others insist it also requires protected rights, social equality or active participation. A dictionary can record the uses but cannot decide which is best, because each interpretation reflects a different view of what is valuable about democracy. Choosing among them requires argument.

Exercise 4

Find the hidden normative premise: "Most economists agree that free trade increases total national income. So the government should remove all tariffs."

Answer

The argument needs a premise such as "the government should adopt whatever policy maximises total national income". This premise ignores how the gains and losses are distributed: free trade may raise total income while some workers lose their jobs. Once the premise is stated, one can ask whether total income is the only thing that matters, or whether fairness to those who lose should also count.

Exercise 5

Describe the method of reflective equilibrium in your own words, and apply it to the principle "a majority may always decide any question".

Answer

Reflective equilibrium means testing general principles against considered judgements about cases, and revising either until they cohere. Test case: a majority votes to deprive a religious minority of the right to worship. Most people judge firmly that this is wrong. We can either keep the principle and accept the conclusion (few will), or revise the principle, for instance to "a majority may decide questions that do not violate the basic rights of others", which matches our judgement. This leads to the idea of constitutional limits on majority rule discussed in Chapter 8.

Exercise 6

Why did some scholars in the 1950s believe that political theory was dead, and what led to its revival?

Answer

Logical positivism treated value statements as meaningless expressions of feeling, and the behavioural revolution in political science favoured measurable behaviour over normative questions. The revival came from urgent public controversies (civil rights, civil disobedience, war, decolonisation), from defences of normative inquiry such as Isaiah Berlin's essay of 1962, and above all from Rawls's A Theory of Justice (1971) and the debates it provoked.
